description: \'e11-Acid Glycoprotein (AAGP) is an acute-phase reactant measured in serum or plasma to aid in assessing inflammatory conditions linked to infections, tissue injury, surgery, sepsis, or certain cancers. Synthesized mainly in the liver, AAGP levels rise significantly during inflammation and reflect the severity and extent of tissue damage or necrosis.

name: AAT Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Level
instructions: Allow specimen to clot completely at room temperature before centrifuging.
description: This test is used in the quantitative determination of \'e11?antitrypsin in serum and plasma.This test is used in the quantitative determination of \'e11?antitrypsin in serum and plasma. "The Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (A1AT) test measures the level of A1AT, a protein produced by the liver that protects the lungs and other tissues from damage caused by enzyme activity during inflammation. It is the body s primary inhibitor of serine proteases, particularly neutrophil elastase, and plays a key role in controlling tissue breakdown and immune regulation. This test is commonly used to screen for or confirm Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency, a hereditary condition that can lead to early-onset emphysema, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and liver disease, including cirrhosis and neonatal hepatitis. Elevated A1AT levels may also be seen in inflammatory conditions, infections, and certain cancers, as it acts as a positive acute-phase reactant. The A1AT test is valuable in diagnosing unexplained liver or lung conditions, assessing disease progression, and supporting treatment decisions. "

description: CSF angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) measures ACE activity in cerebrospinal fluid and may be used as an ancillary test in selected patients with suspected neurosarcoidosis. Its diagnostic sensitivity and specificity are limited, so the result should not be used alone to diagnose or exclude neurosarcoidosis and must be interpreted with neurological findings, MRI, CSF profile and other evidence of sarcoidosis. name: ACE Angiotensin Converting Enzyme (Serum)

description: ACE is an enzyme involved in the renin-angiotensin system, playing a key role in blood pressure regulation by converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Measurement of serum ACE levels is primarily used as a biochemical marker in the diagnosis and monitoring of sarcoidosis, a multisystem granulomatous disease. Elevated ACE levels may also be observed in other conditions such as Gaucher s disease, leprosy, and certain liver disorders, while reduced levels may be associated with ACE inhibitor therapy. The test is useful for supporting clinical suspicion and monitoring response to treatment in patients with sarcoidosis.

name: ACP (Acid Phosphatase)
description: Acid Phosphatase (ACP) is an enzyme assay primarily used to assist in the diagnosis and management of prostate cancer, particularly through measurement of prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP), a tartrate-sensitive form of ACP secreted by the prostate. Elevated PAP levels may indicate metastatic prostate cancer, and while once a key marker, PAP has largely been replaced by PSA as the gold standard. However, PAP can still be useful in monitoring disease progression or recurrence. Total ACP levels may also rise in bone diseases, bone metastases, lysosomal storage disorders, or after prostate manipulation.

name: ACTH - Adrenocorticotropic Hormone
instructions: ;; Collect in K2?EDTA and K3?EDTA plasma. Only use pre-cooled sampling vials . After drawing the blood, put the vials immediately on ice . Use a cooled centrifuge to separate the plasma. Measure samples immediately or freeze them at -20 C
description: The ACTH test measures the level of adrenocorticotropic hormone in the blood. ACTH is produced by the pituitary gland and stimulates the adrenal glands to release cortisol, a hormone essential for stress response, metabolism, and immune function. This test helps evaluate adrenal and pituitary gland function and is often used to diagnose conditions such as Cushing s syndrome, Addison s disease, and secondary adrenal insufficiency. Low ACTH levels usually suggest that the pituitary gland isn t producing enough hormone, often due to high cortisol levels from conditions like Cushing s syndrome or long-term steroid use. High ACTH levels may indicate that the adrenal glands aren t producing enough cortisol, as seen in Addison s disease, or may result from overproduction by a pituitary or ectopic tumor. ACTH results should always be considered alongside cortisol levels for accurate diagnosis. ACTH is used in the assessment of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (HPA axis or HTPA axis) disorders.

name: ADAMTS 13 Autoantibodies (Inhibitor Levels)
instructions: d- 3ml of whole blood in blue top (sodium citrate) tube. - Fill tube completely to ensure correct blood-to-anticoagulant ratio. - Gently invert tube 5-10 times to mix. If submitting to the lab will take more than 1 hour, process as follows: - Centrifuge at 1500 x g for 15 minutes at room temperature. - Transfer supernatant plasma into a plastic, screw-cap vial. - Freeze immediately at -20?C or colder - Ship frozen plasma to the lab
description: The ADAMTS13 autoantibody (inhibitor) test detects inhibitory or non-inhibitory antibodies against the ADAMTS13 enzyme. It is typically performed as a reflex test when ADAMTS13 activity is <30%, and is essential for distinguishing acquired TTP (autoimmune) from congenital TTP in confirming diagnosis of acquired TTP following low ADAMTS13 activity. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: The ADAMTS13 activity assay measures the activity of the ADAMTS13 enzyme, which is responsible for cleaving von Willebrand factor (vWF). This test is essential for diagnosing thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), a rare but potentially life-threatening condition. ADAMTS13 activty at <10% indicates severe deficiency which is highly suggestive of TTP, which requires ADAMTS13 inhibitor assay to assess for autoantibodies for confirmation. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Added PBF Peripheral Blood Film (Test Added to FBC)
description: The Peripheral Blood Film (PBF) is an additional test performed on an already completed Full Blood Count (FBC) at DKL. It involves microscopic examination of a stained peripheral blood smear to assess the morphology of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, including their size, shape, colour, and maturity, as well as the presence of any abnormal or immature forms. This add-on review also includes screening for haemoparasites and other significant morphological abnormalities that may not be detected through automated FBC analysis.

Clinically, it is used in patients with recurrent infections (especially meningococcal), or in disorders of complement regulation such as atypical HUS and C3 glomerulopathy. Low or absent AH50 suggests an alternative pathway defect, while normal results usually exclude complete\\~deficiency. It is commonly used to assess nutritional status and liver function and influences drug pharmacokinetics due to its binding capacity.

Measurement of aldosterone is essential in the evaluation of hypertension, especially when there is suspicion of primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn s syndrome) or secondary causes such as renal artery stenosis or heart failure. When interpreted alongside renin levels, aldosterone testing aids in calculating the aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR), a critical screening tool for autonomous aldosterone secretion.

description: ALP (Alkaline Phosphatase) is an enzyme found mainly in the liver and bones and is used to detect and monitor liver and bone diseases. In the liver, ALP rises with cholestasis and biliary obstruction, especially in obstructive jaundice. In the bones, it increases with osteoblastic activity, seen in conditions like Paget s disease, rickets, osteomalacia, fractures, and bone tumors. Levels may be naturally higher in growing children. Low ALP is rare but may occur in hypophosphatasia, growth hormone deficiency, or multiple myeloma. Though not liver-specific, ALP is a key marker for biliary and bone disorders.

description: dá-Galactosidase A (á-Gal A) Enzyme Activity is the primary biochemical test used in the evaluation of Fabry disease, an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the á-galactosidase A enzyme. Reduced enzyme activity results in progressive accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) and related glycosphingolipids within multiple organs, particularly the kidneys, heart, nervous system, skin, and eyes. This assay measures á-galactosidase A enzyme activity in peripheral blood and is highly sensitive for identifying affected males. In females, normal enzyme activity does not exclude Fabry disease because of variable X-chromosome inactivation; therefore, molecular confirmation by GLA gene analysis may be required where clinical suspicion remains high. Results should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, family history, and, where available, complementary tests such as Lyso-Gb3 and GLA gene mutation analysis. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: Verdana; ;; ALT (Alanine Aminotransferase) is a liver-specific enzyme released into the bloodstream when liver cells are damaged. It is a key marker for detecting and monitoring liver conditions such as acute and chronic viral hepatitis, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), alcohol-related liver disease, ischemic hepatopathy, autoimmune hepatitis, cholestasis, and suspected malignant liver infiltration. ALT is more specific for liver injury than AST, as it is found primarily in the liver and has a longer half-life, while AST is present in multiple organs. ALT elevations are rarely seen outside of liver disease and persist longer than AST in cases of hepatic injury. Quantitative determination of ALT is used in the diagnosis and follow-up of acute and chronic liver injury .

description: Quantitative determination of Ammonia is useful in evaluation of the status of existing liver disease and diagnosis and follow up of in- born errors of metabolism. High ammonia levels (hyperammonemia) can be toxic to the brain and may indicate liver dysfunction. In infants, it can result from inherited urea cycle disorders or Reye s syndrome. In adults, elevated ammonia is often seen in liver failure or hepatic encephalopathy caused by cirrhosis or severe hepatitis.

description: The Amylase (Fluid) test measures the concentration of amylase enzyme in body fluids such as peritoneal, pleural, or pericardial fluid. Elevated amylase levels in non-blood fluids may indicate conditions such as pancreatitis, pancreatic duct leakage, intestinal perforation, or inflammation involving adjacent organs. This test is particularly useful for evaluating abdominal effusions or pleural fluid in patients with suspected pancreatic disease, ruptured viscera, or salivary gland pathology. Amylase levels in fluid are interpreted alongside serum amylase, fluid protein, LDH, and cell count to support differential diagnosis. The ANCA-L substrate helps identify such interference through lymphocyte staining patterns, thereby improving result interpretation. In addition, MPO and PR3 testing is strongly advised for all ANCA-positive patients and is ideally performed on all samples submitted for ANCA testing. description: Anti-Jo-1 antibodies are autoantibodies directed against histidyl-tRNA synthetase, an intracellular enzyme involved in protein synthesis. This test is used to support the diagnosis of autoimmune thyroid dysfunction, especially in patients with abnormal thyroid function tests, goitre, or clinical symptoms suggestive of hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism. Anti-PLA2R autoantibodies are thus highly specific for pMN, of which pMN is the most frequent cause (around 20% of cases) of nephrotic syndrome in adults. The anti-PLA2R test at DKL is performed using chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA) method on Euroimmun platform.

instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Anti-GBM and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: The GBM test quantitatively detection of IgG antibodies against the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) in human serum or plasma, aiding in the diagnosis of Goodpastures syndrome (GP) and differentiating it from other vasculitides. Anti-GBM antibodies are pathogenic markers of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) and Goodpastures syndrome, which may involve both kidneys and lungs (haemorrhagic alveolitis). Early detection is crucial due to the rapid and severe progression of GP. While kidney biopsy with linear immunofluorescence remains the diagnostic gold standard, serologic tests like CLIA or ELISA are highly sensitive (94.7-100%) and specific (90.9-100%) alternatives, particularly when biopsy is not feasible. Anti-GBM antibody levels help assess prognosis and treatment response, especially with plasmapheresis. Around 10-38% of patients with anti-GBM antibodies also have ANCA positivity, commonly against MPO, warranting parallel ANCA testing. Persistent antibody negativity is essential before kidney transplantation to prevent recurrence of the disease in the graft. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Anti-Gliadin IgA (Anti-DGP IgA)
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Anti-Gliadin IgA (Anti-DGP IgA) and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: The Deamidated Gliadin IgA test quantitatively measures IgA antibodies against deamidated gliadin peptides (anti-DGP IgA) in human serum or plasma. It aids in the evaluation of celiac disease (CD) and dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhrings disease) when used alongside other clinical and laboratory data. Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder triggered by gluten in genetically predisposed individuals, primarily linked to HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 genotypes. Gliadin, a gluten protein, undergoes deamidation by tissue transglutaminase (t-TG), forming complexes that activate the immune system, leading to inflammation and potential villous atrophy in the intestines. Serological testing, especially anti-t-TG IgA combined with total IgA measurement, is the recommended first-line approach due to its high sensitivity (96-98%) and specificity (93-95%). Anti-DGP antibodies are highly specific markers for gluten intolerance, with IgA tests showing 86-95% sensitivity and 91-95% specificity, making them particularly useful in children, IgA-deficient individuals, and patients with negative or low anti-t-TG or EMA results. Monitoring anti-DGP and anti-t-TG antibody levels is essential for assessing treatment response in patients adhering to gluten-free diets. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Anti-Gliadin IgG (Anti-DGP IgG)
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Anti-Gliadin IgG (Anti-DGP IgG) and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: The Deamidated Gliadin IgG test quantitatively measures IgG antibodies against deamidated gliadin peptides (anti-DGP IgG) in serum or plasma. It is used alongside other clinical and laboratory findings to support the diagnosis of celiac disease (CD) and dermatitis herpetiformis. CD is an autoimmune condition triggered by gluten in genetically predisposed individuals, primarily linked to HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 genotypes. Gliadin, a gluten-derived protein, undergoes modification by tissue transglutaminase (t-TG), forming complexes that activate immune responses, leading to intestinal inflammation and potential villous atrophy. Serological testing, particularly anti-t-TG IgA and total IgA, remains the first-line diagnostic approach due to its high sensitivity (96-98%) and specificity (93-95%). In cases of IgA deficiency, anti-t-TG IgG and anti-DGP IgG testing is recommended. Anti-DGP IgG antibodies are highly specific for gluten intolerance and are particularly useful in pediatric patients, as they may appear before anti-t-TG antibodies. The test is also beneficial in patients with negative or low anti-t-TG/EMA levels but clinical suspicion of CD. Antibody levels, including anti-DGP IgG, decrease progressively with adherence to a gluten-free diet, although IgG titers decline more slowly compared to IgA. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: Antithrombin (also known as Antithrombin III) is a key inhibitor of several activated coagulation factors, particularly thrombin and factor Xa. It plays a vital role in maintaining the balance between clot formation and breakdown. This test measures the functional activity of antithrombin in plasma to detect deficiencies that may predispose individuals to thrombotic disorders. Antithrombin deficiency can be inherited or acquired (e.g., due to liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, or disseminated intravascular coagulation) and is an important part of a thrombophilia workup in patients with unexplained or recurrent venous thrombosis.

name: Apo A
description: Apolipoprotein A-1 (Apo A-1) is the main protein component of high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and plays a key role in reverse cholesterol transport, helping to remove excess cholesterol from tissues and reduce atherosclerosis risk. Measured in serum or plasma, Apo A-1 aids in identifying dyslipidemias and assessing cardiovascular disease risk. Higher Apo A-1 levels are associated with lower atherogenic risk, especially when paired with low Apo B (a component of LDL). The Apo B/Apo A-1 ratio is a strong predictor of coronary heart disease and stroke, and is recommended for risk assessment by major clinical guidelines.

name: Apo B
description: Apolipoprotein B (Apo B) is the primary protein component of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and is crucial for the transport of cholesterol and triglycerides in the blood. It plays a central role in the development of atherosclerosis by facilitating the accumulation of cholesterol-rich particles in arterial walls. Measured in serum or plasma, Apo B is used to assess cardiovascular risk and diagnose dyslipidemias. Elevated Apo B levels are associated with LDL-related conditions like hypercholesterolemia, type II hyperlipidemia, nephrotic syndrome, and pregnancy, while decreased levels may occur in liver disease, sepsis, or estrogen therapy.

name: APOE Genotyping ( Apolipoprotein E e2/e3/e4 )

instructions: Mix gently by inversion immediately after collection. Send whole blood; do not separate. Provide relevant clinical history and indication for testing. Follow the reference laboratory’s requirements for genetic consent, storage and transport.
description:
APOE genotyping identifies the common apolipoprotein E alleles e2, e3 and e4, reporting the allele pair and e4 carrier status as non-carrier, heterozygous or homozygous. The e4 allele is associated with increased susceptibility to late-onset Alzheimer’s disease, with greater risk generally associated with two copies than one. APOE genotype also informs assessment of the risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), including cerebral oedema and haemorrhage, in patients being considered for anti-amyloid therapy.

This is a susceptibility test and does not independently diagnose Alzheimer’s disease or predict or exclude its future development. Routine predictive testing in asymptomatic individuals is generally not recommended because of limited predictive value. Results should be interpreted alongside clinical findings, family history and relevant diagnostic investigations, with appropriate genetic counselling.

This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

Such infections (e.g. tonsillitis, skin infections) can lead to serious complications like acute rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis, or endocarditis. Elevated ASO levels, found in about 85% of acute rheumatic fever cases, indicate an immune response to streptolysin O toxin.

name: Aspergillus Antibody IgE
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Aspergillus Antibody IgE and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: Aspergillus-specific IgE measures IgE sensitisation to Aspergillus antigens and is useful in the evaluation of allergic Aspergillus disease, including allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis when combined with the appropriate clinical and radiological findings. name: Aspergillus Antibody IgG
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Aspergillus Antibody IgG and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.

name: Aspergillus Antibody IgM
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Aspergillus Antibody IgM and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.

name: Aspergillus Galactomannan
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Aspergillus Galactomannan and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.

Results should be interpreted with host risk, imaging, microbiology and antifungal exposure because false-positive and false-negative results can occur.

This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: AST Aspartate Aminotransferase
instructions: The preferred specimen is serum or plasma collected in a serum separator tube (SST) or green-top tube (sodium or lithium heparin). Allow the specimen to clot at room temperature, separate from cells within 2 hours, and transfer 2 mL (minimum 1 mL) to a transport tube. Samples should be stored and transported refrigerated (2-8\'b0C); freeze if analysis is delayed. Allow serum tube to clot completely at room temperature. Separate serum or plasma from cells within 2 hours of collection.
description: ;; AST (Aspartate Aminotransferase) is an enzyme found in the liver, heart, skeletal muscle, kidneys, brain, and red blood cells. It plays a role in amino acid metabolism and exists in cytoplasmic and mitochondrial forms, the latter increasing with severe liver cell damage. AST is used to diagnose and monitor liver diseases such as viral hepatitis, NAFLD, alcohol-related liver disease, ischemic hepatopathy, autoimmune hepatitis, cholestasis, and malignant infiltration. Though less liver-specific than ALT, AST may be more sensitive in alcohol-related and autoimmune liver conditions. Elevated AST may also indicate cardiac or muscle injury, Quantitative determination of AST is used in the diagnosis and monitoring of acute and chronic liver injury.

name: AST for Gram-Negative Bacterial Isolate – Submitted Culture Isolate (Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing)
synonyms: Automated MIC & Antibiotic Susceptibility Testing;AST by VITEK® 2/Phoenix (Submitted Isolate);
instructions: Sample Type: Pure Gram-negative bacterial isolate on culture plate (non-mixed culture) or pure subculture submitted on appropriate microbiological agar. Turnaround Time (TAT): 24-48 hours from receipt of a suitable pure isolate (may be extended if subculture or purity confirmation is required).
description: This test performs automated antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) on a previously isolated Gram-negative bacterial organism using either the bioM\'e9rieux VITEK\'ae 2 or BD Phoenix\'99 automated microbiology system, depending on laboratory workflow and organism requirements. A standardized bacterial suspension prepared from a pure culture is inoculated into the appropriate AST panel containing multiple antimicrobial agents at defined concentrations. The system determines minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) and categorizes results as Susceptible (S), Susceptible, Increased Exposure (I), or Resistant (R) according to current CLSI or EUCAST interpretive criteria, as configured by the laboratory. Testing is performed only on pure Gram-negative bacterial isolates. Mixed cultures or unsuitable isolates require re-isolation and purification before AST can proceed. The report includes MIC values (where applicable), interpretive susceptibility categories, and may identify clinically significant resistance phenotypes, including important multidrug resistance mechanisms where supported by the testing platform, to assist clinicians in selecting appropriate antimicrobial therapy.

name: Atypical Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome (aHUS) by MLPA
synonyms: Atypical HUS by MLPA, aHUS Copy-Number Analysis, Complement Gene Deletion/Duplication Analysis
instructions: Collect 4 mL of whole blood and mix gently by inversion. Label the tube with two patient identifiers. Include the clinical indication and attach any prior genetic report if requesting confirmation of an NGS finding.
description:
This assay uses Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) to detect deletions and duplications in selected complement gene regions associated with atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (aHUS). It can help investigate suspected complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy and confirm copy-number changes identified by sequencing, where the relevant regions are covered by the assay.

For the current referral, specify confirmation of the suspected homozygous deletion involving CFHR3 and CFHR1. Confirm with the reference laboratory that both genes are covered and that the assay distinguishes a one-copy deletion from a two-copy deletion.

name: Autoimmune Encephalitis Antibodies Panel (CSF)
synonyms: Autoimmune Encephalitis Antibodies – CSF; Neuronal Surface Antibody Panel – CSF; Autoimmune Encephalopathy Panel – CSF
instructions: Submit minimum 1 mL CSF in a sterile, leak-proof plain container. Avoid gross blood contamination where possible. Store and transport refrigerated unless otherwise directed by the referral laboratory. Where clinically appropriate, paired serum and CSF testing may improve diagnostic interpretation.
description: A CSF antibody panel for investigation of suspected autoimmune encephalitis, particularly in patients presenting with subacute encephalopathy, seizures, psychiatric or behavioural disturbance, movement disorders, memory impairment, dysautonomia or other compatible neurological syndromes. The panel includes antibodies to NMDA receptor (NR1), AMPA receptor GluR1, AMPA receptor GluR2, GABA-B receptor, LGI1 and CASPR2. Results should be interpreted with the clinical phenotype, MRI, EEG, CSF findings and other investigations. A negative panel does not exclude autoimmune encephalitis caused by other recognised or currently unidentified neuronal antibodies. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

synonyms: Autoimmune Encephalitis Antibodies – Serum; Neuronal Surface Antibody Panel – Serum; Autoimmune Encephalopathy Panel – Serum
instructions: Submit minimum 3 mL serum. Collect blood into a plain or serum separator tube, allow to clot and separate serum from cells promptly. Avoid gross haemolysis. Paired CSF testing should be considered where clinically indicated
description: A serum autoantibody panel for evaluation of patients with suspected autoimmune encephalitis or neuronal surface antibody-associated neurological disease. Clinical presentations may include rapidly evolving cognitive or behavioural changes, seizures, movement disorders, psychiatric manifestations, sleep disturbance and autonomic dysfunction. The panel detects antibodies to NMDA receptor (NR1), AMPA receptor GluR1, AMPA receptor GluR2, GABA-B receptor, LGI1 and CASPR2. Results require clinical correlation. Depending on the suspected antibody and clinical syndrome, CSF testing may provide additional diagnostic sensitivity or specificity; a negative serum result does not exclude autoimmune encephalitis. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: ;; The Autoimmune Gastrointestinal Diseases IgA provides qualitative in vitro determination of human antibodies of the immunoglobulin class IgA against the three antigens tissue transglutaminase (tTG), gliadin-analogue fusion peptide (GAF-3X) and Mannan from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (ASCA) in serum or plasma to support the diagnosis of gluten-sensitive enteropathy, dermatitis herpetiformis and Crohn\'b4s disease. ASCA are a specific serological marker of Crohn's disease (CD). The use of a combination of P-ANCAs and ASCAs to differentiate between patients with CD and ulcerative colitis (UC) as patients with CD tend to be positive for ASCA and negative for p-ANCA, whereas those with UC are negative for ASCA and positive for p-ANCA.
testDetails: ASCA IgA, GAF-3X IgA, Tissue Transglutaminase IgA

name: Autoimmune Liver Hepatitis Profile x5 Markers
description: The Liver Profile 2 (EUROLINE immunoblot) is a targeted autoantibody panel designed to aid in the diagnosis of autoimmune liver diseases, particularly Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC) and Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH). It detects five key antibodies: AMA-M2 and M2-3E, which are highly specific for PBC and present in the vast majority of cases; LKM-1 and LC-1, which are associated with AIH type 2, most commonly seen in children and young adults; and SLA/LP, a highly specific marker for AIH type 1 that is often linked to a more aggressive disease course or tendency to relapse. A positive AMA strongly supports a diagnosis of PBC in the right clinical setting, while the presence of LKM-1, LC-1, or SLA/LP supports the diagnosis of AIH and helps in distinguishing between its subtypes. Negative results, however, do not completely rule out autoimmune liver disease, as some patients may have seronegative AIH. The test is best interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, liver function tests, immunoglobulin levels, imaging, and histology. In cases of diagnostic uncertainty when the 5 Ag test is negative and overlap syndromes are suspected, a broader panel including other additional markers such as Sp100, gp210, and Ro-52 may be considered for more comprehensive coverage. ASMA is a key diagnostic marker for Type 1 AIH, present in most cases, but its specificity is limited since it can occur in other conditions. It is ordered separately as a standalone marker tather than being part of the panel.
testDetails: Antimitochondrial antIbody (AMA-M2), LC-1 antibody, LKM-1 antibody, M2-3 antibody, SLA/LP antibodies

name: Autoimmune Myositis Panel (Basic) x7 Markers
description: The Autoimmune Myositis Panel (Basic) is a targeted immunoblot assay designed to detect seven clinically significant myositis-specific and myositis-associated autoantibodies associated with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIMs) and overlap connective tissue diseases. The panel includes antibodies against Jo-1, PL-7, PL-12, Mi-2\'e2, Ku, PM-Scl (PM), and Ro52, providing a focused serological assessment for patients with suspected polymyositis, dermatomyositis, anti-synthetase syndrome, overlap myositis, and connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease. Detection of these autoantibodies can support diagnosis, aid disease subclassification, and identify important clinical associations such as interstitial lung disease, characteristic cutaneous manifestations, and overlap syndromes involving systemic sclerosis and other autoimmune rheumatic diseases. Results should be interpreted alongside clinical findings, serum muscle enzyme levels, imaging studies, electromyography, and muscle biopsy findings where indicated, as autoantibody results alone are not diagnostic of inflammatory myopathy.

It is used in the evaluation of suspected idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIMs), including dermatomyositis, polymyositis, anti-synthetase syndrome, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis, and overlap connective tissue disease-associated myositis. The panel includes antibodies against Mi-2a, Mi-2ß, TIF1?, MDA5, NXP2, SAE1, Jo-1, SRP, PL-7, PL-12, EJ, OJ, Ku, PM-Scl75, PM-Scl100, and Ro52. Detection of specific autoantibodies can assist in disease classification, prognostication, and identification of important clinical associations such as interstitial lung disease, malignancy risk, cutaneous manifestations, and overlap autoimmune syndromes. Results should be interpreted in conjunction with the patients clinical presentation, muscle enzyme levels, imaging studies, electromyography, and muscle biopsy findings where applicable, as the presence or absence of autoantibodies alone does not establish or exclude a diagnosis of inflammatory myopathy. name: BCR-ABL by FISH
synonyms: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) FISH; Philadelphia chromosome (Ph)
description: BCR-ABL by FISH is a fluorescence in situ hybridization assay using dual-color, dual-fusion probes targeting the BCR (22q11.2) and ABL1 (9q34) loci to detect the t(9;22)(q34;q11.2) (Philadelphia chromosome). It is used for the diagnosis and classification of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph+ ALL), and for identifying variant or complex rearrangements, using peripheral blood or bone marrow without the need for metaphase cells. Results are reported as positive or negative with the percentage of nuclei showing fusion signals; a positive result confirms a BCR-ABL1 rearrangement in the appropriate clinical context, while a negative result does not exclude low-level disease and should be correlated with morphology, immunophenotyping, cytogenetics, and RT-PCR, which is also required for transcript typing and MRD monitoring.

name: BCR-ABL Quantitative PCR
instructions: Samples should be collected between Monday afternoon and Tuesday morning for delivery to DKL at the lab bench before Tuesday 10am, or collected between Thursday afternoon and Friday morning for delivery to the DKL lab bench before Friday 10am. Ship on ice Avoid Haemolysis (Wrap with a paper towel should not come into direct contact with Ice pack)
description: Quantitative real-time RT-PCR for measurement of BCR:ABL1 transcript burden after the fusion has been identified. Used for baseline quantification and serial monitoring of molecular response, including persistent measurable disease, rising transcript levels, loss of response and molecular relapse. For p210 CML, results are reported on the International Scale (IS) where applicable, allowing standardized assessment of MMR and deeper molecular response. Non-p210 transcripts are quantified according to the assay method in use and are not interchangeable with p210 %IS values. EDTA peripheral blood or bone marrow is accepted. Interpret against known transcript type, prior results and clinical context. If BCR:ABL1 status or transcript type is unknown, request qualitative PCR first.

name: BCR-ABL Tyrosine Kinase Domain (TKD) Mutation Analysis by NGS
synonyms: BCR-ABL Mutation Testing for TKI Resistance in CML;BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase domain mutation testing
description: BCR-ABL1 kinase domain (TKD) mutation analysis by next-generation sequencing (NGS) is performed in patients with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) or Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph+ ALL) who show loss of molecular response, suboptimal response, or disease progression on tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy. TKD mutations are a major mechanism of TKI resistance, and NGS enables sensitive detection (typically down to ~1-3% variant allele frequency) of both dominant and low-level mutations, including multiple coexisting ( compound ) mutations. Identifying the specific mutation helps guide selection of the most appropriate TKI, as certain variants confer resistance to specific agents (e.g., T315I is resistant to imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib, and bosutinib, but sensitive to ponatinib). The report should be interpreted in conjunction with BCR-ABL1 transcript monitoring, cytogenetic findings, and clinical features. Higher VAF mutations are generally more clinically relevant, but emerging low-level mutations may still predict future resistance. Absence of detectable mutations does not rule out TKI resistance from other mechanisms. When mutations are found, results should prompt multidisciplinary review to optimize therapy per current guidelines, and repeat testing is advised if further loss of response occurs.

name: BCR-ABL1 Qualitative PCR (Major-p210, Minor-p190, Micro-p230)
description: Qualitative RT-PCR for detection and characterization of BCR:ABL1 fusion transcripts in Philadelphia chromosome-positive haematological malignancies. Covers the major clinically relevant transcript groups: p210, most often associated with CML; p190, commonly associated with Ph+ ALL; and rare p230, seen in selected BCR:ABL1-positive myeloid neoplasms. Indicated at initial diagnosis, or whenever BCR:ABL1 status or transcript type has not been established. Results are reported as Detected / Not Detected, with transcript group where identified. EDTA peripheral blood or bone marrow is accepted. Once BCR:ABL1-positive disease and transcript type are known, quantitative PCR is the appropriate test for longitudinal molecular monitoring.

name: Blood Culture (Paediatric)
instructions: Collection Instructions The optimal sample for blood culture is one of adequate amount and collected in a manner that prevents contamination of the sample by skin flora. Samples should be collected from peripheral vessels. 1)Apply a tourniquet and identify the blood vessel. 2)Wash the skin with soap and water if it is visibly unclean and wipe dry. 3)Clean the area vigorously with 70% alcohol starting at the intended site of puncture and going outward in concentric circles. 4)Apply 10% povidone iodine over the area of intended puncture. 5)Allow the skin to dry. 6)Remove the caps off blood culture bottles and wipe the top of the vials with an alcohol swab. description: Blood culture involves the aseptic collection of blood into a specialized aerobic culture bottle designed to support the growth of aerobic and facultative anaerobic microorganisms. The specimen is incubated in a continuous-monitoring automated blood culture system, such as the BACTEC blood culture system or BacT/ALERT system, which detects microbial growth based on metabolic activity. When growth is detected, a Gram stain is performed promptly, followed by organism identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) as clinically indicated. The minimum standard incubation period is 5 days (120 hours), which is sufficient to detect the vast majority of clinically significant bloodstream pathogens, most of which flag positive within the first 24-72 hours. Positive results are reported immediately upon detection of growth to facilitate timely targeted therapy. If no growth is detected, the culture is finalized and reported as No growth after 5 days of incubation. Extended incubation (up to 7-14 days) may be undertaken in specific clinical scenarios - such as suspected infections with fastidious organisms (e.g., HACEK group, Brucella) or certain fungal pathogens as per the laboratory protocol.

name: BRAF Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
description: BRAF V600E Immunohistochemistry (IHC) detects expression of the mutant BRAF V600E protein in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue using a mutation-specific antibody. Positive cytoplasmic staining in tumor cells supports the presence of a BRAF V600E mutation, a clinically significant alteration encountered in several neoplasms including melanoma, colorectal carcinoma, papillary thyroid carcinoma, hairy cell leukemia, and selected central nervous system and histiocytic tumors. Identification of BRAF V600E may assist in diagnosis, prognostic stratification, and selection of targeted therapy where appropriate. A negative result suggests absence of detectable BRAF V600E mutant protein, but does not exclude other BRAF mutations or alternative molecular alterations. Although BRAF V600E IHC shows high concordance with molecular testing, confirmatory molecular analysis may be recommended in selected cases, particularly where therapeutic decisions depend on mutation status.

description: This test detects clinically significant BRAF gene mutations in DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissue using a validated PCR-based method. The assay is designed primarily to identify activating mutations in codon 600 (including V600E and related variants), which occur in a range of malignancies such as melanoma, colorectal carcinoma, papillary thyroid carcinoma, and selected brain and hematologic tumors. Detection of a BRAF mutation may support diagnosis and has important therapeutic implications, including eligibility for targeted BRAF inhibitor therapy in appropriate clinical settings. A negative result indicates that no detectable BRAF mutation within the regions covered by the assay was identified but does not exclude mutations outside the tested regions or the presence of other oncogenic drivers. Results should be interpreted in conjunction with histopathological and clinical findings, and additional molecular testing may be recommended where clinically indicated. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: BRCA 1 and BRCA 2 Germline
description: Symbol; The BRCA germline mutation test is a DNA analysis hHereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome is a type of familial cancer, and is linked to mutations in two genes called BRCA1 and BRCA2 . BRCA1 and BRCA2 are known as tumour suppressor genes - they prevent cells from growing too rapidly or in an uncontrolled way. Thousands of mutations have been found in these genes, but only some have been linked to an increased risk of cancer. Women with a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation are at increased risk of cancer of the fallopian tubes, pancreas, and peritoneum (the membrane that lines the abdomen and the organs in the abdomen). Men with a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation are at increased risk of cancer of the breast, prostate and pancreas. BRCA gene mutation testing is recommended if you have any of the following: -360 1. A personal or family history of breast and/or ovarian cancer. -360 2. If you were younger than 50 years of age when breast cancer was diagnosed. 3. If you have had breast cancer diagnosed more than once (in the same breast or in both breasts). 4. If you are a man and diagnosed with breast cancer at any age. 5. If you have a close relative with a known BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation.

name: Calcium (24 Hrs Urine)
instructions: Preferred start collection time is morning Collect in 24 hour urine container with 20?30 mL of 6 mol/L HCl to prevent calcium salt precipitation. Addition of HCl after collection may not completely dissolve precipitated calcium and is therefore discouraged. Empty the bladder first thing in the morning or at the start time and discard this urine. Note the time as this is the start time of the 24 hours. For example 6:00 am Collect every drop of urine voided over the next 24 hours (i.e. upto the next morning e.g. 6:am on a Tuesday to 6:00 am Wednesday). Should one need to defecate and urinate at the same time, this urine should also be collected. Try as much as possible not to contaminate the urine with faeces. Keep the urine cold either on ice or refigerated. Stop time should be within 20 minutes of the start time the day before. E.g. if start time was 6:00 am Tuesday, stop time is between 5:50 am and 6:10 am during which time any urine passed must be collected. FOR SUBMITTING LABORATORIES /HOSPITALS If submitting an aliquot of the 24 hour urine, note the volume of 24 hour urine submited. Mix the sample well to a homogenous mixture and aliquote into a clean container. Submit the aliquot with clear documentation of the duration of collection and the volume of the 24 hour urine. Sample (Primary sample and alliquot) should be kept at 2?8 \'b0C
description: Determination of 24 hour urine calcium is useful in the evaluation of nephrolithiasis, renal disease, hyperparathyroidism, hyper/hypocalcaemia and hypercalciuria.

Elevated levels indicate the presence of neutrophil-driven inflammation in the gastrointestinal tract.

instructions: Collect 3?5 mL peripheral blood in an EDTA tube; a minimum of 1 mL may be acceptable. Alternatively, submit 1?2 mL bone marrow aspirate in EDTA. name: C-ANCA, PR3-II (Proteinase 3)
instructions: Performed on serum or plasma(EDTA or Sodium Citrate)
description: The c-ANCA (cytoplasmic Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody) test measures IgG antibodies which target proteinase 3 in the cytoplasm of neytrophils.It is used in diagnosing and monitoring disease progression in patient with autoimmune vasculitides especially Wegener's granulomatosis.This test was perfomed using Euroimmun chemoliminescence(ChLIA) assay on the IDS-iSYS platform. The PR3 II test quantitatively detect IgG antibodies against proteinase 3 (PR3) in human serum or plasma, aiding in the evaluation of ANCA-associated vasculitides (AAVs), particularly Wegener s granulomatosis (WG). Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) are key markers for necrotizing vasculitides affecting small- and medium-sized blood vessels, including WG, microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), pauci-immune necrotizing glomerulonephritis (PING), and Churg-Strauss syndrome (CSS). PR3, a serine protease in granulocytes and monocytes, contributes to antimicrobial activity but can cause tissue damage when uncontrolled. c-ANCA patterns are typically associated with PR3 antibodies, while p-ANCA patterns often involve MPO antibodies. ANCA titres often correlate with disease activity, making quantitative PR3 testing valuable for monitoring patients. While PR3-ANCA is strongly associated with WG, it cannot differentiate between all AAV subtypes. A positive result must be interpreted alongside clinical findings due to possible ANCA positivity in other conditions, such as infections or bacterial endocarditis, and a negative result does not entirely rule out AAV in symptomatic patients.

description: This test qualitatively detects the presence of Candida albicans DNA using real-time Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) methodology. Candida albicans is the commonest cause of Vulvovaginal Candidiasis and may also be associated with mucocutaneous, genitourinary, and invasive fungal infections depending on the clinical context. The assay offers rapid and highly sensitive molecular detection and may be particularly useful in patients with recurrent or persistent symptoms, equivocal microscopy/culture findings, prior antifungal exposure, or suspected low organism burden. Detection of Candida DNA should always be interpreted alongside the patients clinical presentation, as asymptomatic colonization may occur, especially in genital specimens. Negative results do not entirely exclude fungal infection where organism burden is below the assay detection threshold or sampling is suboptimal. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: A test that detects the amount of IgA autoantibodies against cardiolipin.Cardiolipin is a fat molecule found on cell membranes and platelets.Anti Cardiolipin IgA is ordered as part of the diagnostic work up for evaluation of patients with Antiphospholipid Syndrome(APS) especially in patients with symptoms of APS, but IgG and IgM tests are negative and other autoimmune disorders eg SLE.The Anti Cardiolipin IgA test at DKL is performed using chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA) method on ids-isys platform. name: Cardiolipin IgG (Anti-Cardiolipin Antiphospholipid Antibody)
instructions: Use human serum or plasma(EDTA,heparin)
description: A test that detects the amount of IgG autoantibodies against cardiolipin.Cardiolipin is a fat molecule found on cell membranes and platelets.Anti Cardiolipin IgG is ordered as part of the diagnostic work up for evaluation of patients with Antiphospholipid Syndrome(APS) and other autoimmune disorders.The Anti Cardiolipin IgG test at DKL is performed using chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA) method on ids-isys platform . Anti-cardiolipin antibodies are autoantibodies directed against phospholipids, commonly associated with antiphospholipid syndrome (APS)-an autoimmune condition that increases the risk of thrombosis, pregnancy complications, and recurrent miscarriages. This test specifically detects the IgG isotype, which is considered clinically significant and more strongly associated with thrombotic events than IgM or IgA. It is often requested as part of a broader antiphospholipid antibody panel in the investigation of unexplained blood clots, recurrent pregnancy loss, prolonged aPTT, or systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

name: Cardiolipin IgM (Anti-Cardiolipin Antiphospholipid Antibody)
description: A test that detects the amount of IgM autoantibodies against cardiolipin.Cardiolipin is a fat molecule found on cell membranes and platelets.Anti Cardiolipin IgM is ordered as part of the diagnostic work up for evaluation of patients with Antiphospholipid Syndrome(APS) and other autoimmune disorders eg SLE.The Anti Cardiolipin IgM test at DKL is performed using chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA) method on ids-isys platform. Anti-cardiolipin antibodies of the IgM isotype are part of the antiphospholipid antibody group and are commonly assessed in the diagnosis of antiphospholipid syndrome (APS). While IgG isotypes are more strongly associated with clinical events, elevated IgM levels may also be seen in thrombotic conditions, recurrent pregnancy loss, or autoimmune disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The test is useful in evaluating patients with unexplained blood clots, prolonged aPTT, or recurrent fetal loss, and is typically ordered alongside IgG and IgA to provide a comprehensive antiphospholipid antibody profile.

description: The Expanded Carrier Screening Panel (~2000 Genes) NGS with MLPA/CNV Analysis is a comprehensive pan-ethnic expanded carrier screening assay designed to detect carrier status for a wide range of inherited genetic disorders. It utilizes high-depth next-generation sequencing (NGS) to identify single nucleotide variants and small insertions/deletions across approximately 2000 clinically relevant genes, with integrated copy number variation (CNV) analysis (via MLPA or validated NGS-based methods) for genes where deletions or duplications are a key disease mechanism. The panel covers autosomal recessive, X-linked, and selected dominant conditions relevant to reproductive risk assessment. Results are reported as carrier detected, no clinically significant variant detected (residual risk remains), or, where appropriate, variants of uncertain significance. This test is indicated for preconception and prenatal screening, with recommendation for partner testing and genetic counseling if a pathogenic variant is identified. Limitations include inability to detect all variant types (e.g., deep intronic or complex rearrangements), and a negative result does not eliminate carrier risk. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Catecholamines (Plasma)
instructions: Patient Preparation Patient should ideally fast for 8 to 12 hours prior to sample collection (water allowed). Avoid caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, strenuous exercise, and emotional stress for at least 24 hours before sampling, as these may falsely elevate catecholamine levels. If clinically feasible and under physician guidance, medications that may interfere with catecholamine levels (e.g. sympathomimetics, decongestants, tricyclic antidepressants, levodopa, amphetamines, beta blockers) should be reviewed prior to testing. Patient should rest quietly in a supine position for at least 20-30 minutes before blood collection. Sample Requirements Specimen: EDTA plasma Collection tube should be placed immediately on ice after collection. Sample must be transported rapidly under cold conditions and plasma separated promptly. Frozen plasma preferred for referral transport.
description: Plasma Catecholamines is a specialized biochemical assay that quantitatively measures circulating catecholamines including epinephrine (adrenaline), norepinephrine (noradrenaline), and dopamine in plasma. These hormones are produced by the adrenal medulla and sympathetic nervous system and play a central role in cardiovascular and neuroendocrine regulation. The test is primarily used in the evaluation of suspected pheochromocytoma, paraganglioma, neuroblastoma, autonomic dysfunction, and catecholamine-secreting tumors. Because catecholamine levels are highly sensitive to physiological stress, posture, medications, exercise, and dietary factors, strict patient preparation and specimen handling requirements are critical to minimize false elevations and ensure accurate interpretation. name: Chloride (24 Hrs Urine)
instructions: Instructions for collection: Preferred start collection time is morning. Collect 24?hour urine without additives. Empty the bladder first thing in the morning or at the start time and discard this urine. Note the time as this is the start time of the 24 hours. For example 6:00 am Collect every drop of urine voided over the next 24 hours (e.g. 6:am on a Tuesday to 6:00 am Wednesday). Should one need to defecate and urinate at the same time, this urine should also be collected. Try as much as possible not to contaminate the urine with faeces. Keep the urine cold either on ice or refigerated. Stop time should be within 20 minutes of the start time the day before. E.g. if start time was 6:00 am Tuesday, stop time is between 5:50 am and 6:10 am during which time any urine passed must be collected. FOR SUBMITTING LABORATORIES /HOSPITALS If submitting an aliquot of the 24 hour urine, note the volume of 24 hour urine submited. Mix the sample well to a homogenous mixture and aliquote into a clean container. Submit the aliquot with clear documentation of the duration of collection and the volume of the 24 hour urine. Sample (Primary sample and alliquot) should be kept at 2?8 \'b0C

synonyms: Low resolution microarray CMA Chromosomal Microarray
instructions: For chromosomal microarray (CMA) testing on products of conception (POC), submit fresh fetal tissue-preferably chorionic villi or fetal parts-in sterile saline or transport media, avoiding maternal decidua and blood clots. Ensure the sample is properly labeled and accompanied by a completed requisition form and relevant clinical history, including gestational age and any notable findings. Keep the specimen refrigerated (not frozen) and deliver to the lab within 24-48 hours. If fresh tissue is unavailable, FFPE blocks may be submitted, though DNA quality may be limited. Maternal cell contamination testing may be performed to confirm fetal origin.
description: Chromosomal microarray (CMA) testing for products of conception (POC) is a high-resolution genetic test used to detect chromosomal abnormalities, including aneuploidies and submicroscopic copy number variants, that may have contributed to pregnancy loss. It offers greater diagnostic yield compared to conventional karyotyping and does not require viable cells, making it suitable for both fresh and formalin-fixed tissue. CMA helps provide insight into the genetic causes of miscarriage, guides counseling for recurrence risk, and informs future pregnancy management. Both 315K and 750K array platforms are effective for identifying aneuploidies and large copy number variants (CNVs). The 750K array provides greater diagnostic yield, especially in complex cases such as recurrent pregnancy loss or when detailed genomic analysis is needed wwith large CNVs. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Chromosomal Microarray 315K (Cytogenetics) Blood

instructions: 2-5 mL of EDTA whole blood
description: Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) 315K is a genomic test that detects larger copy number variations (CNVs), including submicroscopic deletions and duplications, across the genome. When performed on peripheral blood, CMA is commonly used in the evaluation of patients with developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorders, multiple congenital anomalies, and unexplained dysmorphic features. It may also be employed in the context of hematological malignancies to detect somatic chromosomal imbalances. Peripheral blood is the standard source for germline CMA testing. The test provides superior resolution compared to conventional karyotyping and can uncover clinically significant variants that are not visible by traditional cytogenetics. However, CMA does not detect balanced translocations, low-level mosaicism, or point mutations. Results must be interpreted in the context of clinical findings, family history, and other genetic studies. Incidental findings or variants of uncertain significance (VUS) may be identified, and appropriate pre- and post-test genetic counseling is recommended. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

Incidental findings or variants of uncertain significance (VUS) may be identified, and appropriate pre- and post-test genetic counseling is recommended. name: Chromosomal Microarray 750 K (Cytogenetics) POC
synonyms: POC - MICROARRAY; Products of Conception Microarray, peripheral blood micro-array High resolution Micro-array CMA POC Chromosomal Microarray
instructions: For chromosomal microarray (CMA) testing on products of conception (POC), submit fresh fetal tissue-preferably chorionic villi or fetal parts-in sterile saline or transport media, avoiding maternal decidua and blood clots. Ensure the sample is properly labeled and accompanied by a completed requisition form and relevant clinical history, including gestational age and any notable findings. Keep the specimen refrigerated (not frozen) and deliver to the lab within 24-48 hours. If fresh tissue is unavailable, FFPE blocks may be submitted, though DNA quality may be limited. Maternal cell contamination testing may be performed to confirm fetal origin.
description: Chromosomal microarray (CMA) testing for products of conception (POC) is a high-resolution genetic test used to detect chromosomal abnormalities, including aneuploidies and submicroscopic copy number variants, that may have contributed to pregnancy loss. It offers greater diagnostic yield compared to conventional karyotyping and does not require viable cells, making it suitable for both fresh and formalin-fixed tissue. CMA helps provide insight into the genetic causes of miscarriage, guides counseling for recurrence risk, and informs future pregnancy management. The 750K chromosomal microarray offers higher resolution and broader genomic coverage compared to the 315K array, allowing for more sensitive detection of smaller copy number variants (CNVs) and subtle chromosomal abnormalities. While both platforms are effective for identifying aneuploidies and large CNVs, the 750K array provides greater diagnostic yield, especially in complex cases such as recurrent pregnancy loss or when detailed genomic analysis is needed. Previous research indicates that more than 60% of first trimester miscarriages occurred due to chromosomal anomalies including aneuploidies, triploidy, uniparental disomy (UPD), etc. Traditional cytogenetic analysis of these samples is challenging due to high degrees of maternal cell contamination and culture failure, results in long turn-around time. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: Chromosome-breakage testing for Fanconi anaemia assesses cellular hypersensitivity to DNA cross-linking agents by demonstrating excessive chromosome breaks and radial formations after induced stress. description: The CLL FISH Panel is a molecular cytogenetic test used to detect common chromosomal abnormalities associated with Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia. The test utilizes Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH) to identify specific genetic alterations in interphase cells without the need for cell culture. This panel typically evaluates key abnormalities including deletions of 13q, 11q, and 17p, as well as trisomy 12. These genetic findings play an important role in diagnosis, prognosis, and risk stratification, and may guide treatment decisions. FISH analysis is highly sensitive and can detect abnormalities even when conventional cytogenetics is normal or when dividing cells are limited. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: Autoimmune Nodopathy / Paranodal Antibody Panel is a serum autoantibody panel used in the evaluation of suspected autoimmune nodopathies (paranodopathies), a distinct group of immune-mediated neuropies within the CIDP spectrum associated with antibodies directed against nodal and paranodal proteins of peripheral nerves. The panel typically includes Neurofascin-155 (NF155), Neurofascin-186 (NF186), Contactin-1 (CNTN1), and CASPR1 antibodies, usually detected using cell-based assay (CBA) methodologies. These antibodies are associated with atypical or treatment-refractory demyelinating neuropathies presenting with features such as progressive weakness, sensory ataxia, tremor, distal neuropathy, cranial nerve involvement, or acute/subacute inflammatory neuropathy. Identification of specific nodal/paranodal antibodies may help refine diagnosis, prognostication, and therapeutic selection, particularly in patients with poor response to standard IVIg therapy and possible responsiveness to B-cell-directed therapies such as rituximab. Preferred specimen is serum. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: CK-MB
instructions: CK?MB is temperature-sensitive. To prevent inaccurate results, avoid keeping the sample at or above 32?\'b0C.
description: CK-MB is the muscle-brain isoenzyme of creatine kinase and serves as a key biomarker for diagnosing acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and other cardiac injuries such as myocarditis and heart failure. It becomes detectable in serum within 3-8 hours after symptom onset and remains elevated depending on disease progression. Though cardiac troponins are now the preferred and more specific markers for myocardial injury, CK-MB remains a valuable alternative when troponin assays are unavailable, particularly when measured using mass assays. CK-MB may also rise in non-cardiac conditions like rhabdomyolysis and stroke, so it is often interpreted alongside other markers such as total CK, myoglobin, and troponin.

Staining is interpreted based on the presence, intensity (weak/moderate/strong), and percentage of tumor cells demonstrating membranous positivity, using clinically validated scoring thresholds. name: CMV (Cytomegalovirus) RT-PCR
description: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA PCR is a real-time polymerase chain reaction assay used for the qualitative and/or quantitative detection of CMV viral DNA in clinical specimens, commonly EDTA plasma, whole blood, cerebrospinal fluid, or urine depending on clinical indication. The test targets conserved regions of the CMV genome and provides a sensitive and specific method for detecting active viral replication. Quantitative results, typically reported in IU/mL or copies/mL depending on assay calibration, allow assessment of viral load and are useful for monitoring disease progression and response to antiviral therapy. CMV PCR is primarily indicated for the diagnosis and monitoring of CMV infection in immunocompromised patients, including transplant recipients and individuals with HIV, as well as for evaluation of suspected congenital CMV infection in neonates. The assay plays a critical role in guiding initiation and adjustment of antiviral treatment. Proper specimen collection in EDTA tubes and timely transport under appropriate conditions are essential to ensure sample integrity and reliable amplification results.

The presence of CMV-specific IgG antibodies indicates past exposure to the virus and the development of immune memory. CMV is a common herpesvirus that, while usually harmless in healthy individuals, can cause serious complications in pregnant women and immunocompromised patients.

name: CMV IgM (Cytomegalovirus IgM)
instructions: Serum collected using standard sampling tubes or tubes containing separating gel. (SST)
description: "The Cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgM Antibody Test is a qualitative test used to detect IgM antibodies against CMV in human serum or plasma. The presence of CMV-specific IgM antibodies typically indicates a recent or current infection, as IgM is the first antibody produced by the immune system in response to CMV exposure.This test is commonly used in pregnant women, organ transplant candidates or recipients, and patients with unexplained mononucleosis-like symptoms, where identifying active or primary CMV infection is clinically important. A positive CMV IgM result may suggest a primary CMV infection, reactivation of latent infection, or, in some cases, false positives due to cross-reactivity with other viruses. Because CMV IgM can persist for several months and does not always indicate an acute infection on its own, results should be interpreted in combination with CMV IgG and clinical findings for accurate diagnosis."

name: Coxiella burnetii IgG Antibody Test
synonyms: Q Fever Serology (IgG); Coxiella burnetii IgG Antibodies; Coxiella IgG Antibody Assay; Phase I & Phase II Coxiella burnetii IgG Antibodies
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Coxiella Burnetii IgG Antibody Test and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: The Coxiella burnetii IgG Antibody Test is a serological assay used to detect IgG antibodies directed against Coxiella burnetii, the causative agent of Q fever. The test assists in the evaluation of prior exposure, recent infection, chronic Q fever, or immune response following infection. Depending on the assay methodology and clinical context, antibodies against both Phase I and Phase II antigens may be assessed to help differentiate acute from chronic infection patterns. Q fever is a zoonotic infection commonly associated with exposure to livestock such as cattle, sheep, and goats, particularly through inhalation of contaminated aerosols, animal birth products, dust, or unpasteurized dairy products. Clinical manifestations may range from asymptomatic infection to acute febrile illness, atypical pneumonia, hepatitis, or chronic infections including endocarditis and vascular infection. Serological interpretation should always be correlated with clinical findings, exposure history, imaging, and other laboratory investigations. Early acute infection may yield negative serology prior to seroconversion; repeat testing after 2?3 weeks may be clinically indicated where suspicion remains high. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Coxiella burnetii IgM Antibody Test
synonyms: Q Fever Serology (IgM); Coxiella burnetii IgM Antibodies; Coxiella IgM Antibody Assay; Phase I & Phase II Coxiella burnetii IgM Antibodies
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Coxiella Burnetii IgM Antibody Test and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: The Coxiella burnetii IgM Antibody Test is a serological assay used to detect IgM antibodies against Coxiella burnetii, the etiologic agent of Q fever. Detection of IgM antibodies may support the diagnosis of recent or acute infection, particularly when interpreted together with clinical presentation and complementary serological findings including IgG antibody patterns. Q fever is a zoonotic infection transmitted primarily through inhalation of aerosols contaminated by infected livestock, especially cattle, sheep, and goats. Acute infection may present with non-specific febrile illness, severe headache, atypical pneumonia, hepatitis, or flu-like symptoms. IgM antibodies generally appear early during infection; however, isolated IgM reactivity should be interpreted cautiously due to the possibility of cross-reactivity or non-specific serological responses. Confirmation with paired acute and convalescent sera demonstrating seroconversion or rising antibody titres may be recommended where clinically indicated. Serological results should be interpreted in conjunction with exposure history, clinical findings, and other laboratory investigations. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: The creatine phosphokinase (CPK) enzyme has three isoenzymes: CPK-MM (muscle), CPK-MB (cardiac), and CPK-BB (brain). The CPK-MM fraction test checks for the predominant form found in skeletal muscle and to a lesser extent in cardiac muscle. Elevated CPK-MM levels indicate skeletal muscle injury, breakdown, or disease. Common causes include trauma, strenuous exercise, muscular dystrophies, myositis, rhabdomyolysis, and certain drug/toxin exposures. Clinically, CPK-MM helps differentiate muscle-derived enzyme elevation from cardiac (CPK-MB) or neurologic (CPK-BB) sources. Persistently high levels warrant evaluation for ongoing muscle damage, while correlation with clinical history, physical findings, and additional tests (e.g., renal function, urine myoglobin, EMG, biopsy) is important for accurate diagnosis\\~and\\~management. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Creatine Kinase - Total
description: Creatine kinase (CK) is a dimeric enzyme measured in serum or plasma to aid in the diagnosis of muscle injuries, myocardial infarction, and neuromuscular disorders. It exists as three cytosolic isoenzymes CK-MM (skeletal muscle), CK-MB (cardiac muscle), and CK-BB (brain) as well as a mitochondrial isoenzyme. CK levels rise significantly in skeletal muscle damage (e.g., rhabdomyolysis, Duchenne muscular dystrophy) and in cardiac injury, where levels increase within 4 hours of myocardial infarction, peak at 12 24 hours, and normalize within 3 4 days. Although troponins are now preferred for cardiac diagnostics due to greater specificity, CK remains valuable for evaluating chronic myopathies, statin-induced myotoxicity, and drug-related muscle effects. Monitoring CK is recommended before and during lipid-lowering therapy in patients with muscle-related symptoms.

description: The C-terminal telopeptide (CTX) test measures type I collagen breakdown products to assess bone resorption, aiding in the evaluation of osteoporosis, metabolic bone diseases, or bone metastases, and monitoring antiresorptive therapy efficacy. Plasma CTX (preferred) uses a fasting morning blood sample (7-10 AM), offering higher precision (<15% variability) and is ideal for detailed assessment or research, with reference ranges for premenopausal women, postmenopausal women, and men. Urine CTX, collected from a second-morning void or 24-hour sample (normalized to creatinine), is non-invasive but less precise (23-48% variability), suitable for routine monitoring when blood draws are impractical. Elevated levels indicate increased bone resorption; a 25-40% decrease post-therapy suggests effective treatment. Blood CTX (EDTA plasma) is favored in clinic settings for its accuracy, with results interpreted alongside clinical history and other tests (e.g., DEXA, P1NP). This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: Cyclosporine is an immunosuppressant medication that is primarily used to prevent organ rejection following organ transplants (such as kidney, liver, and heart transplants). It works by suppressing the immune system, specifically targeting T-cells, which are part of the body's immune response that can attack transplanted organs. By inhibiting the activity of these immune cells, cyclosporine helps prevent the body from rejecting the new organ.The dosage needs to be carefully monitored, as cyclosporine can have serious side effects, including kidney damage, high blood pressure, and increased risk of infections. Regular blood tests are necessary to ensure the drug is at the correct level in the body. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: CYP11B1 / CYP11B2 Chimeric Gene by PCR
synonyms: CYP11B1 / CYP11B2 Molecular Assay for Glucocorticoid-Remediable Aldosteronism;Familial Hyperaldosteronism Type I
description: This PCR-based assay detects the presence of a CYP11B1/CYP11B2 chimeric gene, the characteristic genetic abnormality in familial hyperaldosteronism type I (FH-I), also known as glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism (GRA). The test is performed on peripheral blood DNA and targets the hybrid gene formed by unequal crossover between the 11\'e2-hydroxylase and aldosterone synthase genes, resulting in ACTH-regulated aldosterone overproduction. It is indicated in patients with early-onset or familial hypertension, suppressed renin with inappropriately normal or elevated aldosterone, and in children or young adults with suspected primary aldosteronism. A positive result confirms FH-I and enables targeted management with low-dose glucocorticoids and/or mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and facilitates family cascade testing. A negative result excludes FH-I but does not rule out other causes of primary aldosteronism, including sporadic aldosterone-producing adenomas, bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, and other familial subtypes. Where clinical suspicion remains high despite a negative PCR result, next-generation sequencing (NGS) -based clinical exome seuqncing (CES) targeting genes implicated in primary aldosteronism (e.g., KCNJ5, CACNA1D, CACNA1H, ATP1A1, ATP2B3) may be used as an alternative or complementary approach to detect point mutations, small insertions/deletions, or atypical rearrangements that are not detectable by conventional PCR

name: Cysticercosis IgG (Taenia Solium IgG) CSF
synonyms: Cysticercus IgG Antibodies Test: Pig Tapeworm Antibodies Test
instructions: CSF 3-5 mL
description: The Cysticercosis IgG antibody test is a serologic assay used to support the diagnosis of cysticercosis, especially neurocysticercosis, caused by Taenia solium larvae. It detects IgG antibodies in serum or CSF. A positive result suggests prior or active infection but must be interpreted alongside clinical findings and neuroimaging, as it cannot distinguish between active and past infection. False positives may occur due to cross-reactivity with other parasitic infections, while false negatives are possible in cases of localized lesions, early infection, or immunosuppression. The test is most useful in patients from endemic regions who present with unexplained seizures or intracranial cystic/ring-enhancing lesions. However, it is not suitable as a screening tool in asymptomatic individuals due to high background seroprevalence. Negative results do not rule out disease, especially in cases with single or calcified lesions. A positive test should prompt further diagnostic evaluation including brain imaging and possible CSF analysis, with management guided by a multidisciplinary team. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: DHEA-S (Dehydroepiandrosterone Sulphate)
instructions: Serum. Plasma: Li?heparin, K2?EDTA and K3?EDTA plasma.
description: The DHEA-S test measures the level of dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, a hormone produced mainly by the adrenal glands. DHEA-S serves as a precursor to male and female sex hormones (androgens and estrogens) and plays a role in puberty, reproductive function, and overall hormonal balance. This test is often used to evaluate adrenal gland function and investigate symptoms of hormone imbalances such as excessive hair growth (hirsutism), irregular menstrual cycles, infertility, or early or delayed puberty. Low levels of DHEA-S may indicate underactive adrenal glands (adrenal insufficiency), aging, or pituitary dysfunction that reduces hormone production. They can also occur due to chronic illness or long-term use of corticosteroids. On the other hand, high DHEA-S levels are often linked to conditions that cause excessive androgen production, such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), adrenal tumors, or congenital adrenal hyperplasia. In rare cases, elevated levels may suggest an adrenal cancer. Because DHEA-S is produced almost exclusively by the adrenal glands, abnormal levels can provide important insight into adrenal health and hormonal balance. Together, these markers provide valuable insight into the interplay between diabetes and cardiovascular health. This panel is recommended for diabetic patients during routine monitoring or when assessing cardiovascular risk. The addition of a Lipid Profile (total cholesterol, HDL, LDL, and triglycerides) helps identify atherogenic dyslipidemia commonly associated with diabetes, guiding both risk stratification and therapeutic interventions.
