name: DNA Maternity Test x2 (Mother & Child)
synonyms: Maternity Test; DNA test (Mother and Child)
instructions: DNA Paternity Testing Specimen - Buccal Swab (Cotton Swab) or dried blood spot on treated or untreated paper. Buccal Swab Specimen Collection Instructions 1. Prepare the Collection Kit: Ensure the kit contains sterile buccal swabs (minimum 2 per individual), labeled collection envelopes or tubes, gloves, and a consent form. 2. Label each envelope or tube clearly with the individual's full name, date of birth, and collection date. 3. Ensure Proper Identification: Verify and record the identity of each donor using a valid form of identification. 4. Complete the chain-of-custody form if required. 5. Pre-Collection Instructions: Do not eat, drink, smoke, chew gum, or brush teeth for at least 30 minutes prior to sample collection. Rinse the mouth with clean water and wait 10 minutes before swabbing. 6. Swab Collection Procedure: Wear gloves throughout the procedure. Using one sterile swab, firmly rub the inside of the cheek in a back-and-forth motion for 30-60 seconds to collect epithelial cells. Repeat with a second swab on the opposite cheek. Allow swabs to air dry for at least 15-20 minutes. Do not blow on or touch the swab head. 7. Packaging the Samples: Place the dried swabs into the labeled paper envelope or specimen tube (do not use plastic bags or airtight containers). 8. Ensure each sample is properly sealed and labeled. 9. Documentation: Complete and sign all required documentation, including consent and identification forms. Ensure accurate linkage of sample ID to the donor's identity. 10. Transport to Laboratory: Place all labeled envelopes, consent forms, and chain-of-custody documents in the collection kit or transport bag. Deliver to the laboratory under standard room temperature conditions. Avoid exposure to moisture or heat.

description: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a molecule that carries our genetic code and is unique to each of us. Almost every cell in the body contains a complete set of DNA that is inherited from our biological parents. A person gets half of their DNA from their mother and half from their father. Paternity testing compares DNA from different individuals to find out if they are biologically related. The most common reason for paternity testing is to identify a child s biological father. A complete paternity test must test samples from the alleged father, the mother and the child. By testing the mother, we can see which half of the DNA she contributed to the child. Once this is determined, the remaining DNA contribution (other half) is only compared to the alleged father s DNA.

name: Drug Allergy Antibiotics Panel x28 Drugs
synonyms: Antibiotic Allergy Panel; Drug-Specific IgE Panel; 28-Drug Allergy Panel; Antibiotic Hypersensitivity Panel; Antibiotic IgE Allergy Testing;
instructions: Collect blood in 2 Serum Separator Tubes (SSTs) to obtain a minimum of 5 mL serum. Allow blood to clot, centrifuge and separate serum into appropriately labelled containers. Avoid haemolysed or contaminated specimens.
description: The Drug Allergy Antibiotics Panel (28 Drugs) is a serum-based enzyme immunoassay (EIA) that measures drug-specific immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies against 28 antibiotic and related drug antigens. The panel includes penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, sulfonamides and other antimicrobial agents. Results are reported quantitatively in IU/mL and classified into seven IgE reactivity classes (0 6), ranging from clinically insignificant to extremely high according to the reference laboratory's assay-specific thresholds. The test is intended as an adjunct in the evaluation of suspected IgE-mediated antibiotic hypersensitivity, particularly in patients with a history of allergic reactions following antibiotic exposure. Results require correlation with the implicated medication, clinical presentation, timing and severity of the reaction, and previous drug exposures. A positive result indicates detectable IgE reactivity but does not independently confirm clinical drug allergy, while a negative result does not exclude drug hypersensitivity, including non-IgE-mediated reactions. The clinical diagnostic performance of individual drug assays may be limited or inadequately validated. Specialist allergy assessment, including validated skin testing or supervised drug provocation where appropriate, may be necessary to establish the diagnosis and guide safe antibiotic selection. Test is performed at our reference lab network. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: The Drug Allergy Panel (10 Drugs) is a serum-based immunoassay panel that measures drug-specific immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies against ten commonly used antibiotics and analgesic/antipyretic medications. The panel includes six antibiotics (Amoxicillin, Ciprofloxacin, Ampicillin, Cloxacillin, Erythromycin and Ofloxacin) and four analgesic/antipyretic agents (Ibuprofen, Diclofenac, Paracetamol and Aspirin). Total serum IgE measurement is also included. Drug-specific IgE antibodies are measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), while total IgE is measured using chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA). Results are reported quantitatively in IU/mL, with drug-specific IgE concentrations classified into seven reactivity classes (0 6) according to the reference laboratory's assay-specific thresholds. The panel is intended as an adjunct in evaluating suspected immediate drug hypersensitivity reactions, including urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis and other symptoms occurring after exposure to the listed medications. It covers selected antibiotic and analgesic agents, although aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) hypersensitivity reactions are frequently mediated by non-IgE mechanisms and cannot be reliably diagnosed or excluded using serum-specific IgE testing. Results require careful correlation with the clinical history, implicated medication and timing of symptoms. A positive result does not independently confirm clinical allergy, while a negative result does not exclude drug hypersensitivity. Specialist allergy assessment, including validated skin testing or supervised drug provocation where appropriate, may be required to establish the diagnosis and guide safe medication selection. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: The Drug Allergy Panel (7 Drugs) is a serum-based immunoassay panel that measures drug-specific immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies against seven medications: Penicillin G, Penicillin V, Ampicillin, Amoxicillin, Neomycin, Gentamicin and Paracetamol. Clinical indications include suspected medication-related urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis or other immediate allergic reactions. Results must be interpreted alongside the patient's medication exposure history, timing and nature of symptoms, and previous allergic reactions. A positive result indicates detectable IgE reactivity but does not independently establish clinical drug allergy, while a negative result does not exclude drug hypersensitivity, including delayed or non-IgE-mediated reactions. description: The Du test (Weak D test) detects weak or partial expression of the RhD antigen using the indirect antiglobulin method. It is primarily used in RhD typing of blood donors, pregnant women, and transfusion candidates. Donors with weak D are classified as RhD positive, while recipients and pregnant women may be managed as RhD negative to prevent alloimmunization. Molecular genotyping may be advised for accurate classification.

description: EBV EBNA-1 IgG is an antibody that appears approximately 6-12 weeks after primary Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) infection and remains positive for life, indicating past infection or latency. Its presence-with absence of VCA IgM-helps confirm previous exposure and excludes acute primary infection, while also supporting identification of reactivation in immunocompromised individuals. Detection of EBNA-1 IgG is therefore essential for assessing immune status and differentiating stages of EBV infection. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: The Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) DNA Quantitative PCR test is a molecular diagnostic assay used to detect and quantify EBV DNA in clinical specimens such as whole blood, plasma, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), or tissue. Using real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR), this test provides an accurate measurement of EBV viral load. It is highly sensitive and specific, allowing for early detection of viral replication even before clinical symptoms appear. This test is primarily used to monitor EBV infection in immunocompromised patients, particularly transplant recipients at risk for post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD), and in the evaluation of EBV-associated malignancies or chronic active EBV infection. Quantitative PCR enables serial monitoring of viral load over time, aiding in diagnosis, prognosis, and response to therapy. Results should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings and other laboratory tests. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: EBV EA IgG Antibodies
synonyms: EBV Early Antigen D Antibodies EBV Early Antigen Diffuse Antibodies
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for EBV EA IgG Antibodies and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: Epstein-Barr virus early-antigen IgG (EBV EA IgG) supports interpretation of EBV serology when assessed together with VCA IgM, VCA IgG and EBNA antibodies. EA IgG commonly appears during acute infection and may also be detected during reactivation. EA IgG is not, by itself, proof of active EBV replication because it can persist in a proportion of healthy individuals after past infection. Interpret the overall EBV antibody pattern and clinical presentation rather than this marker in isolation.

name: EBV IgM Antibody
synonyms: Anti-EBV IgM AntibodyEbstein Barr Virus IgM Antibody
description: EBV VCA?IgM is a qualitative immunoassay for IgM antibodies to Epstein-Barr virus, typically detectable at symptom onset during primary infection (infectious mononucleosis). It peaks within the first few weeks and usually disappears within 2-6 months. Its presence-especially when combined with VCA?IgG and absence of EBNA?1 IgG-helps confirm acute EBV infection, differentiate from other mononucleosis-like illnesses (e.g., CMV, HIV, toxoplasmosis), and assess immune status in transplant and immunocompromised patients. Negative IgM with positive IgG markers signifies past infection or latency.

description: Immunohistochemistry for EBV evaluates expression of this marker in tissue sections to support diagnosis, classification, and, where relevant, prognostic or predictive assessment. description: The EGFR test on liquid biopsy is used to monitor for development of EGFR T790M drug-resistant mutation in patients administered tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy for EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer. The EGFR mutations are commonly seen in lung adenocarcinomas, and less frequently in adenosquamous carcinoma but are extremely rare in squamous cell carcinoma. name: Electron Microscopy (Tissue)
instructions: Submit tissue biopsies immediately in 3% buffered glutaraldehyde solution. Ensure the specimen is fully immersed in fixative and appropriately labelled. Do not place tissue intended for electron microscopy in formalin.
description: Electron microscopy (EM) is a specialized ultrastructural examination used to assess cellular and subcellular morphology at high resolution. It may be performed on appropriately collected tissue or cellular specimens where detailed evaluation of organelles, membranes, inclusions, deposits, cilia or other ultrastructural features may assist in diagnosis. Findings are interpreted in conjunction with the clinical information, light microscopy, immunohistochemistry and other relevant laboratory investigations. Diagnostic yield depends on appropriate specimen selection, fixation and preservation. EM is particularly valuable in the diagnosis and classification of mitochondrial myopathies, congenital myopathies, myofibrillar myopathies, inclusion body myositis, storage disorders, vacuolar myopathies and selected muscular dystrophies. It is performed as an adjunct to routine histology, histochemistry, immunohistochemistry and molecular genetic testing to provide comprehensive clinicopathological correlation.

name: Electron Microscopy Renal Biopsy (Specimen in EM Fixative)
instructions: Submit Kidney biopsy in 3% Buffered Glutaraldehyde solution.
description: Electron microscopy (EM) of renal biopsy is a specialised ultrastructural examination performed to evaluate the glomeruli, tubules, interstitium and blood vessels at very high magnification. It enables detailed assessment of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), podocyte foot processes, mesangium, endothelial cells, immune deposits and other ultrastructural features that are not detectable by routine light microscopy or immunofluorescence. EM is an essential component of the diagnostic work-up for many medical renal diseases, including minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), membranous nephropathy, hereditary nephropathies (e.g. Alport syndrome and thin basement membrane nephropathy), complement-mediated glomerulopathies and selected immune complex-mediated diseases. It is interpreted alongside clinical information, light microscopy and immunofluorescence findings to provide an integrated clinicopathological diagnosis. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) Panel
instructions: Collect the approved blood and any other listed specimens for Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) Panel. Fast only if the request or a component test requires it. Label all containers with patient and collection details.
description: The Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) Panel is a non-invasive serum test that assesses the severity of liver fibrosis by measuring Hyaluronic Acid (HA), Amino-terminal Propeptide of Type III Procollagen (PIIINP), and Tissue Inhibitor of Metalloproteinases-1 (TIMP-1). These biomarkers reflect extracellular matrix turnover and fibrogenesis, and are combined into a calculated ELF score that correlates with fibrosis stage, aiding in the management of chronic liver diseases such as NAFLD/MASLD, viral hepatitis, alcohol-related liver disease, and autoimmune liver conditions. The ELF score helps suggest the degree of minimal fibrosis, minimum vs ndeterminate vs advanced fibrosis. While the test is useful for non-invasive fibrosis assessment and monitoring, it should be interpreted alongside clinical evaluation, imaging, and other investigations, as it cannot determine disease etiology and may be influenced by systemic fibrotic or inflammatory\\~conditions. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: ERG (ETS-Related Gene) is a nuclear immunohistochemical marker used in the evaluation of selected neoplasms. It is a highly sensitive marker of endothelial differentiation and is useful in confirming vascular tumours such as angiosarcoma, epithelioid hemangioendothelioma and Kaposi sarcoma. ERG is also expressed in approximately 40-60% of prostate adenocarcinomas due to TMPRSS2-ERG gene fusion and may support a prostatic origin when interpreted alongside morphology and other prostate markers (e.g. NKX3.1, PSA and PSMA). Results should always be interpreted in conjunction with the histopathological findings and the full immunohistochemical panel. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Extended Paternity Testing
instructions: DNA Paternity Testing Specimen - Buccal Swab (Cotton Swab) or dried blood spot on treated or untreated paper. Buccal Swab Specimen Collection Instructions 1. Prepare the Collection Kit: Ensure the kit contains sterile buccal swabs (minimum 2 per individual), labeled collection envelopes or tubes, gloves, and a consent form. 2. Label each envelope or tube clearly with the individual's full name, date of birth, and collection date. 3. Ensure Proper Identification: Verify and record the identity of each donor using a valid form of identification. 4. Complete the chain-of-custody form if required. 5. Pre-Collection Instructions: Do not eat, drink, smoke, chew gum, or brush teeth for at least 30 minutes prior to sample collection. Rinse the mouth with clean water and wait 10 minutes before swabbing. 6. Swab Collection Procedure: Wear gloves throughout the procedure. Using one sterile swab, firmly rub the inside of the cheek in a back-and-forth motion for 30-60 seconds to collect epithelial cells. Repeat with a second swab on the opposite cheek. Allow swabs to air dry for at least 15-20 minutes. Do not blow on or touch the swab head. 7. Packaging the Samples: Place the dried swabs into the labeled paper envelope or specimen tube (do not use plastic bags or airtight containers). 8. Ensure each sample is properly sealed and labeled. 9. Documentation: Complete and sign all required documentation, including consent and identification forms. Ensure accurate linkage of sample ID to the donor's identity. 10. Transport to Laboratory: Place all labeled envelopes, consent forms, and chain-of-custody documents in the collection kit or transport bag. Deliver to the laboratory under standard room temperature conditions. Avoid exposure to moisture or heat.

name: Factor IX
instructions: Inform your clinician if you are on any anticoagulant therapy.
description: A coagulation screening test used to evaluate patients with suspected factor deficiencies(hereditary or acquired Haemophilia B),family history of factor deficiencies or unexplained bleeding disorders suspected to be caused by factor IX deficiency. Factor IX is a vitamin K-dependent clotting factor that plays a critical role in the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade. It is essential for the activation of factor X, ultimately leading to the formation of a stable fibrin clot. This test measures the activity of Factor IX in plasma and is primarily used to diagnose and monitor Hemophilia B (Christmas disease), a bleeding disorder caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of Factor IX. It may also be ordered in cases of unexplained bleeding, prolonged aPTT, or to assess for acquired deficiencies or the presence of inhibitors.

description: Factor V Leiden mutation testing detects the F5 G1691A variant that causes activated protein C resistance. The mutation is an inherited risk factor for venous thromboembolism and should be interpreted with the patient s thrombotic history, family history and other thrombophilia findings.

name: Factor VIII

This test measures the activity of Factor VIII in plasma and is used primarily in the diagnosis and monitoring of Hemophilia A, a genetic bleeding disorder caused by Factor VIII deficiency. It is also useful in evaluating unexplained bleeding, prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), or assessing acquired deficiencies due to conditions such as liver disease, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), or the presence of inhibitors.

name: Factor XIII Activity Assay (FXIII:C)
synonyms: Factor XIII Functional Assay; Coagulation Factor XIII Activity; Factor XIII (13) Activity
instructions: Sample Instructions: Collect 3 mL whole blood in one Blue Top (3.2% sodium citrate) tube. Mix gently by inversion immediately after collection. Centrifuge within 1 hour of collection to prepare platelet-poor plasma (PPP). Transfer plasma into a properly labelled plastic transport tube and freeze if transport to the reference laboratory will be delayed. Avoid haemolysed, lipaemic or clotted specimens. Clinical history, including bleeding manifestations, family history, recent surgery or trauma, and any recent plasma products or Factor XIII replacement therapy, should accompany the request.
description: The Factor XIII Activity Assay (FXIII:C) is a quantitative functional assay used to evaluate the activity of coagulation Factor XIII, the enzyme responsible for stabilising fibrin clots by cross-linking fibrin strands after clot formation. Factor XIII deficiency is a rare but important cause of bleeding in patients with normal PT/INR and APTT results, as routine coagulation tests do not assess Factor XIII function. This assay is indicated in patients with unexplained delayed postoperative or post-traumatic bleeding, recurrent soft tissue or intracranial haemorrhage, umbilical stump bleeding in neonates, poor wound healing, recurrent pregnancy loss, or suspected congenital or acquired Factor XIII deficiency. Reduced activity may require follow-up testing with Factor XIII antigen assays, Factor XIII inhibitor studies, and, where clinically indicated, F13A1/F13B genetic testing This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: The Full Blood Count (FBC) with Peripheral Blood Film (PBF) includes a complete quantitative analysis of blood cells together with a microscopic morphological review of the blood smear. name: Ferritin - Inflammatory Marker
description: Ferritin is a protein that stores iron and is primarily located in the liver, spleen, muscles, and bone marrow, with small amounts circulating in blood. Serum ferritin levels correlate with total body iron stores and are used to diagnose iron deficiency (e.g. iron deficiency anemia) and iron overload (e.g. hemochromatosis). A level below 15 \'ecg/L confirms iron deficiency, while elevated levels can indicate iron overload or act as an acute phase reactant in cases of inflammation, infection, liver or renal disease, and malignancy.

It is also useful in monitoring patients with cardiovascular disease or those undergoing major surgery. The test is performed using a high-precision clot-based method that delivers fast and reliable results.

name: Filaria Antibody
synonyms: Filarial Antibody Test; Filaria IgG Antibody; Filarial Serology
instructions: Collect 2?3 mL blood in a plain or serum separator tube. No specific time-of-day collection is required. Where possible, provide relevant travel or residence history, suspected filarial species, clinical presentation and previous antifilarial treatment, as these materially affect interpretation.
description: Serological detection of antibodies to filarial parasites, used as supportive evidence of exposure or infection in patients with suspected filariasis. Depending on the assay, antibodies may be detected in infections caused by filarial nematodes such as Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia spp., Loa loa, Onchocerca volvulus and Mansonella spp. The exact species coverage and degree of cross-reactivity depend on the antigen composition of the assay. A positive antibody result indicates exposure to filarial antigens but does not reliably distinguish active from past infection, and antibodies may persist after successful treatment. Cross-reactivity between different filarial species and, with some assays, other helminths may occur. A negative result does not completely exclude infection, particularly in early disease or immunologically hyporesponsive patients. Results should therefore be interpreted with clinical and epidemiological findings and, where appropriate, microfilaria microscopy, circulating filarial antigen testing and/or molecular testing. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Filaria Antigen
synonyms: Circulating Filarial Antigen (CFA); Wuchereria bancrofti Antigen; Lymphatic Filariasis Antigen
instructions: Collect blood at any time of day. Unlike microfilaria microscopy, nocturnal collection is not required, because circulating filarial antigen does not show the same clinically important periodicity as circulating microfilariae. Where possible, document relevant travel/residence history, previous antifilarial treatment and clinical suspicion of lymphatic filariasis.
description: Detection of circulating filarial antigen for investigation of lymphatic filariasis due principally to Wuchereria bancrofti. Antigen testing detects products of adult filarial worms and may therefore identify infection even when peripheral microfilariae are absent or below the detection threshold of microscopy. W. bancrofti causes approximately 90% of lymphatic filariasis worldwide. This test is not a general screen for all filarial infections. Standard circulating filarial antigen assays are primarily directed at W. bancrofti and should not be relied upon to diagnose Brugia malayi, Brugia timori, Loa loa, Onchocerca volvulus or Mansonella infections. Microscopy and/or species-appropriate serological or molecular testing should be considered where these infections are suspected. A positive antigen result supports current or recent W. bancrofti infection, although antigen may persist after treatment or loss of reproductive adult worms. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Filarial PCR
synonyms: Filaria DNA PCR; Filariasis PCR; Lymphatic Filariasis PCR; Wuchereria bancrofti PCR; Brugia malayi PCR
instructions: Collect 3?5 mL peripheral venous blood in a sterile EDTA tube and gently invert to mix. Avoid haemolysis and clot formation. For suspected Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia infection, document collection time and consider nocturnal collection where clinically appropriate. Confirm the referral laboratory's current specimen, timing and transport requirements.
description: This test is a molecular qualitative PCR assay used for the detection of filarial parasite DNA in clinical specimens for the diagnosis of filariasis. Depending on assay design and laboratory capability, the test may detect and/or differentiate major human pathogenic filarial species including Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, and occasionally other filarial nematodes. PCR offers high analytical sensitivity and specificity and may be useful in cases with low microfilarial burden, occult infection, atypical presentations, partially treated disease, or when smear microscopy is negative despite strong clinical suspicion. The test is primarily used as an adjunctive or confirmatory investigation and does not replace routine conventional methods such as peripheral blood smear microscopy, circulating filarial antigen (CFA) assays, or filarial antibody testing, which remain the standard frontline diagnostic approaches in most clinical settings. Filarial PCR is generally not a routine mainstream commercial assay and is mainly available in selected specialized reference, research, tropical medicine, or public health laboratories. Clinical correlation with travel history, eosinophilia, lymphatic manifestations, and other parasitological/serological findings is recommended. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: T-lymphocyte subset analysis on bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid is performed using multiparametric flow cytometry to characterize cellular immune populations within the lower respiratory tract. The assay identifies and quantifies T lymphocytes based on surface antigen expression, primarily CD3 (total T cells), CD4 (T-helper cells), and CD8 (cytotoxic T cells). Results are reported as percentages of gated lymphocytes and, where applicable, as absolute counts, providing insight into the local immune milieu of the lung. This test is clinically useful in the evaluation of interstitial lung diseases, sarcoidosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, pulmonary infections (including opportunistic infections in immunocompromised patients), and immune-mediated or transplant-related pulmonary conditions. Interpretation should be correlated with clinical findings, radiologic features, microbiological results, and histopathology, as BAL lymphocyte subset distributions reflect localized immune responses rather than systemic immune status.

instructions: Collect the approved blood or named specimen for FLT3 ITD & TKD (D835Y) Mutations. Send with the clinical indication and any prior molecular results. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: FLT3 mutation testing identifies activating alterations in the FLT3 receptor tyrosine kinase, a key prognostic and therapeutic biomarker in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The two clinically relevant mutations are FLT3-ITD (internal tandem duplication) involving the juxtamembrane domain, and FLT3-TKD mutations, most commonly D835Y, within the tyrosine kinase domain. Both result in constitutive FLT3 signaling and are associated with aggressive disease biology, high leukemic burden, and increased relapse risk, particularly for FLT3-ITD. Detection of FLT3 mutations informs risk stratification, treatment selection, and transplant planning. FLT3-ITD is generally associated with adverse risk (context-dependent), while FLT3-TKD confers intermediate risk. Identification of either mutation supports the use of FLT3 inhibitors (e.g., midostaurin in frontline therapy; gilteritinib in relapsed/refractory disease) and guides monitoring for acquired resistance, especially emergence of TKD mutations during therapy. Results should be interpreted alongside co-mutations (e.g., NPM1) and reported with variant allele frequency or allelic ratio where available. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

It is indicated in women with premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), unexplained infertility, or relevant family history. Testing is performed by TP-PCR with capillary electrophoresis, with reflex methods for large expansions if required. Detection of a premutation supports Fragile Xassociated POI (FXPOI) and has key reproductive implications, including risk of expansion in offspring. Results are reported as CGG repeat number with interpretation; genetic counseling is recommended for positive findings. name: Folate Levels (Serum)
description: The Folate test is a quantitatively measures folate (vitamin B9) levels in the human serum, aiding in the diagnosis and management of anemia and nutritional deficiencies. Folate plays a vital role in DNA synthesis, methylation, redox reactions, and amino acid metabolism. Deficiency may result from poor diet, malabsorption, increased demand (e.g., pregnancy), liver disease, or drug interactions, and is associated with megaloblastic anemia, cardiovascular disease, and neural tube defects. Hemolyzed samples are unsuitable due to high folate content in red blood cells. Samples should be collected from fasting individuals, protected from light, and processed promptly. When evaluating folate status, concurrent B12 testing is recommended due to overlapping clinical presentations.

This test evaluates FRá protein expression by immunohistochemistry (IHC) on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue sections. Expression is assessed in a semi-quantitative manner, incorporating the proportion of tumor cells demonstrating membranous staining and staining intensity, typically reported using a validated scoring system (e.g., percentage positivity and/or composite score). The assay is primarily indicated to identify patients eligible for FRá-targeted therapies (e.g., antibody-drug conjugates such as mirvetuximab soravtansine) and may also provide supportive diagnostic or prognostic information in selected tumor types. Interpretation should be performed in the context of tumor histology, clinical findings, and other relevant biomarkers. It plays a critical role in the inactivation of coagulation factors Va and VIIIa, helping to prevent excessive clot formation. This test measures the functional activity of free Protein S in plasma to identify hereditary or acquired deficiencies, which are associated with an increased risk of venous thromboembolism. It is especially useful in patients with unexplained or recurrent thrombosis, during thrombophilia investigations, or in evaluating coagulation disorders related to pregnancy, liver disease, or oral anticoagulant therapy.

It complements HbA1c in monitoring glycemic trends and treatment effectiveness.

Low or absent fructose can suggest ejaculatory duct obstruction, seminal-vesicle dysfunction or congenital absence of the vas deferens when interpreted with semen volume and other findings.

name: FSH (Follicle Stimulating Hormone) - Endocrine
instructions: Serum collected using standard sampling tubes or tubes containing separating gel. Li?heparin, K2?EDTA and K3?EDTA plasma.
description: Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH) is hormone produced by the anterior pituitary. Acting together with luteinizing hormone (LH), it stimulates the growth and function of the gonads. In women, it promotes follicular development and the production of estrogen, with levels peaking around mid-cycle and rising significantly during menopause due to reduced estrogen feedback. In men, FSH supports spermatogenesis by acting on the seminiferous tubules. Measurement of FSH levels, often in conjunction with LH, is useful in evaluating conditions such as menstrual irregularities, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), menopausal status, infertility, and gonadal dysfunction. Low FSH levels in men may be associated with azoospermia.

name: G6PD Qualitative Screening Test
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for G6PD Qualitative Screening Test and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: Qualitative G6PD screening assesses whether red-cell glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity is sufficiently reduced to suggest G6PD deficiency. It is used to identify patients at risk of oxidant-induced haemolysis; borderline or clinically discordant results may require quantitative confirmation.

name: G6PD Quantitative Confirmatory Test
synonyms: G6PD Quant Test; G6PD Confirmatory Test
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for G6PD Quantitative Confirmatory Test and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: Quantitative G6PD testing measures red-cell glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity to confirm or exclude G6PD deficiency. Results can be falsely normal during or soon after acute haemolysis or transfusion and should be interpreted with clinical history.

name: GAD Glutamic Acid Decarboxylase Antibody

Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: GAD(Glutamic Acid Decarboxylase) is an enzyme involved in producing GABA, a neurotransmitter that regulates nerve activity. In autoimmune diseases, antibodies are produced against GAD. A GAD (Glutamic Acid Decarboxylase) antibody test measures the presence of GAD antibodies in the blood which are associated with autoimmune disorders, particularly in type 1 diabetes and Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS).The test is used to diagnose and distinguish between Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes.It is also used in asssesing the risk of developing type 1 diabetes, especially in individuals with a family history of the disease alongside other islet cell autoantibodies and in diagnosis of Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS). This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Galactosemia (GALT) Gene Mutation
instructions: Collect EDTA whole blood for Galactosemia (GALT) Gene Mutation.

name: Ganglioside Antibody Profile IgG

It is used in risk assessment and prognostication in cardiovascular disease.

name: Genetic Test NGS Lung Cancer Panel Liquid Biopsy x50 Markers

description: The Oncomine Precision Assay is a validated liquid-biopsy next-generation sequencing panel that interrogates 50 cancer-related genes (78 variants) in circulating cell-free/tumour-derived nucleic acids. MAPK/RAS?RAF?MEK coverage includes KRAS, NRAS, HRAS, BRAF, ARAF, RAF1, MAP2K1 and MAP2K2; PI3K/AKT/mTOR genes include PIK3CA, PTEN, AKT1, AKT2, AKT3 and MTOR. Receptor tyrosine kinases and fusion drivers include EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB3, ERBB4, ALK, ROS1, RET, MET, FGFR1?4, NTRK1?3, KIT, PDGFRA, FLT3 and NRG1. Additional targets include CTNNB1, RSPO2, RSPO3, GNA11, GNAQ, GNAS, SMO, AR, ESR1, CDK4, CDKN2A, CHEK2, TP53, IDH1, IDH2, CD274 (PD-L1) and NUTM1. The assay evaluates DNA hotspot variants in 45 genes, copy-number changes in 14 genes and fusion rearrangements involving 19 genes. Results may support molecular classification and targeted-treatment decisions. A negative liquid-biopsy result does not exclude a tumour alteration because circulating tumour DNA shedding varies; tissue testing should be considered when clinically appropriate.

The alteration classes reported for individual genes are those defined by the validated referral-laboratory assay.

name: Genome-wide DNA Methylation Profiling (CNS Tumor Classifier)
synonyms: CNS Tumor DNA Methylation Profiling; Brain Tumor DNA Methylation Array; Heidelberg CNS Tumor Classifier
instructions: FFPE with > 30% tumor content
description: Genome-wide DNA Methylation Profiling (CNS Tumor Classifier) is an advanced molecular diagnostic assay that analyzes genome-wide epigenetic patterns using an Illumina EPIC (850K) methylation array with validated classifier algorithms (e.g., Heidelberg CNS tumor classifier). This test enables objective, biology-based classification of central nervous system tumors by comparing the tumors methylation signature to a large reference dataset, thereby refining or resolving diagnoses that are morphologically and genetically ambiguous. This assay is particularly indicated in high-grade gliomas where there is overlap between adult-type glioblastoma (IDH-wildtype) and pediatric-type high-grade glioma (H3-wildtype/IDH-wildtype). It allows definitive distinction between these entities and further subclassifies pediatric-type tumors into clinically relevant molecular subgroups (RTK1, RTK2, MYCN). The test complements histopathology and targeted NGS panels but is essential for accurate integrated diagnosis and risk stratification in such cases. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: GGT Gamma Glutamyltransferase
instructions: Allow serum tube to clot completely at room temperature. Separate serum or plasma from cells within 2 hours of collection.
description: Gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) is an enzyme measured in serum or plasma to aid in the diagnosis and monitoring of hepatobiliary diseases and serves as a screening tool for alcohol abuse. Although present in multiple tissues, serum GGT primarily reflects liver activity. GGT testing is often performed alongside ALT, AST, ALP, bilirubin, and albumin during liver function assessment. Elevated levels are associated with among others liver disease, excessive alcohol intake, obesity, and the use of certain drugs. It is one of the most sensitive markers for alcohol-related liver damage.

A negative result does not exclude infection if clinical suspicion remains high, and repeat or alternative testing may be appropriate. name: Gilbert Syndrome (UGT1A1 Genotyping)

name: GLDH Glutamate Dehydrogenase
description: GLDH is a mitochondrial enzyme primarily found in the liver and to a lesser degree in kidneys and in the heart muscle. GLDH is more specific to liver injury than ALT. description: This assay quantitatively measures human growth hormone in serum and plasma. hGH, secreted by the pituitary gland, plays a vital role in stimulating growth, especially bone elongation, through the production of IGF-1 in the liver. Its secretion is pulsatile and regulated by factors such as GHRH, somatostatin, sleep, exercise, and glucose levels. hGH levels vary by age, sex, and physiological state, peaking in adolescence and declining with age. Excess hGH can lead to gigantism (in children) or acromegaly (in adults), often caused by pituitary adenomas, while deficiency can cause growth retardation in children and metabolic disturbances in adults. name: Gut health by LC-MS/MS
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Gut Health by LC-MS/MS and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: Gut Health by LC-MS/MS is a urine-based metabolic profile that measures selected organic acid biomarkers associated with intestinal microbial metabolism and gut microbiome balance. The assay is performed by liquid chromatographytandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), with results expressed relative to urinary creatinine. The profile includes markers associated with intestinal fungal overgrowth and microbiome dysbiosis, including citramalic acid, tartaric acid, hippuric acid, 4-methylhippuric acid, 2-hydroxyphenylacetic acid, 4-hydroxybenzoic acid, 3-indoleacetic acid, 4-hydroxyphenylacetic acid, 3-hydroxybutyric acid, succinic acid, orotic acid, pyroglutamic acid, homovanillic acid and adipic acid. Alterations in these metabolites may reflect changes in microbial metabolism, intestinal dysbiosis, oxidative stress and related metabolic pathways. In particular, the reference laboratory interprets increased succinic and adipic acids as biochemical findings that may be associated with gut dysbiosis and increased oxidative or inflammatory activity. This test is intended as an adjunctive metabolic assessment and should be interpreted alongside the patients clinical presentation, dietary history and other relevant laboratory or gastrointestinal investigations. It does not directly identify or quantify individual microorganisms and should not be used in isolation to diagnose a specific gastrointestinal infection or disease. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Gut Microbiome Analysis and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: The Gut Microbiome Analysis is an advanced molecular stool test designed to characterize the composition and diversity of microorganisms inhabiting the gastrointestinal tract, collectively referred to as the gut microbiome. Using next-generation sequencing (NGS) and/or targeted microbial genomic analysis, the test evaluates the relative abundance of key bacterial taxa and commensal microbial populations, providing insights into microbial balance (eubiosis), dysbiosis, microbial diversity, and selected gut ecosystem patterns associated with gastrointestinal and systemic health. This assay may assist in the evaluation of conditions associated with altered gut microbiota, including chronic gastrointestinal symptoms, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), post-antibiotic dysbiosis, metabolic disorders, immune dysregulation, and selected nutrition or wellness assessments. Results should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, dietary factors, medications (especially antibiotics and probiotics), and other laboratory investigations. This test is not intended as a standalone diagnostic assay for infectious gastroenteritis or specific gastrointestinal diseases. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: The Hantavirus RNA Detection by Real-Time RT-PCR assay is a qualitative molecular test used for the detection of Hantavirus viral RNA in clinical specimens. The test assists in the early diagnosis of acute hantavirus infection, including Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS) and Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), particularly during the early viremic phase before antibody seroconversion occurs. Clinical features may include acute febrile illness, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, respiratory distress, pulmonary edema, hemorrhagic manifestations, and history of rodent exposure. Detection of Hantavirus RNA supports active or recent infection. A negative result does not completely exclude infection and should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, exposure history, imaging studies, and serological testing (Hantavirus IgM/IgG), especially in late-stage disease or low viral load states. The assay is performed using real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) technology on validated clinical specimens including whole blood, plasma, serum, respiratory specimens, or tissue samples. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: Qunatitative determination of Haptoglobin is used to detect and assess hemolysis. Haptoglobin is a liver-derived glycoprotein that binds free hemoglobin released during red blood cell destruction, forming complexes cleared by the liver. Its levels drop in hemolytic anemia or liver dysfunction due to rapid consumption, while they increase during inflammation as it is an acute phase reactant. Therefore, haptoglobin measurement in serum or plasma helps diagnose and monitor hemolysis, inflammation, and liver conditions. Low levels can also occur in cirrhosis, splenomegaly, or malnutrition, while elevated levels may be seen in infections, cancer, or tissue damage.

This quantitative CLIA assay should always be interpreted in conjunction with the patient's clinical probability (e.g. 4Ts score), timing of heparin exposure, platelet count trend, and evidence of thrombosis. A positive result indicates the presence of anti-PF4/heparin IgG antibodies but does not by itself confirm clinically significant HIT. Where indicated, confirmation with a functional platelet activation assay may be recommended. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

instructions: Sample type: EDTA plasma preferred; serum acceptable. Provide any available HBV DNA viral-load result. Low viral loads may result in amplification failure or incomplete resistance profiling. Collect 3?5 mL whole blood in an EDTA tube for plasma. Centrifuge promptly and separate plasma within 6 hours. Avoid haemolysis and repeated freeze?thaw cycles. Store at 2?8?C for up to 72 hours or freeze at -20?C or lower. Maintain the cold chain during transport.
description: This test performs HBV antiviral drug-resistance sequencing together with HBV genotype determination. If an adequate prior HBV DNA viral-load result is supplied, that result is used to assess suitability for sequencing. If no viral-load result is supplied, HBV DNA is measured first and resistance sequencing with genotyping is performed reflexively when the viral load is adequate, typically at or above 1,000 IU/mL. Interpret resistance findings with treatment history, current antiviral therapy, HBV DNA level and clinical context. name: Hepatitis B (HBV) Genotyping (including HBV Viral Load)
synonyms: HBV genotype; HBV genotyping; HBV DNA viral load and genotype; HBV Genotype Testing New
instructions: Sample type: EDTA plasma preferred; serum acceptable. Collect 3?5 mL whole blood in an EDTA tube. Centrifuge promptly and separate plasma within 6 hours. Avoid haemolysis and repeated freeze?thaw cycles. Store at room temperature or 2?8 ?C for up to 72 hours, or freeze at -20 ?C or lower. Maintain the cold chain during transport. HBV viral load (HBV DNA) is performed first. Genotyping is carried out reflexively if the viral load is adequate (typically =1,000 IU/mL). Low viral load may result in genotyping failure. Confirm the referral laboratory's current specimen and transport requirements before collection.
description: This assay provides a comprehensive molecular evaluation of hepatitis B virus (HBV), combining quantitative HBV DNA viral load measurement with reflex genotyping by PCR-based sequencing to determine the viral genotype (A?J). The viral load component quantifies circulating HBV DNA and is used for diagnosis, assessment of infectivity, and monitoring of antiviral therapy. Genotyping is performed on samples with sufficient viral load and may inform therapy selection, predicted treatment response (including interferon sensitivity), and prognosis, including risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Accurate genotyping requires adequate circulating viral DNA; low viral loads may fail amplification. The combined workflow is useful when no recent viral load result is available, so that quantification and genotype can be obtained from one referral. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Hepatitis B (HBV) Genotyping (reflex test on recent HBV Viral Load)
instructions: Sample Type: EDTA Plasma (preferred), Serum (acceptable) Collection & Handling: Performed on an already submitted sample; no additional collection required NOTE: This is a REFLEX TEST performed on samples with a recent detectable HBV viral load Adequate viral load is required for successful genotyping (typically =1,000 IU/mL); lower levels may result in amplification failure The existing HBV DNA result will be utilized for this analysis
description: This assay performs molecular genotyping of Hepatitis B virus (HBV) using PCR-based sequencing methods to determine the viral genotype (AJ). It is conducted as a reflex test on samples with a recent detectable HBV viral load. HBV genotyping provides clinically relevant information for guiding antiviral therapy selection, predicting treatment response (e.g., interferon sensitivity), and offering prognostic insight into disease progression, including the risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Successful analysis requires sufficient circulating viral DNA; low viral loads may lead to test failure. This test is intended for use in patients with confirmed HBV infection and detectable viremia. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Hepatitis B Surface Antibody (Anti-HBs)
synonyms: ANTI HBsAnti Hepatitis B Surface Antibody
description: The Hepatitis B Surface Antibody (Anti-HBs) test measures the presence and level of antibodies against the hepatitis B surface antigen, reflecting immunity status. A positive Anti-HBs result indicates immunity to hepatitis B virus (HBV), either from past infection or successful vaccination. Levels ?10 mIU/mL are generally considered protective. In patients post-vaccination, Anti-HBs testing can confirm adequate immune response, especially in high-risk individuals (e.g., healthcare workers, immunocompromised patients). A negative result (Anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL) suggests susceptibility to HBV infection, warranting vaccination if not previously done or revaccination in non-responders. Anti-HBs testing should be interpreted alongside other hepatitis B markers (e.g., HBsAg, Anti-HBc) for a comprehensive assessment of HBV status.

description: Hepatitis E Virus (HEV) RNA Detection by PCR is a highly sensitive molecular assay used for the direct detection of HEV RNA in blood specimens. The test confirms active HEV infection and is particularly useful in patients with suspected acute hepatitis E, immunocompromised individuals, transplant recipients, and cases where serological findings are inconclusive. Detection of viral RNA provides evidence of ongoing infection and may identify cases before antibody responses become detectable. This assay complements HEV serology (IgM and IgG) and is considered the preferred method for diagnosing active infection in patients with impaired immune responses. HEV RNA testing may also be used for monitoring persistent or chronic HEV infection, particularly in immunosuppressed patients. Results should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, liver function tests, epidemiological risk factors, and other hepatitis investigations. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Her2 Neu by Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
description: HER2 immunohistochemistry (IHC) evaluates overexpression of the HER2 (ERBB2) transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase on tumor cells, most commonly in breast and gastroesophageal adenocarcinomas. In normal tissue, HER2 expression is low to absent. In tumor samples, staining is assessed based on the intensity and completeness of membranous staining in viable tumor cells. A score of 0 or 1+ (faint or incomplete membranous staining) is considered negative, 2+ (weak to moderate complete membranous staining) is equivocal and typically warrants reflex testing by in situ hybridization (ISH), and 3+ (strong, complete circumferential membranous staining in >10% of tumor cells) is considered positive.

specimenReqQuantity: FFPE tumour tissue block,Cytology cell block (validated specimens),Plasma cfDNA / liquid biopsy
instructions: Submit representative tumour tissue (usually an FFPE block or approved alternative) with the histological diagnosis and estimated tumour content. Provide the clinical indication and any prior molecular or pathology results. Follow current laboratory or referral-laboratory collection requirements. description: This test performs molecular analysis of the HER2/ERBB2 oncogene using targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) to detect clinically significant genomic alterations including ERBB2 amplification (copy number gain), activating mutations, and selected insertions/deletions/fusions depending on panel design. HER2 alterations are important predictive biomarkers in multiple solid tumours including breast carcinoma, gastric/gastro-oesophageal adenocarcinoma, non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC), colorectal carcinoma, endometrial carcinoma, and other advanced malignancies. The assay assists in identifying patients who may benefit from HER2-targeted therapies such as trastuzumab, pertuzumab, trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd), tucatinib, lapatinib, neratinib, and other anti-HER2 agents, as guided by tumour type and current oncology guidelines. Results should be interpreted in conjunction with histopathology, immunohistochemistry (IHC), FISH/ISH findings where applicable, tumour percentage, and overall clinical context. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

instructions: Serum collected using standard sampling tubes or tubes containing separating gel. Li?heparin, K2?EDTA and K3?EDTA plasma.
description: "The Herpes Simplex Virus Type 1 (HSV-1) IgG Antibody Test detects IgG antibodies specific to HSV-1, a virus most commonly associated with oral herpes. HSV-1 is highly prevalent worldwide, with most people acquiring the infection in childhood through non-sexual contact. It typically causes cold sores or fever blisters around the mouth but can also be responsible for genital infections, especially through oral-genital contact.This test helps determine whether an individual has been previously exposed to HSV-1, even if they have never experienced noticeable symptoms. IgG antibodies usually appear within a few weeks after infection and remain in the body for life, making this test useful for detecting past or silent infections. The HSV-1 IgG test is particularly helpful in cases where clinical symptoms are unclear, when screening individuals who may be at risk of transmitting the virus, and in evaluating exposure in pregnant women to support perinatal care. It can also be used to distinguish HSV-1 from HSV-2 when both types are possible causes of infection.By identifying long-term immunity or prior infection, the HSV-1 IgG Antibody Test supports accurate diagnosis, patient counseling, and appropriate management of herpes-related conditions."

name: Herpes IgG(HSV2)
instructions: Serum collected using standard sampling tubes or tubes containing separating gel. Li?heparin, K2?EDTA and K3?EDTA plasma.
description: "The Herpes Simplex Virus Type 2 (HSV-2) IgG Antibody Test is used to detect IgG antibodies specific to HSV-2, the virus most commonly associated with genital herpes. HSV-2 is a lifelong viral infection that often goes unrecognized, as many individuals may have mild or no symptoms. Despite the absence of symptoms, the virus can still be transmitted through subclinical viral shedding, making serologic testing important for diagnosis, screening, and management. This test identifies past exposure to HSV-2 by detecting IgG antibodies, which typically develop within a few weeks of infection and remain in the bloodstream for life. As such, the HSV-2 IgG test is useful for confirming prior infection, even in asymptomatic individuals or those with non-specific symptoms. The test is particularly valuable in evaluating patients with unexplained genital ulcers or recurrent symptoms, screening sexual partners of individuals with confirmed HSV-2, and assessing risk in pregnant women to help reduce the chance of neonatal herpes. It is also helpful in guiding patient counseling and treatment decisions. Because it is type-specific, this test can distinguish HSV-2 from HSV-1, enhancing diagnostic accuracy.Overall, the HSV-2 IgG Antibody Test provides a reliable method for detecting silent or past infections and plays a critical role in comprehensive sexual health care"

description: The Histoplasma Antibody test uses immunodiffusion to detect antibodies against Histoplasma capsulatum, the causative organism of histoplasmosis. It is indicated in patients with suspected pulmonary or disseminated histoplasmosis, particularly those presenting with persistent respiratory symptoms, pulmonary nodules, granulomatous lung lesions or relevant environmental exposure. Detection of H and/or M precipitin bands supports exposure or infection, with H-band antibodies more suggestive of active disease and M-band antibodies potentially persisting following previous infection. A positive result should be interpreted alongside clinical presentation, radiological findings and other laboratory investigations, as seropositivity alone does not establish active infection. A negative result does not exclude histoplasmosis, particularly in early infection, immunocompromised patients or localised disease. Where clinical suspicion persists, additional investigations such as Histoplasma urine or serum antigen testing, fungal culture, molecular testing or tissue biopsy with histopathological examination may be necessary to establish the diagnosis and guide antifungal treatment decisions. name: HIV PCR Qualitative RNA Detection
description:
The cobas® HIV-1/HIV-2 Qualitative assay uses real-time reverse transcription PCR to detect and distinguish HIV-1 and HIV-2. It detects viral RNA in serum or EDTA plasma. Dried blood spots (DBS) may also be tested when the laboratory uses the assay version that includes DBS in its intended use. The test aids diagnosis in adults and children, including infants with perinatal HIV exposure. It can also help identify acute infection before antibodies are detectable and clarify HIV type following a reactive antigen/antibody screening result.

Results are reported separately for HIV-1 and HIV-2. Detection of either target indicates infection with the corresponding HIV type. A negative result means the assay did not detect either target in the specimen tested. Infection may still be present if the amount of viral nucleic acid is below the assay’s detection limit. This qualitative test does not provide a viral load. A quantitative HIV RNA assay is used to monitor response to antiretroviral therapy.

In infants born to HIV-infected mothers and who have maternal antibodies to HIV-1 or HIV-2, the presence of HIV nucleic acid is indicative of active infection.

This test may also be used to confirm HIV-1 or HIV-2 infection in an individual with specimens reactive for HIV-1 or HIV-2 antibodies or antigens.

instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for HMGCR Antibody (Anti?3-Hydroxy-3-Methylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Antibodies) and label it with patient identity and collection time. description: The HMGCR antibody test detects autoantibodies directed against 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase, the key enzyme in cholesterol synthesis. The presence of these antibodies is strongly associated with immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM), particularly in patients with prior statin exposure, though cases also occur in statin-naïve individuals, especially younger patients. Clinically, affected patients typically present with progressive proximal muscle weakness, markedly elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels, and muscle fiber necrosis with minimal inflammation on biopsy. Unlike statin-related toxic myopathy, HMGCR antibodyassociated IMNM usually persists or progresses despite statin withdrawal and often requires immunosuppressive therapy. A positive test supports the diagnosis of HMGCR-associated IMNM, while a negative result does not exclude other inflammatory or necrotizing myopathies such as SRP-positive IMNM or paraneoplastic forms. The antibody may remain detectable despite clinical improvement and is not reliable for disease monitoring. Interpretation should always be integrated with the clinical picture, CK levels, muscle biopsy findings, and other myositis-specific antibody\\~results. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: HOMA-IR (Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance) is a calculated index derived from fasting plasma glucose and fasting insulin concentrations, used as a surrogate marker of insulin resistance. It reflects the balance between hepatic glucose output and pancreatic \'e2-cell insulin secretion under fasting steady-state conditions. Elevated HOMA-IR values indicate reduced insulin sensitivity, typically associated with compensatory hyperinsulinemia, and are commonly seen in obesity, metabolic syndrome, prediabetes, and related cardiometabolic disorders. Clinically, HOMA-IR provides a practical, non-invasive, and cost-effective method for assessing insulin resistance in routine laboratory practice. It is particularly useful for early detection of metabolic dysfunction in patients with normal glucose levels but underlying hyperinsulinemia. However, as a static model, it does not capture dynamic insulin responses and may be less reliable in advanced diabetes or conditions affecting \'e2-cell function. Results should therefore be interpreted in conjunction with clinical context, glycaemic indices (e.g., HbA1c), and other metabolic parameters such as lipid profile.

name: Homologous Recombination Deficiency (HRD) Assay
description:
HRD testing assesses defects in the homologous recombination DNA repair pathway in tumour cells, which may predict sensitivity to platinum-based chemotherapy and PARP inhibitors. Comprehensive HRD testing evaluates genomic instability markers, including loss of heterozygosity (LOH), telomeric allelic imbalance (TAI), and large-scale state transitions (LST), often alongside BRCA1/2 mutation analysis.

Unlike Homologous Recombination Repair (HRR) gene panel testing, which identifies mutations in DNA repair genes, comprehensive HRD testing assesses the genomic consequences of defective DNA repair and may identify HRD-positive tumours even without detectable BRCA1/2 mutations. An HRR gene panel alone does not establish HRD status.

name: HPV DNA PCR
instructions:

description:
HPV is a viral infection that causes common skin and mucous membrane warts. Certain high-risk strains are known to progress cancer. It is now well-established that a persistent infection with a high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) genotype is the main cause of cervical cancer. It is possible to have an HPV infection without any cytologic abnormalities.

 

Checking for HR-HPV genotypes is a reliable and accurate primary screening tool for cervical cancer in women between 25 and 65 years without need for Pap smear while those under 25 years are recommended to have Pap smear. Detection of one or more high risk genotypes is associated with an increased risk of development of cervical cancer.

 

The HPV DNA PCR test at Dr. Kalebi Labs (DKL) has been performed using the FDA approved Cobas 5800 assay which automatically detects 14 HR - HPV genotypes (16, 18, 31, 33, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66 and 68) with individual typing of HPV 16 and HPV 18 simultaneously.

This test is not intended for women who have undergone full hysterectomy.

The HPV DNA PCR test at Dr. Kalebi Labs (DKL) has been performed using the FDA approved Cobas 5800 assay which automatically detects 14 HR - HPV genotypes (16, 18, 31, 33, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66 and 68) with individual typing of HPV 16 and HPV 18 simultaneously. description:
HRR (Homologous Recombination Repair) genetic testing plays an important role in the management of prostate cancer, particularly in men with metastatic disease. Mutations in HRR pathway genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, PALB2, and RAD51 occur in a significant proportion of patients and are clinically relevant for both treatment selection and prognosis. Current guidelines recommend HRR testing for all men with metastatic prostate cancer, ideally through both germline testing (blood or saliva, to detect inherited mutations) and somatic testing (tumor tissue or circulating tumor DNA, to detect acquired mutations).

 

Identifying HRR mutations has direct therapeutic implications, as these patients are more likely to benefit from PARP inhibitors (e.g., olaparib, rucaparib) and may also show increased sensitivity to platinum-based chemotherapy. Beyond guiding treatment, HRR testing provides prognostic information-particularly as BRCA2 mutations are associated with more aggressive disease-and informs family counseling when germline mutations are detected. Testing is typically performed using NGS-based multigene panels covering the relevant HRR genes.

 

This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: The Insulinoma-Associated-2 Antibody (IA-2 Ab) test is used to aid in diagnosing autoimmune Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM). IA-2 is a protein tyrosine phosphatase located in pancreatic ß-cell secretory granules, and the presence of antibodies against IA-2 indicates autoimmune destruction of ß-cells. IA-2 antibodies are typically found in individuals with new-onset T1DM and, like other diabetes-related autoantibodies, their detection helps distinguish T1DM from Type 2 or other non-autoimmune diabetes forms. A positive IA-2 antibody result supports a diagnosis of autoimmune T1DM, especially when combined with other autoantibodies such as GAD65, ZNT8, and insulin autoantibodies. Multiple positive antibodies increase diagnostic confidence and predict higher risk of progression in at-risk individuals. A negative IA-2 result does not exclude T1DM, as not all patients develop detectable levels of this antibody. Interpretation should always be integrated with clinical findings. name: IGHV Mutation Status by NGS
description: IGHV Mutation Status by NGS is a molecular assay used in the diagnostic and prognostic work-up of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). Using next-generation sequencing, the test analyzes the immunoglobulin heavy chain variable (IGHV) gene rearrangement in leukemic B cells and compares it with the closest germline IGHV sequence to determine the degree of somatic hypermutation. Cases with <98% identity are reported as mutated IGHV, while those with ?98% identity are unmutated IGHV, in line with iwCLL/WHO/ICC recommendations. IGHV status is a stable, disease-defining biomarker with major clinical impact: mutated IGHV is associated with indolent disease and longer progression-free and overall survival, whereas unmutated IGHV predicts more aggressive behavior and earlier need for therapy. Results inform risk stratification at diagnosis and may influence treatment selection (e.g., likelihood of durable response to chemo-immunotherapy versus preference for targeted agents). The test requires peripheral blood or bone marrow with adequate tumor burden and is typically performed once, as IGHV status does not change over the disease course.

name: IGHV Mutation Status by Sanger Sequencing

description: IGHV Mutation Status by Sanger Sequencing is a molecular assay used in the diagnostic and prognostic evaluation of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). The test involves PCR amplification of the rearranged immunoglobulin heavy chain variable (IGHV) gene from leukemic B cells, followed by Sanger sequencing and comparison with the closest germline IGHV sequence in international databases (e.g., IMGT). A sequence identity of <98% defines mutated IGHV, while ?98% defines unmutated IGHV, in accordance with iwCLL, WHO, and ICC criteria. IGHV mutation status is a robust, stable prognostic biomarker in CLL: mutated IGHV is associated with more indolent disease and prolonged survival, whereas unmutated IGHV correlates with aggressive disease and earlier treatment requirement. Results support baseline risk stratification and may guide therapeutic decisions, including the expected durability of response to chemo-immunotherapy versus targeted agents. The assay is typically performed once per patient, as IGHV status remains stable over time, and requires peripheral blood or bone marrow with sufficient clonal B-cell burden.

instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Insulin Autoantibodies (IAA) and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: The Insulin Autoantibody (IAA) test detects antibodies directed against endogenous insulin and is primarily used in the evaluation of autoimmune Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM), particularly in young children. IAA is often the first autoantibody to appear in genetically susceptible individuals and is most commonly seen in children under five years old with new-onset T1DM. The presence of IAA indicates an autoimmune response targeting insulin-producing ß-cells. A positive IAA result supports the diagnosis of autoimmune T1DM, especially when detected alongside other antibodies such as GAD65, IA-2, and ZNT8. Its diagnostic utility decreases with age and in individuals who have been treated with exogenous insulin, as this can induce antibody formation. A negative IAA result does not rule out T1DM, and the test should be interpreted in the clinical context along with other autoantibody and metabolic markers. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: Insulin-like Growth Factor Binding Protein 3 (IGFBP-3) is the major carrier protein for insulin-like growth factors (IGF-I and IGF-II) in circulation and reflects growth hormone (GH) activity. Measurement of IGFBP-3 provides a stable and reliable indicator of the GH-IGF axis, as its levels are less affected by short-term physiological fluctuations compared to IGF-1. This makes IGFBP-3 particularly useful in the evaluation of suspected growth hormone deficiency (GHD) and growth hormone excess (e.g., acromegaly or gigantism), especially in pediatric populations. Clinically, IGFBP-3 is used alongside IGF-1 to assess disorders of growth and development, including short stature, delayed puberty, and suspected pituitary dysfunction. Low levels are suggestive of growth hormone deficiency, malnutrition, or chronic systemic illness, while elevated levels may be seen in conditions of GH excess. Interpretation should be age- and sex-specific, and results are best considered in conjunction with clinical findings and other endocrine investigations. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

instructions: Collect the approved blood or named specimen for JAK2 Second-Line Testing Exon 12 Mutation Detection. Send with the clinical indication and any prior molecular results. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: JAK2 exon 12 mutation analysis detects a group of less common activating variants in the JAK2 gene that are primarily associated with polycythemia vera (PV), particularly in cases where the more common JAK2 V617F mutation is not identified. These mutations are found in a small subset of patients with PV and are characteristically associated with isolated erythrocytosis, often with low serum erythropoietin levels. This test is recommended as a second-line investigation in patients with a strong clinical suspicion of PV who test negative for JAK2 V617F. A positive result supports the diagnosis of a clonal erythrocytosis consistent with PV and should be interpreted in the context of clinical findings, hematologic parameters, and bone marrow morphology. A negative result does not exclude PV or other myeloproliferative neoplasms; additional molecular testing (e.g., CALR, MPL) or further hematologic evaluation may be required depending on the clinical scenario. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: The JAK2 V617F mutation is a recurrent somatic variant in the JAK2 gene and serves as a key diagnostic marker for myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs). It is present in the majority of patients with polycythemia vera and in a significant proportion of those with essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis. This test is recommended as a first-line molecular investigation in patients with unexplained erythrocytosis, thrombocytosis, or other clinical features suggestive of an MPN. Detection of the mutation supports a clonal myeloid process and contributes to diagnostic classification in conjunction with clinical and hematologic findings. A positive result is highly indicative of an MPN but should be interpreted alongside full blood count parameters, bone marrow findings, and other relevant investigations. A negative result does not exclude an MPN; in cases with strong clinical suspicion-particularly suspected polycythemia vera-further testing for less common mutations (e.g., JAK2 exon 12) or additional markers (such as CALR or MPL) may be warranted.

name: JC virus (JCV) PCR Test {Blood}

description: The JC virus (JCV) PCR test on blood is used in the evaluation of patients at risk for JC virus reactivation, particularly those who are immunocompromised due to advanced HIV, post-transplant immunosuppression, or treatment with monoclonal antibody therapies such as natalizumab or rituximab. The assay detects JCV DNA in plasma or whole blood using real-time PCR, providing high specificity and good sensitivity for monitoring systemic viral presence and risk of progression to central nervous system (CNS) disease. A positive result indicates active JC viremia and may support risk stratification for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) in the appropriate clinical context. However, detection in blood does not confirm CNS involvement, and correlation with neurological symptoms and imaging is essential. A negative result reduces but does not fully exclude the possibility of JC virus infection or PML, especially if clinical suspicion remains high. Follow-up testing or CSF analysis may still be warranted in such cases. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: The JC virus (JCV) PCR test on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is used in the evaluation of patients with suspected progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a demyelinating CNS infection seen in immunocompromised individuals such as those with advanced HIV, post-transplant immunosuppression, or on monoclonal antibody therapies like natalizumab or rituximab. The assay detects JCV DNA by real-time PCR, offering high specificity and good sensitivity, though detection depends on viral load and disease stage. A positive result in the appropriate clinical and radiological setting strongly supports a diagnosis of PML, while a negative result does not fully exclude the disease, particularly early on or in patients with low viral burden. If suspicion remains high, repeat CSF testing or brain biopsy may be indicated. Interpretation should always be made in correlation with neurological findings and MRI features of multifocal non-enhancing white matter lesions. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: The JC virus (JCV) PCR test on urine is primarily used to detect viral shedding in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with advanced HIV, transplant recipients, or patients receiving monoclonal antibody therapies (e.g., natalizumab, rituximab). The assay identifies JCV DNA in urine using real-time PCR, which offers high sensitivity for detecting latent or reactivated infection since the virus commonly reactivates in the kidneys before systemic spread. A positive result indicates urinary shedding of JCV and supports the presence of active or latent infection but does not, by itself, confirm central nervous system (CNS) disease or progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). A negative urine PCR reduces the likelihood of viral reactivation but does not completely rule it out, particularly in patients with ongoing risk factors. Results should always be interpreted in conjunction with blood or CSF testing, neurological assessment, and imaging where clinically indicated. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.
