name: Karyotyping - Bone marrow/Haemat Malignancy
instructions: Collect 1?3 mL of bone marrow aspirate into a sodium heparin (green top) tube for cytogenetic karyotyping analysis. Immediately after collection, gently invert the tube 8?10 times to ensure proper mixing with the anticoagulant; avoid vigorous shaking to prevent cellular damage and reduced viability. Ensure the specimen is clearly labeled and free from clots or excessive peripheral blood dilution. Transport the sample to the laboratory as soon as possible at room temperature (18?25?C). Do not refrigerate or freeze the specimen, as this may compromise cell culture viability. For optimal chromosome growth and metaphase yield, the specimen should ideally reach the laboratory and be processed within 24 hours of collection.
description: Bone marrow karyotyping is a cytogenetic test used to evaluate the number and structure of chromosomes in dividing bone marrow cells. The test helps detect chromosomal abnormalities associated with hematological disorders such as leukemias, lymphomas, myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs), aplastic anemia, and other bone marrow malignancies. Chromosomal analysis assists in diagnosis, prognosis, disease classification, treatment selection, and monitoring of disease progression or response to therapy. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Karyotyping - Peripheral Blood
instructions: Collect 3-5 mL of peripheral blood into a sodium heparin (green top) tube, or a bone marrow aspirate where indicated, especially for hematological malignancies. Immediately after collection, gently invert the tube 8-10 times to mix; avoid vigorous shaking to prevent cell damage. Ensure the sample is properly labeled and free from clots. Transport the specimen to the laboratory as soon as possible while maintaining room temperature (18-25?C). Do not refrigerate or freeze the sample. The specimen should ideally be processed within 24 hours to ensure viable cells for culture and analysis.
description: Karyotyping is a cytogenetic test used to evaluate the number and structure of chromosomes in a patients cells. It allows for the detection of chromosomal abnormalities such as aneuploidies, deletions, duplications, translocations, and other structural rearrangements. This test is commonly used in the evaluation of hematological malignancies, including conditions such as Chronic Myeloid Leukemia, as well as in cases of congenital abnormalities, infertility, and recurrent pregnancy loss. It provides a global view of the genome and is often used alongside more targeted techniques such as FISH for comprehensive analysis. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Karyotyping - POC
instructions: Sample Collection Instructions for POC Karyotyping Tissue Type: Submit chorionic villi or fetal tissue (preferably placental villi, not maternal decidua). Avoid blood clots and maternal tissue. Container: Use a sterile, screw-cap container. Transport Medium: Place the sample in sterile saline or transport medium (e.g., RPMI or Hanks Balanced Salt Solution). Do not use formalin or fixatives. Volume: A tissue piece about 2-4 cm³ is usually sufficient. Labeling: Clearly label the container with patient identifiers and indicate it is a POC specimen. Timing: Deliver to the lab as soon as possible (ideally within 24 hours) at room temperature or refrigerated (4-8?C). Do not freeze. Requisition: Include clinical details, gestational age, reason for testing (e.g., recurrent miscarriage), and contact information.
description: Karyotyping of POC is a cytogenetic analysis used to detect chromosomal abnormalities that may underlie miscarriage or pregnancy loss. It helps identify aneuploidies (e.g., trisomy 13, 18, 21, monosomy X), polyploidies, and structural chromosomal anomalies. The test is most informative in recurrent pregnancy loss, second-trimester losses, or when fetal anomalies are suspected. Ideally, fresh tissue should be submitted promptly in sterile conditions to optimize cell culture success. Limitations include culture failure and maternal cell contamination. Molecular techniques (e.g., chromosomal microarray) may be considered where available for higher resolution and better diagnostic yield. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Kinship Studies x2 Individuals
instructions: DNA Kinship Testing Specimen - Buccal Swab (Cotton Swab) or dried blood spot on treated or untreated paper. Buccal Swab Specimen Collection Instructions 1. Prepare the Collection Kit: Ensure the kit contains sterile buccal swabs (minimum 2 per individual), labeled collection envelopes or tubes, gloves, and a consent form. 2. Label each envelope or tube clearly with the individual's full name, date of birth, and collection date. 3. Ensure Proper Identification: Verify and record the identity of each donor using a valid form of identification. 4. Complete the chain-of-custody form if required. 5. Pre-Collection Instructions: Do not eat, drink, smoke, chew gum, or brush teeth for at least 30 minutes prior to sample collection. Rinse the mouth with clean water and wait 10 minutes before swabbing. 6. Swab Collection Procedure: Wear gloves throughout the procedure. Using one sterile swab, firmly rub the inside of the cheek in a back-and-forth motion for 30-60 seconds to collect epithelial cells. Repeat with a second swab on the opposite cheek. Allow swabs to air dry for at least 15-20 minutes. Do not blow on or touch the swab head. 7. Packaging the Samples: Place the dried swabs into the labeled paper envelope or specimen tube (do not use plastic bags or airtight containers). 8. Ensure each sample is properly sealed and labeled. 9. Documentation: Complete and sign all required documentation, including consent and identification forms. Ensure accurate linkage of sample ID to the donor's identity. 10. Transport to Laboratory: Place all labeled envelopes, consent forms, and chain-of-custody documents in the collection kit or transport bag. Deliver to the laboratory under standard room temperature conditions. Avoid exposure to moisture or heat.

name: Lacosamide (TDM by LC-MS/MS)
instructions: Serum in red top.
description: Lacosamide (TDM by LC-MS/MS) is a test that checks for Lacosamide as an antiepileptic used in focal epilepsy. Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) supports dose optimization, checks adherence, and helps assess toxicity, especially with comorbidities, drug interactions, or breakthrough seizures. Clinical response and tolerability remain paramount. Higher levels may increase risk of dizziness, diplopia, ataxia, or cardiac conduction effects. Results should be interpreted in context of dosage, timing of sampling, and patient-specific\\~factors. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Lactate (Fluid)
description: "The Lactate (Fluid) test measures the concentration of lactate in body fluids such as pleural, peritoneal, or synovial fluid. Lactate is a byproduct of anaerobic metabolism and serves as a sensitive marker of local tissue hypoxia, inflammation, or infection within the fluid compartment. Elevated lactate levels in body fluids may indicate bacterial peritonitis, empyema, intestinal ischemia, or septic arthritis, and can aid in differentiating infectious from non-infectious causes of effusion. This test is especially useful in critically ill patients or when evaluating unexplained fluid accumulation. Proper collection into sterile containers and rapid transport to the lab (ideally on ice) are essential, as lactate is metabolically active and may degrade if delayed"

name: Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH), CSF
synonyms: CSF LDH; LDH CSF; Lactate Dehydrogenase CSF; Cerebrospinal Fluid LDH; LDH – Cerebrospinal Fluid
description: Cerebrospinal fluid lactate dehydrogenase (CSF LDH) measures the activity of the intracellular enzyme lactate dehydrogenase within cerebrospinal fluid. LDH may be released into CSF following cellular injury, inflammation or increased cellular turnover within the central nervous system. Increased CSF LDH concentrations have been described in association with central nervous system infections, particularly bacterial meningitis, intracranial haemorrhage, malignant involvement of the central nervous system and other conditions causing tissue or cellular injury. CSF LDH is a non-specific biochemical marker and should not be used independently to establish a diagnosis. Results should be interpreted together with the patient's clinical presentation and other CSF investigations, particularly total and differential cell counts, protein, glucose, Gram stain/culture or molecular microbiological investigations, and cytology or flow cytometry where malignancy is suspected. Blood contamination of CSF may increase LDH activity and should be considered when interpreting an elevated result. Testing is performed by a kinetic photometric enzymatic method based on the IFCC principle using the Roche cobas c 503 clinical chemistry system. The cobas c 503 platform accommodates CSF specimens; however, the Roche LDHI2 reagent manufacturer's stated intended specimen types are serum and plasma. Use of the assay for CSF should therefore be supported by the laboratory's documented verification of the alternative specimen application and locally verified or appropriately adopted reference values.

name: Lactate Level (Blood)
instructions: Specimen Instructions - Lactate (Roche cobas c503) The patient should be at complete rest for at least 15-30 minutes prior to specimen collection and should avoid exercise or repeated use of the arm or hand before and during phlebotomy. Where clinically feasible, a fasting sample is preferred. Blood should be drawn without the use of a tourniquet where possible, or within three minutes of tourniquet application, while avoiding fist clenching and excessive venous stasis. The specimen should be centrifuged and plasma separated as soon as possible, preferably within 15-30 minutes of collection. If immediate processing is not possible, the specimen should be maintained at 2-8 degrees centigrade and transported promptly. Rapid processing and proper handling are essential to minimize falsely elevated lactate results caused by ongoing cellular metabolism.
description: Lactate is produced during anaerobic metabolism and is an important marker of tissue hypoxia and impaired oxidative metabolism. Measurement of blood lactate is primarily used in the evaluation and monitoring of sepsis, shock, hypoxia, and metabolic acidosis, and may also assist in the investigation of mitochondrial disorders and inborn errors of metabolism. Serial lactate measurements are useful for assessing disease severity and response to treatment in critically ill patients. Testing is performed on the Roche cobas c503 analyzer using an enzymatic method. Accurate results require proper patient preparation and prompt specimen processing, as prolonged venous stasis or delayed plasma separation may lead to falsely elevated lactate levels.

name: Lactate Level (CSF)
description: The CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) lactate test measures the concentration of lactate in the cerebrospinal fluid, which surrounds the brain and spinal cord. It is primarily used to help differentiate between bacterial and viral meningitis, as lactate levels tend to be significantly higher in bacterial infections. Elevated CSF lactate may also indicate other conditions such as brain hypoxia, mitochondrial disorders, or central nervous system trauma. It provides valuable information about metabolic activity and oxygen utilization in the brain.

name: Lamotrigine
instructions: Collect 3-5 mL of venous blood in a plain (red-top) tube or serum separator tube (SST). The sample should be drawn just before the next scheduled dose (trough level) to obtain an accurate assessment of steady-state concentration. After collection, allow the sample to clot, centrifuge, and separate serum promptly. Avoid hemolyzed or lipemic samples. Clearly indicate the time of last dose and the time of sample collection on the request form to aid in accurate interpretation.
description: The Lamotrigine test is used to measure and monitor the concentration of lamotrigine in a patients blood. Lamotrigine is an anticonvulsant medication commonly prescribed for the management of epilepsy and bipolar disorder. Monitoring lamotrigine levels helps clinicians ensure therapeutic effectiveness while minimizing the risk of toxicity or subtherapeutic dosing. The test is particularly useful in cases of suspected non-compliance, drug interactions, dose adjustments, pregnancy, or when patients present with signs of toxicity such as dizziness, blurred vision, or skin rashes. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Langerin Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
instructions: For Langerin Immunohistochemistry (IHC), submit representative tissue in approved fixative, or the specified paraffin block and slides. Label the anatomical site and provide relevant clinical, imaging, and previous pathology information. Follow current laboratory collection requirements. Confirm the referral laboratory's current specimen and transport requirements before collection.
description: Immunohistochemistry for Langerin evaluates expression of this marker in tissue sections to support diagnosis, classification, and, where relevant, prognostic or predictive assessment. Interpret with morphology, the remainder of the immunopanel, and clinical / imaging findings. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: LAP Leucocyte Alkaline Phosphotase
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for LAP Leucocyte Alkaline Phosphatase and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: Leucocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) testing assesses alkaline phosphatase activity in neutrophils. Historically it has been used to help distinguish reactive neutrophilia/leukaemoid reactions from chronic myeloid leukaemia, although molecular testing now provides more definitive diagnosis.

name: LDH - Pleural Fluid
description: The LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) level in pleural fluid is a key laboratory test used to help determine the cause of a pleural effusion. It is primarily used as part of Light s criteria to differentiate between exudative and transudative effusions. Elevated pleural fluid LDH especially when the pleural fluid/serum LDH ratio is >0.6 or when the absolute LDH level exceeds two-thirds of the serum upper limit of normal suggests an exudative effusion, which is commonly associated with conditions such as infection, malignancy, or inflammatory diseases. Conversely, lower LDH levels in pleural fluid are more consistent with transudative effusions, which typically result from systemic conditions like heart failure, cirrhosis, or nephrotic syndrome. LDH is a marker of cell turnover and inflammation, so increased levels in pleural fluid indicate a higher degree of cellular activity or damage in the pleural space. The LDH test is often performed alongside measurements of total protein in both pleural fluid and serum to apply Light s criteria accurately.
testDetails: Pleural fluid LDH

name: LDH (Serum)
instructions: Allow serum tube to clot completely. Separate serum or plasma from cells within 2 hours of collection. In certain diseases such as hepatobiliary, skeletal and malignant tumors LDH 4 and LDH 5 are unstable in colled and frozen samples leading to an incorrect LDH value in these conditions. Seperated plasma and serum MUST be free from cells to prevent a spuriously elevated LDH.
description: ;; Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is an enzyme found throughout the body, especially in the heart, liver, muscles, and kidneys. levated LDH levels in the blood are associated with various conditions, including megaloblastic anemia, heart attacks, certain cancers such as leukemia and disseminated carcinoma, and trauma. Milder increases may be seen in hemolytic anemia, muscular dystrophy, pulmonary infarction, liver diseases like hepatitis and cirrhosis, and kidney conditions such as nephrotic syndrome.

name: LDL Cholesterol Measured (Serum)
instructions: Allow serum tube to clot completely at room temperature. Separate serum or plasma from cells within 2 hours of collection. Fasting and Non-fasting sample acceptable
description: ;; Low Density Lipoproteins (LDL) play a key role in causing and influencing the progression of atherosclerosis and, in particular, coronary sclerosis. This test is used to assess cardiovascular disease risk and guide therapy. LDL-cholesterol is a type of cholesterol that contributes significantly to plaque buildup in the arteries, raising the risk of heart disease, stroke, and other cardiovascular conditions. Often referred to as "bad" cholesterol, elevated LDL levels are associated with arterial narrowing and inflammation. Testing LDL-cholesterol is important for diagnosing lipid disorders and assessing cardiovascular risk, including atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease

name: Lead (24hr Urine)
instructions: Proper collection over a full 24-hour period is essential for reliable results. Ensure the patient uses an acid-washed container and that the total volume is recorded.
description: 24-hour urine lead testing is used to assess total lead excretion and is more accurate than spot urine for evaluating body burden, especially in individuals with known or suspected chronic exposure. It is also useful for monitoring chelation therapy efficacy. Elevated values indicating significant exposure or mobilization of lead stores. While 24-hour urine lead testing provides more precise exposure assessment than spot samples, it should still be interpreted alongside clinical findings and blood lead levels, particularly for guiding treatment and public health interventions. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Lead (Blood)
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Lead (Blood) and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: Blood lead level (BLL) testing is the gold standard for diagnosing lead exposure and toxicity. It reflects recent or ongoing exposure and is used for both screening and monitoring, particularly in children, pregnant women, and workers in high-risk occupations. BLL is reported in micrograms per deciliter (µg/dL), with any detectable level considered abnormal in children, as no safe threshold has been established. Elevated BLLs should prompt evaluation of exposure sources, clinical assessment for toxicity, and possible environmental or occupational interventions. In symptomatic individuals or those with very high levels, further evaluation including renal function, hemoglobin, and chelation eligibility may be necessary. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Lead (Spot Urine)
instructions: Sample Collection: Use a clean, acid-washed plastic container to avoid contamination. Collect preferably the first morning void to reduce diurnal variation.
description: Spot urine lead testing is a screening tool for recent or ongoing lead exposure, often used in occupational health or where blood sampling is not immediately feasible. Results should be interpreted relative to urine creatinine (µg/g creatinine) to account for dilution. Elevated levels require confirmation with venous blood lead testing, which remains the gold standard for diagnosis and assessment of body burden. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Lead Compounds in water (Environmental Testing)
instructions: Collect the water specimen in the referral laboratory-approved container. Record the sample source/location, date/time and collection method. Confirm the required volume, preservative and transport conditions with the referral laboratory before collection.
description: Water lead testing quantifies lead in an environmental water sample to assess contamination and potential toxic exposure risk. Results should be compared with the applicable drinking-water or environmental standard, recognising that sampling location, plumbing and collection technique can materially affect the measured concentration. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Legionella pneumophila Antigen, Urine
synonyms: Legionella Urinary Antigen; Legionella pneumophila Urine Antigen; Legionella UAT
instructions: Specimen Instructions Submit 1-2 mL of freshly collected random urine in a clean, sterile, leak-proof urine container without preservative. Refrigerate the specimen if transport is delayed.
description: A qualitative immunochromatographic assay for detection of Legionella pneumophila antigen in urine. It is useful in the investigation of suspected Legionnaires disease, particularly in patients with severe, hospital-acquired or travel-associated pneumonia. Most assays primarily detect L. pneumophila serogroup 1. A negative result does not exclude infection caused by other serogroups or other Legionella species. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Legionella pneumophila IgG Antibody, Serum
synonyms: Legionella IgG Antibody; Anti-Legionella IgG; Legionella IgG Serology
instructions: Specimen Instructions Submit 3 mL of separated serum in a properly labelled, leak-proof transport tube. Collect blood in a plain or serum-separator tube, allow it to clot, centrifuge and separate the serum from the cells. Refrigerate pending transport.
description: An enzyme immunoassay for detection of IgG antibodies to Legionella pneumophila. The test is mainly useful for supportive or retrospective investigation of suspected Legionella infection and for paired acute and convalescent serology. A single positive IgG result may indicate previous exposure and does not independently confirm acute infection. Results should be interpreted with clinical findings and direct detection tests such as urinary antigen, respiratory PCR or culture. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Legionella pneumophila IgM Antibody, Serum
synonyms: Legionella IgM Antibody; Anti-Legionella IgM; Legionella IgM Serology
instructions: Specimen Instructions Submit 3 mL of separated serum in a properly labelled, leak-proof transport tube. Collect blood in a plain or serum-separator tube, allow it to clot, centrifuge and separate the serum from the cells. Refrigerate pending transport.
description: An enzyme immunoassay for detection of IgM antibodies to Legionella pneumophila. IgM antibodies may support recent infection but may be absent early in the illness, persist after infection or show nonspecific reactivity. An isolated positive IgM result is not independently diagnostic of acute Legionnaires disease. Correlation with urinary antigen testing, respiratory PCR or culture is recommended. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Leishmania PCR
instructions: Collect the approved blood or named specimen for Leishmania PCR. Send with the clinical indication and any prior molecular results. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: Leishmania spp. DNA Detection by Real-Time PCR (qPCR) is a highly sensitive and specific molecular assay used for the qualitative detection of Leishmania DNA in clinical specimens. The test employs nucleic acid extraction followed by real-time PCR amplification targeting conserved genomic regions (such as kinetoplast DNA or ribosomal DNA), enabling reliable detection even in cases with low parasite burden. It is applicable to a variety of specimen types including whole blood, bone marrow aspirate, tissue biopsies, and lesion aspirates, depending on the clinical presentation. This assay is indicated for the diagnosis and confirmation of suspected leishmaniasis (visceral, cutaneous, or mucocutaneous), particularly where conventional methods such as microscopy are inconclusive or insensitive. A Detected result supports the presence of active infection and should be interpreted in clinical context, while a Not Detected result does not fully exclude disease, especially in low-level or localized infection. The test is also useful for assessing suspected relapse. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Leptin (Serum)
instructions: Collect serum in a plain or serum-separator tube for Leptin (Serum). Confirm the current referral-laboratory specimen requirement before collection.
description: Leptin (Serum) measures the level of leptin, a hormone produced by fat tissue that regulates appetite, body weight, and energy balance. It is useful in the evaluation of obesity, metabolic syndrome, PCOS, leptin deficiency or resistance, and disorders of appetite regulation. Abnormal leptin levels may indicate impaired communication between fat stores and the brain and can be associated with difficulty managing weight, hormonal imbalance, or insulin resistance. The test requires a serum sample, and results are typically available within 1-3 days. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Leptospirosis IgM

description: Leptospira IgM detects an early antibody response that can support diagnosis of recent leptospirosis after the first several days of illness. Results should be interpreted with exposure history and timing; PCR early in disease or confirmatory microscopic-agglutination/paired serology may be required. description: Liquid-Based Cytology (LBC) Pap smear is a cervical cancer screening test in which exfoliated cells from the transformation zone of the cervix are collected and preserved in a liquid medium, allowing for improved sample quality, standardized preparation, and enhanced detection of epithelial abnormalities. Compared to conventional smears, LBC reduces obscuring factors such as blood, mucus, and inflammation, and provides a more uniform cellular distribution, thereby improving diagnostic accuracy and adequacy rates. The residual sample also permits ancillary testing, including high-risk HPV DNA testing where indicated. Reporting is performed in accordance with the The Bethesda System. Results should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, prior cytology/HPV status, and current screening guidelines. Abnormal results may require further evaluation with HPV testing, colposcopy, or biopsy depending on the category and patient risk profile.

name: LKM-1 Liver Kidney Microsomal Antibodies
description: The LKM-1 (Liver Kidney Microsomes type 1) test quantitatively detects IgG antibodies against LKM-1 in human serum or plasma, serving as an aid in diagnosing type 2 Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH). AIH is a chronic autoimmune liver disease, often seen in females, characterized by elevated gamma globulins, specific autoantibodies, and histological liver changes. It is classified into three types based on antibody profiles: type 1 (ANA and SMA), type 2 (LKM-1), and type 3 (anti-SLA/LP). LKM-1 antibodies target cytochrome P4502D6 and are detected in about 90% of type 2 AIH cases, making them a key diagnostic marker. However, they can also appear in 5-10% of chronic hepatitis C patients, though the epitopes differ from those in AIH. Detecting LKM-1 antibodies is crucial for distinguishing type 2 AIH from other liver diseases and autoimmune conditions.

High LP-PLA2 activity suggests increased atherothrombotic risk, while low/normal levels indicate lower vascular inflammatory burden. Results should be interpreted alongside lipids, hs-CRP, and overall ASCVD risk profile. Although not recommended for routine screening, it can provide added value in select clinical contexts. name: Magnesium (24 Hrs Urine)
instructions: General instructions : Preferred start collection time is morning. Collect urine in a 24 hour metal free urine container. Urine is acidified to pH 1 with concentrated HCl to prevent precipitation of magnesium ammonium phosphate. Empty the bladder first thing in the morning or at the start time and discard this urine. Note the time, as this is the start time of the 24 hours. (For example 6:00 am) Collect every drop of urine voided over the next 24 hours (e.g. 6:am on a Tuesday to 6:00 am Wednesday). Should one need to defecate and urinate at the same time, this urine should also be collected. Try as much as possible not to contaminate the urine with faeces. Keep the urine cold either on ice or refigerated. Stop time should be within 20 minutes of the start time the day before. E.g. if start time was 6:00 am Tuesday, stop time is between 5:50 am and 6:10 am during which time any urine passed must be collected. FOR SUBMITTING LABORATORIES /HOSPITALS If submitting an aliquot of the 24 hour urine, note the volume of 24 hour urine submited. Mix the sample well to a homogenous mixture and aliquote into a clean container. Submit the aliquot with clear documentation of the duration of collection and the volume of the 24 hour urine.
description: 24 hour urine is used to distinguish between renal and GIT losses of Magnesium in hypomagnesemia.

The test assesses the risk of chromosomal abnormalities, primarily Trisomy 21 and Trisomy 18. Risk calculation incorporates maternal age, weight, gestational age, and other clinical factors. It is a screening tool; abnormal results should be followed by appropriate diagnostic procedures. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

It measures three biomarkers: alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), and unconjugated estriol (uE3). This test estimates the risk of fetal chromosomal abnormalities (such as Trisomy 21 and Trisomy 18) and neural tube defects. Results are interpreted in the context of maternal age, weight, gestational age, and other clinical factors. It is a non-diagnostic screening tool and abnormal results should prompt further diagnostic evaluation (e.g., ultrasound, amniocentesis). This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

This test estimates the risk of fetal chromosomal abnormalities (such as Trisomy 21 and Trisomy 18) and neural tube defects. Risk assessment incorporates maternal demographics and gestational age. It is a non-diagnostic screening tool; abnormal results warrant further evaluation through targeted ultrasound or diagnostic testing. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Measles IgM Antibodies
description: The Measles IgM test quantitatively detect IgM antibodies against the measles virus in serum or plasma, aiding in the diagnosis of recent or ongoing infection. Measles is a highly contagious viral disease caused by the Morbillivirus of the Paramyxoviridae family, transmitted via respiratory droplets or direct contact with secretions. It presents with fever, cough, conjunctivitis, Koplik s spots, and a generalized rash, with complications such as pneumonia, diarrhea, and rarely subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE). IgM antibodies typically appear at the onset of the rash, persist for 3-6 weeks, and are the preferred marker for diagnosing acute measles, whereas IgG antibodies indicate past infection or vaccination but require paired serum samples for confirmation.

description: The Membranous Nephropathy IHC Panel comprises a panel of tissue immunohistochemical markers used in the evaluation and further classification of membranous nephropathy and selected associated renal pathological processes. Results should be interpreted in conjunction with light microscopy, immunofluorescence and, where available, electron microscopy, serum antibody studies and the clinical setting. Identification of a characteristic antigen-staining pattern may assist in distinguishing PLA2R-associated membranous nephropathy from other antigen-defined or potentially secondary forms and may guide further clinical investigation.

Management decisions should follow disease-specific targets and the patient s clinical and nutritional status. Abnormal results should prompt clinical correlation and consideration of specialist metabolic assessment and confirmatory investigations. For treatment decisions in established disorders of methionine metabolism, plasma methionine and total homocysteine are generally more directly informative; urine methionine serves as a complementary investigation. description: MGMT Promoter Methylation Analysis (Tumor Tissue) assay detects methylation of the MGMT gene promoter in tumor DNA (typically from FFPE tissue) using PCR- or pyrosequencing-based methods. Promoter methylation leads to reduced MGMT expression and impaired DNA repair capacity. Clinically, in Glioblastoma and other high-grade gliomas, MGMT promoter methylation is a predictive biomarker of improved response to alkylating chemotherapy such as Temozolomide and is associated with better prognosis; results should be interpreted in conjunction with histologic and molecular findings, including IDH status. NB: This test is different from Global methylation profiling which is a diagnostic genome-wide classifier based on DNA methylation microarray technology. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: Anti-Mi-2 myositis-specific autoantibody is a highly specific serologic marker for dermatomyositis (DM). Its presence supports the diagnosis in patients with compatible clinical features such as proximal muscle weakness and characteristic cutaneous manifestations (e.g., Gottron papules, heliotrope rash). Anti-Mi-2 antibodies are most commonly detected in classic adult DM and are infrequently seen in polymyositis or other connective tissue diseases, enhancing their diagnostic utility. Clinically, Anti-Mi-2 positivity is associated with a more favorable prognosis, including good response to corticosteroids and immunosuppressive therapy, lower risk of interstitial lung disease, and reduced malignancy association compared with other myositis-specific antibodies. While titers are not routinely used for disease monitoring, results should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, muscle enzymes, imaging, and histopathology where indicated. name: Mitochondrial DNA Genome Sequencing (mtDNA)
instructions: Sample Types: Peripheral Blood in EDTA, Amniotic Fluid, Chorionic Villi
description: Mitochondrial DNA sequencing is a molecular diagnostic test that evaluates the entire mitochondrial genome or targeted regions to detect pathogenic variants associated with mitochondrial disorders. It is indicated in patients with unexplained multi-systemic presentations such as progressive myopathy, encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes, optic neuropathy, hearing loss, cardiomyopathy, or maternal inheritance patterns of disease. The test can identify point mutations, small insertions/deletions, and heteroplasmy (the proportion of mutant vs wild-type mtDNA), which is a critical factor influencing disease severity and penetrance. Results should be interpreted in the context of clinical presentation, biochemical findings (e.g., elevated lactate), and additional nuclear gene testing, since many mitochondrial disorders arise from nuclear-encoded genes that affect mitochondrial function. A positive result confirming a pathogenic mtDNA variant provides a definitive diagnosis, guides management, and enables genetic counseling regarding maternal transmission risk. Negative or inconclusive results do not exclude a mitochondrial disorder, and further nuclear DNA sequencing or functional studies may be warranted. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Mpox
instructions: The preferred specimen is skin lesion material. Gently clean the lesion with sterile saline, then vigorously swab vesicular, pustular, or ulcerative lesions using a synthetic fibre swab (Dacron/polyester/nylon) with a rigid plastic shaft. Where possible, collect from 2-3 lesions at different sites or stages. Vigorous swabbing may naturally unroof the lesion; do not intentionally unroof or incise lesions, and do not use scalpels, needles, or other sharp instruments. Do not use cotton or wooden-shafted swabs. An oropharyngeal (throat) swab may be collected as a supplementary specimen when skin lesions are absent or limited. Place the swab in a sterile, leak-proof, screw-cap tube (dry or in VTM/UTM as per laboratory protocol). Clearly label each specimen with at least two patient identifiers and ensure the details match the request form. Securely seal and transport using triple packaging (UN3373 - Biological Substance, Category B) at 2-8?C. For prolonged storage, store at -70?C and avoid repeated freeze-thaw cycles. IMPORTANT: Do not open the specimen container during accessioning or routine sample reception. Keep the specimen sealed and forward it directly to the designated testing area for processing under appropriate biosafety precautions.
description: This assay detects Monkeypox virus (MPXV) DNA by real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) from clinical specimens and is the preferred laboratory method for confirming suspected mpox infection. Skin lesion material (vesicle, pustule or crust/lesion swabs) is the specimen of choice and provides the highest diagnostic sensitivity. Oropharyngeal swabs may be submitted as supplementary specimens where clinically indicated but have lower sensitivity than lesion specimens. A positive result confirms the presence of MPXV DNA in the submitted specimen and should be interpreted in conjunction with the patients clinical presentation and epidemiological risk factors. A negative result does not completely exclude mpox, particularly if specimen collection is suboptimal, sampling is performed very early or late in the course of illness, or viral DNA is below the assays limit of detection. Appropriate infection prevention and public health measures should be followed in accordance with national guidelines. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: MRD Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) by Multiparametric Flow Cytometry
synonyms: AML MRD by Flow Cytometry;Minimal Residual Disease (MRD) AML; Measurable Residual Disease (MRD) AML; Residual AML Detection by Flow Cytometry; Post-treatment AML Flow Cytometry; Leukemia MRD Panel AML;
description: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) Minimal Residual Disease (MRD) by Multiparametric Flow Cytometry is a high-sensitivity assay used for detection and quantification of residual leukemic myeloid blasts following therapy in patients with AML. The assay utilizes advanced multicolor flow cytometry to identify aberrant leukemia-associated immunophenotypes (LAIP) and/or abnormal immature myeloid blast populations that differ from normal regenerating myeloid precursors using both leukemia-associated and different-from-normal analytical approaches. This test is primarily performed for post-induction, consolidation, maintenance, relapse assessment, and treatment response monitoring in AML. MRD status is a major independent prognostic marker and is widely used for risk stratification, evaluation of therapeutic response, transplant decision-making, and relapse prediction. Analytical sensitivity typically ranges from 10^4 to 10^5 depending on specimen quality, cellularity, and assay design. Fresh bone marrow aspirate is the preferred specimen. Concurrent review of prior diagnostic immunophenotyping, cytogenetic/molecular findings, and treatment history is strongly recommended for accurate interpretation.

The assay utilizes advanced multicolor flow cytometry to identify aberrant leukemia-associated immunophenotypes (LAIP) and/or abnormal immature T-cell populations that differ from normal thymic or regenerating T-cell precursors using both leukemia-associated and different-from-normal analytical approaches. This test is primarily performed for post-induction, consolidation, maintenance, relapse assessment, and treatment response monitoring in T-ALL. MRD status is a major independent prognostic marker and is widely used for risk stratification, evaluation of therapeutic response, transplant decision-making, and relapse prediction. Analytical sensitivity typically ranges from 10^4m to 10^5 depending on specimen quality, cellularity, and assay design. Fresh bone marrow aspirate is the preferred specimen. Concurrent review of prior diagnostic immunophenotyping and treatment history is strongly recommended for accurate interpretation.

name: MRD Mature B-Cell Neoplasm / CLL by Multiparametric Flow Cytometry
synonyms: Mature B-Cell Neoplasm MRD by Flow Cytometry; B-Cell Lymphoma MRD by Flow Cytometry; Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) MRD by Flow Cytometry; Minimal Residual Disease (MRD) Mature B-Cell Neoplasm; Measurable Residual Disease (MRD) B-Cell Lymphoma; Residual B-Cell Neoplasm Detection by Flow Cytometry; Post-treatment B-Cell Neoplasm Flow Cytometry;
description: Mature B-Cell Neoplasm Minimal Residual Disease (MRD) by Multiparametric Flow Cytometry is a high-sensitivity assay used for detection and quantification of residual clonal mature B-cell populations following therapy in patients with mature B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders including chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), mantle cell lymphoma, follicular lymphoma, hairy cell leukemia, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, and other mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas with peripheral blood and/or bone marrow involvement. The assay utilizes advanced multicolor flow cytometry to identify persistent abnormal B-cell populations based on aberrant antigen expression patterns and light-chain restriction. This test is primarily performed for post-treatment response assessment, remission monitoring, relapse detection, and therapeutic response evaluation in mature B-cell neoplasms. MRD assessment is increasingly used for prognostication, treatment stratification, evaluation of depth of remission, and monitoring response to targeted therapies and stem cell transplantation. Analytical sensitivity typically ranges from 10^4 to 10^5 depending on specimen quality, cellularity, and assay design. Bone marrow aspirate is generally preferred for highest sensitivity, although peripheral blood may be acceptable in selected disorders such as CLL. Concurrent review of prior diagnostic immunophenotyping, molecular/cytogenetic findings, and treatment history is strongly recommended for accurate interpretation.

name: MRD T-Lymphoblastic Leukemia (T-ALL) by Multiparametric Flow Cytometry
synonyms: T-ALL MRD by Flow Cytometry; Minimal Residual Disease (MRD) T-ALL; Measurable Residual Disease (MRD) T-ALL;Residual T-ALL Detection by Flow Cytometry; Post-treatment T-ALL Flow Cytometry; Leukemia MRD Panel T-ALL;
description: T-Lymphoblastic Leukemia / Lymphoma Minimal Residual Disease (MRD) by Multiparametric Flow Cytometry is a high-sensitivity assay used for detection and quantification of residual leukemic T-lymphoblasts following therapy in patients with T-acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL/LBL). The assay utilizes advanced multicolor flow cytometry to identify aberrant leukemia-associated immunophenotypes (LAIP) and/or abnormal immature T-cell populations that differ from normal thymic or regenerating T-cell precursors using both leukemia-associated and different-from-normal analytical approaches. This test is primarily performed for post-induction, consolidation, maintenance, relapse assessment, and treatment response monitoring in T-ALL. MRD status is a major independent prognostic marker and is widely used for risk stratification, evaluation of therapeutic response, transplant decision-making, and relapse prediction. Analytical sensitivity typically ranges from 10^4m to 10^5 depending on specimen quality, cellularity, and assay design. Fresh bone marrow aspirate is the preferred specimen. Concurrent review of prior diagnostic immunophenotyping and treatment history is strongly recommended for accurate interpretation

description: The Multiple Myeloma FISH Panel panel detects key cytogenetic abnormalities in plasma cell myeloma to support diagnosis, prognostic risk stratification, and treatment planning. It is performed on bone marrow aspirate (preferred) or plasma cell-enriched specimens and should be interpreted alongside morphology, flow cytometry, and serum/urine protein studies. Service parameters (targets) include 1q amplification/1p deletion, DLEU/12 centromere (13q deletion/trisomy 12), ATM deletion (11q deletion), TP53 deletion (17p deletion), IGH rearrangement, MYEOV::IGH t(11;14), FGFR3::IGH t(4;14), and MAF::IGH t(14;16). High-risk findings include del(17p)/TP53, t(4;14), t(14;16), and 1q gain/amplification, while t(11;14) may have therapeutic relevance. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Mumps IgG Antibodies (Serum)
description: The Mumps IgG test quantitatively detects IgG antibodies against the mumps virus in serum or plasma, helping assess immunity or past infection. Mumps is a contagious viral disease caused by the Rubulavirus, transmitted via respiratory droplets, with peak infectivity occurring about 48 hours before symptom onset. It primarily causes parotid gland swelling but may also present with mild respiratory symptoms or be asymptomatic. IgG antibodies typically appear 7-10 days after infection and persist for years, providing lifelong immunity. When interpreted alongside IgM results, the test helps distinguish between primary infection, past infection, or susceptibility.

name: Mumps IgM Antibodies
description: The Mumps IgM test detects recent mumps infection by identifying IgM antibodies in serum or plasma. Mumps, caused by the Rubulavirus, spreads via respiratory droplets and often causes parotid gland swelling, though many cases are mild or asymptomatic. IgM antibodies appear 3-4 days after symptoms, peak within a week, and persist for up to 12 weeks, while IgG antibodies develop later and confer lifelong immunity. Diagnosis is confirmed by detecting IgM or a rise in IgG titers, especially in atypical or vaccinated cases.

name: Muscle Biopsy Electron Microscopy

description: Electron microscopy (EM) of skeletal muscle biopsy is a specialised ultrastructural examination performed to evaluate muscle fibres, neuromuscular junctions and associated cellular organelles at high magnification. It provides detailed assessment of sarcomere architecture, mitochondria, glycogen, lipid droplets, lysosomes, autophagic vacuoles, myofibrils, nuclei and basement membranes, and can identify characteristic ultrastructural abnormalities not visible on routine light microscopy. EM is particularly valuable in the diagnosis and classification of mitochondrial myopathies, congenital myopathies, myofibrillar myopathies, inclusion body myositis, storage disorders, vacuolar myopathies and selected muscular dystrophies. It is performed as an adjunct to routine histology, histochemistry, immunohistochemistry and molecular genetic testing to provide comprehensive clinicopathological correlation. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Myelin-Associated Glycoprotein (MAG) Antibody
synonyms: Anti-MAG Antibody IgM;Anti-Myelin Associated Glycoprotein Antibody;Anti-MAG Neuropathy Antibody;
description: This assay detects IgM autoantibodies directed against myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG), a component of peripheral nerve myelin involved in Schwann cell-axon interactions and maintenance of myelin integrity. Anti-MAG antibodies are associated with autoimmune demyelinating peripheral neuropathies, particularly distal acquired demyelinating symmetric neuropathy (DADS) and IgM paraproteinaemic neuropathy, commonly occurring in association with monoclonal IgM gammopathies such as IgM MGUS or Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia. The test is useful in the diagnostic evaluation of patients with chronic slowly progressive sensory or sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy, sensory ataxia, tremor, or demyelinating neuropathy identified on nerve conduction studies. Testing is typically performed using ELISA or immunoblot-based methodologies. Results should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, electrophysiologic studies, serum protein electrophoresis/immunofixation, serum free light chain analysis, and other relevant neurologic and haematologic investigations

name: MYO (Myoglobin)
description: Myoglobin is a small oxygen-binding protein (17.8 kDa) found in cardiac and skeletal muscle, measured in serum or plasma to aid in the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction (AMI). It is rapidly released into the bloodstream within ~2 hours of myocardial injury and peaks within 3 hours, especially after reperfusion therapy. Because of its quick rise and elimination (via kidneys within 24 hours), it serves as an early but non-specific marker for myocardial damage. Elevated levels can also result from skeletal muscle injury or renal impairment.

description: Urine myoglobin is a test used to detect myoglobin released into the urine following skeletal muscle injury, most commonly in suspected rhabdomyolysis. It is performed on a fresh urine sample using an immunoassay method. Clinically, it is indicated in patients with dark urine, muscle injury, or unexplained acute kidney injury, especially when urine dipstick is positive for blood but microscopy shows few or no red blood cells. A positive result supports muscle breakdown and signals risk of myoglobin-induced acute kidney injury. Interpretation should be correlated with serum creatine kinase, myoglobin in blood and renal function. Because myoglobin is rapidly cleared and unstable, early sample collection and prompt analysis are essential to avoid false-negative results. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: The EGFR gene mutation test detects presence of specific genetic mutations in non-small cell lung cancer tumor cells that are in turn useful in determining whether the cancer can be treated with EGFR-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as gefitinib and erlotinib. The EGFR mutations are commonly seen in lung adenocarcinomas, and less frequently in adenosquamous carcinoma but are extremely rare in squamous cell carcinoma. Some mutations in EGFR, such as the L858R mutation and exon 19 deletion, have been shown to be predictive of response to EGFR-directed tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) in patients with non-small cell lung cancer. Other EGFR mutations, such as T790M and exon 20 insertion, are associated with resistance to EGFR TKIs. For testing on tissue biopsy, histologic section of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue is examined by a pathologist to confirm presence of tumor then DNA is extracted analysis of the EGFR mutations. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: NGS KRAS Mutation Analysis
synonyms: KRAS mutation analysis by next-generation sequencing; Genetic Test NGS KRAS; KRAS NGS; KRAS Mutation – Colorectal Cancer; KRAS Mutation – Solid Tumour
instructions: Submit a representative FFPE tumour block containing adequate viable tumour or appropriately prepared unstained sections from the tumour block. A corresponding H&E-stained slide and histopathology report should be provided where available to support assessment of tumour adequacy and selection of the appropriate tumour-rich area for testing. Specimens with extensive necrosis, very low tumour cellularity, insufficient tissue or significantly degraded DNA may be unsuitable for analysis or may require repeat sampling.
description: KRAS mutation analysis by next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a targeted molecular test for detection of clinically significant somatic variants in the KRAS gene from tumour tissue. KRAS is an important oncogenic driver in several solid tumours, particularly colorectal cancer, and mutation status may provide predictive and therapeutic information. In colorectal cancer, activating KRAS mutations are associated with lack of benefit from anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody therapy such as cetuximab and panitumumab. NGS provides broader sequence interrogation than conventional targeted PCR assays and may detect a wider spectrum of KRAS variants within the regions covered by the validated assay. Results should be interpreted together with the tumour type, histopathological findings and clinical context. A negative result indicates that no clinically relevant KRAS variant was detected within the analytical scope of the assay and does not exclude alterations outside the regions tested. Where comprehensive RAS or broader tumour profiling is required, extended KRAS/NRAS/HRAS/BRAF pathway testing or a multigene solid-tumour NGS panel may be more appropriate. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

Where possible, the specimen should contain adequate viable tumour for molecular analysis. A corresponding H&E-stained slide and histopathology report should accompany the specimen where available. Tumour-rich areas may be selected or macrodissected where required to optimise tumour content.
description: The NGS KRAS/NRAS/HRAS/BRAF/PIK3CA/TP53 Extended 6-Gene Panel is a targeted next-generation sequencing assay for detection of clinically relevant somatic mutations in KRAS, NRAS, HRAS, BRAF, PIK3CA and TP53 in solid tumours. The panel evaluates key molecular alterations involving the RAS/MAPK and PI3K signalling pathways together with TP53 tumour-suppressor abnormalities, which may have diagnostic, prognostic, predictive or therapeutic significance depending on the tumour type and clinical context. The assay is particularly useful in the molecular characterisation of colorectal carcinoma, including extended RAS and BRAF assessment, and may also be applicable to other solid tumours such as lung, pancreatic, thyroid and endometrial carcinomas, melanoma, and other malignancies in which alterations involving these genes may influence targeted therapy selection, treatment response, resistance profiling or tumour classification. The assay primarily detects single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and small insertions/deletions (indels) within the targeted genomic regions analysed. Results should be interpreted together with the histopathological diagnosis, tumour type, tumour cellularity, clinical context and other relevant molecular or immunohistochemical findings. This is a focused six-gene targeted panel and does not constitute comprehensive genomic profiling. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: The RAS/RAF Extended NGS Panel is a focused targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) assay for detection of clinically significant somatic mutations in selected solid tumors using formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissue. The assay specifically evaluates hotspot regions and coding sequences within six clinically important cancer-associated genes: KRAS, NRAS, HRAS, BRAF, PIK3CA, and TP53. This panel is primarily designed to assess alterations involving the RAS/MAPK signaling pathway together with selected PI3K pathway and tumor suppressor genes relevant to oncogenesis, prognosis, targeted therapy selection, resistance profiling, and eligibility for precision oncology protocols. The assay detects single nucleotide variants (SNVs), small insertions/deletions (indels), and selected copy number alterations where technically feasible using massively parallel sequencing technology. Clinically relevant applications include molecular characterization of colorectal carcinoma, endometrial carcinoma, lung carcinoma, melanoma, thyroid carcinoma, pancreatic carcinoma, and other solid tumors in which RAS/RAF pathway alterations may influence therapeutic decision-making. Results should be interpreted in conjunction with histopathological findings, tumor type, clinical context, and other relevant molecular or immunohistochemical studies. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Nickel (Serum)
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Nickel (Serum) and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: The serum nickel test measures the concentration of nickel circulating in the bloodstream, providing an indication of recent or ongoing systemic exposure. It is typically requested when significant acute exposure is suspected, such as in industrial accidents, ingestion of nickel-containing substances, or complications from nickel-containing implants or prosthetic devices. Unlike urine testing, serum nickel reflects circulating levels at the time of sampling but does not directly correlate with total body burden. Reference values vary, and interpretation should consider local reference ranges, exposure history, and clinical presentation. Elevated serum nickel may be associated with systemic symptoms like allergic reactions, respiratory issues, gastrointestinal irritation, or in rare cases, systemic toxicity. Persistently elevated serum levels suggest ongoing exposure or accumulation, particularly from internal sources like implants. The test is not routinely used for occupational monitoring but may aid in acute exposure assessment or medical device surveillance. No specific patient preparation is required before sample collection. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Nickel (Urine)

description: The urine nickel test assesses recent exposure to nickel by measuring its concentration in urine, typically reflecting exposure over the past few days. It is primarily used in evaluating occupational or environmental exposure, particularly in individuals working in industries like electroplating, welding, battery production, or mining. Results from spot urine samples should ideally be corrected for creatinine to account for urine concentration variability, while 24-hour urine collections may offer greater accuracy in certain situations. Interpretation requires correlation with exposure history and clinical findings, as mild elevations can also occur due to dietary sources or nickel-containing medical devices. Clinically, elevated urine nickel levels should be assessed alongside potential symptoms such as dermatitis, respiratory irritation, or systemic toxicity in significant exposures. Persistently high levels warrant investigation for ongoing exposure and may require referral to occupational health or toxicology specialists. Reference intervals differ across laboratories, and results should be interpreted within the appropriate regulatory and clinical context. No special patient preparation is needed prior to testing. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: Non-invasive prenatal screening test performed on maternal peripheral blood cell-free fetal DNA for selected recurrent fetal chromosomal microdeletion syndromes. Whole blood from the mother, which contains fragments of DNA from the fetus, can be collected as early as 10 weeks into the pregnancy, and is used to analyze for these specific congenital disorders. The most common sex chromosome conditions are Turner syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome, Triple X syndrome and XYY syndrome. NIPT S test screens for: Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Trisomy 18, Trisomy 13, Disorders affecting sex chromosomes (X and Y) and any disorders in other chromosomes. description: N-MYC (MYCN) amplification analysis by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is performed for prognostic risk stratification in neuroblastoma. The assay uses dual-color probes targeting the MYCN locus at chromosome 2p24 and a chromosome 2 reference probe, allowing assessment of MYCN gene copy number relative to chromosome 2 in interphase tumor nuclei from FFPE tissue or cytology specimens with adequate tumor cellularity. MYCN amplification is defined by a marked increase in MYCN signals relative to the chromosome 2 control (or the presence of MYCN signal clusters) and is a well-established adverse prognostic marker, associated with aggressive tumor biology and high-risk disease irrespective of age or stage. The result directly informs treatment intensity and clinical risk group assignment. Findings should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical stage, histology, DNA ploidy, and other genomic abnormalities (e.g., segmental chromosomal aberrations). This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: Non-switched memory B-cell testing quantifies memory B cells that retain IgM and/or IgD expression as part of detailed B-cell immunophenotyping. description: NPM1 Gene Mutation Quantitative PCR (qPCR) is a sensitive molecular test used to detect and quantify NPM1 gene mutations, most commonly seen in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). These mutations, typically involving exon 12 insertions, occur in about 30?35% of adult AML and define a biologically and prognostically distinct subgroup. The assay is mutation-specific and can detect very low levels of mutated transcripts, with analytical sensitivity reaching 10?4 to 10?5. The test is primarily used for measurable residual disease (MRD) monitoring. Serial measurement of NPM1-mutated transcript levels allows assessment of treatment response and early detection of molecular relapse, often before clinical or hematologic recurrence. Persistent or rising transcript levels are associated with increased relapse risk, while deep molecular remission correlates with favorable prognosis. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: Anti-nRNP antibodies target components of the U1 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP) complex involved in RNA splicing. These autoantibodies are frequently associated with mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) and may also be seen in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis. Detection of Anti-nRNP is useful in diagnosing and classifying connective tissue diseases, especially when clinical features overlap. In MCTD, high titers of Anti-U1 RNP are a defining serological hallmark and aid in distinguishing it from other autoimmune disorders. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: NTRK gene fusion analysis by RNA-based next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a high-sensitivity, definitive molecular assay for the detection of oncogenic fusions involving NTRK1, NTRK2, and NTRK3. These gene rearrangements result in constitutive activation of TRK signaling pathways and are actionable biomarkers predictive of response to targeted TRK inhibitors such as Larotrectinib and Entrectinib. RNA-based platforms are preferred as they directly detect expressed fusion transcripts, enabling identification of both known and novel fusion partners with high analytical sensitivity. This assay is indicated for patients with advanced or metastatic solid tumors where identification of targetable alterations may impact therapeutic decision-making, particularly in tumors enriched for NTRK fusions or those negative for other common driver mutations. Results should be interpreted in conjunction with histopathological and clinical findings. In cases with prior positive Pan-TRK IHC screening, this test serves as confirmatory molecular validation, while a negative result effectively excludes clinically significant NTRK fusions within the assays detection limits. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: The Oncotype DX® Breast Recurrence Score is a quantitative RT-PCR-based genomic assay performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissue from patients with early-stage, estrogen receptor (ER)-positive, HER2-negative invasive breast carcinoma. The test analyzes the expression of 21 genes (16 cancer-related genes and 5 reference genes) to generate a Recurrence Score® result ranging from 0-100. This score provides prognostic information regarding the risk of distant recurrence at 9-10 years and predicts the potential benefit of adjuvant chemotherapy when added to endocrine therapy. The assay is performed at a centralized reference laboratory (Exact Sciences) and requires submission of tumor tissue block with a completed requisition form. Results are reported as a numeric Recurrence Score with interpretive categories and clinical guidance based on established clinical trial validation studies (e.g., TAILORx). This test is intended for use in appropriately selected patients as part of multidisciplinary treatment planning. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: Urine Organic Acids analysis is used to detect abnormal excretion of organic acids, which may indicate underlying inborn errors of metabolism. It is particularly useful in the evaluation of unexplained metabolic acidosis, developmental delay, or suspected metabolic disorders. This test aids in the diagnosis of a wide range of inherited metabolic conditions affecting amino acid, carbohydrate, and fatty acid metabolism. description: Dried-blood-spot newborn screening for Ornithine Transcarbamylase Deficiency evaluates decreased citrulline to identify infants at increased risk of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, an X-linked urea-cycle disorder that can cause hyperammonaemia; low citrulline is not specific and requires urgent confirmatory testing. name: Orotic Acid, Urine
instructions: Collect 15-20 mL of a random urine sample in a sterile, preservative-free container; first morning or timed collections may be used if clinically indicated. Keep refrigerated if transport is delayed, and samples should be transported refrigerated (preferred). Avoid contaminated specimens. Indicate relevant clinical details, such as hyperammonemia or suspected urea cycle disorder, to assist interpretation.
description: The urinary orotic acid test measures levels of orotic acid, a byproduct of pyrimidine metabolism, to aid in the evaluation of urea cycle disorders-particularly ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency-as well as certain metabolic conditions like hereditary orotic aciduria. Elevated orotic acid in the presence of hyperammonemia suggests OTC deficiency, while persistent elevation without hyperammonemia may indicate defects in pyrimidine synthesis. The test is typically performed via quantitative mass spectrometry on a random or timed urine sample. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Osmolality (Urine)

These conditions apply to urine organic acids, orotic acid, and urine osmolality testing. Clinical history should be provided to support interpretation, particularly for suspected metabolic disorders, renal concentrating defects, or polyuria-related conditions. Early or symptomatic collection may improve diagnostic yield where applicable.
description: Urine Osmolality measures the concentration of solutes in urine and reflects the kidneys ability to concentrate or dilute urine. name: Oxalate (24 Hrs Urine)
instructions: Collect urine over 24 hours in a clean container pre-supplied with 10 mL of 6N HCl as preservative (do not discard). Discard the first morning urine, then collect all urine for the next 24 hours including the following mornings first sample. Keep the container tightly closed and refrigerated or in a cool place during the collection. Avoid spilling the acid and handle the container carefully; do not void directly into the container. Maintain adequate hydration and avoid high-oxalate foods (e.g., spinach, nuts, tea, chocolate) for at least 48 hours before and during collection unless otherwise advised.
description: This test measures the total oxalate excretion in a 24-hour urine sample. Elevated levels may indicate primary or secondary hyperoxaluria, malabsorption syndromes, or increased risk of calcium oxalate kidney stones. It is particularly useful in the metabolic evaluation of patients with recurrent nephrolithiasis. Monitoring urinary oxalate can guide dietary modification and therapeutic interventions, and helps in assessing the effectiveness of stone-prevention strategies. Results should be interpreted alongside other metabolic urine parameters. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: Random urine oxalate measures oxalate excretion in a spot urine specimen and can support evaluation of hyperoxaluria or kidney-stone risk. Interpretation is strengthened by urine creatinine, dietary history and, when indicated, a 24-hour urine oxalate measurement.

name: Oxcarbazepine (Trileptal)

description: Oxcarbazepine is an anticonvulsant used in the management of seizure disorders, and its therapeutic monitoring is performed by measuring the serum concentration of its active metabolite, 10-monohydroxy derivative (MHD). The usual therapeutic range for MHD is approximately 10?35 mcg/mL, though this may vary depending on the laboratory reference values. Measurement of MHD levels is clinically useful to evaluate medication adherence, adequacy of dosing, and risk of toxicity. Sub-therapeutic levels may explain breakthrough seizures or inadequate seizure control, whereas supra-therapeutic levels can be associated with adverse central nervous system effects such as dizziness, drowsiness, diplopia, and ataxia, as well as systemic complications like hyponatremia. Interpretation of the oxcarbazepine/MHD level should therefore be integrated with the patients clinical status, seizure frequency, reported side effects, and potential drug interactions. Dose adjustments or other therapeutic decisions should be guided by both the laboratory result and the overall clinical context. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: p53 Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
description: p53 Immunohistochemistry (IHC) acts as a rapid surrogate for TP53 dysfunction in tumors from suspected Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) cases (germline TP53 pathogenic variants). In LFS-associated tumors (e.g., early-onset breast cancer, sarcomas, brain tumors, adrenocortical carcinoma), aberrant patterns-strong diffuse nuclear overexpression (>50-80% intense positivity, common with missense variants stabilizing mutant protein) or complete null/absent staining (<1% positivity, typical of truncating/non-missense variants)-strongly suggest TP53 alteration and warrant germline TP53 testing, especially in young patients with LFS-spectrum cancers or family history. A normal/wild-type pattern (scattered weak-moderate nuclear staining in few cells) does not exclude LFS. p53 IHC is not diagnostic of germline status - germline confirmation requires blood-based genetic testing - but aberrant results provide a quick, cost-effective trigger for genetic counseling and surveillance in confirmed carriers.

description: This test is used for quantitative determination of IgG antibodies directed against myeloperoxidase,a protein produced by white blood cells.It is used in conjuction with other tests for diagnosis of autoimmune vasculitis.A positive p-anca may also be associated with inflammatory bowel disease.This test is perfomed using chemiluminescent(chLIA) under IDS-ISYS platform. The MPO test quantitatively detect IgG antibodies against myeloperoxidase (MPO) in human serum or plasma, aiding in the evaluation of ANCA-associated vasculitides (AAVs), especially microscopic polyangiitis (MPA). MPO, along with proteinase 3 (PR3), is a primary antigen target of antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), which are key markers for necrotizing vasculitides such as Wegener s granulomatosis (WG), MPA, pauci-immune necrotizing glomerulonephritis (PING), and Churg-Strauss syndrome (CSS). MPO-ANCA is typically associated with a p-ANCA fluorescence pattern and is more common in MPA and PING, while PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) is linked to WG. ANCA titers often correlate with disease activity, making this test useful for both diagnosis and monitoring.

description: Pan-TRK immunohistochemistry using the EPR17341 detects expression of TRK proteins (TRKA, TRKB, TRKC) encoded by NTRK1, NTRK2, and NTRK3. It serves as a screening assay for tumors harboring oncogenic NTRK gene fusions, which are actionable alterations associated with response to targeted TRK inhibitors such as Larotrectinib and Entrectinib. The test is particularly useful in selected tumor types including secretory carcinomas, pediatric sarcomas, and other malignancies where NTRK fusions are enriched or therapeutically relevant. Interpretation is based on staining pattern and intensity (cytoplasmic and/or nuclear), and results should be correlated with tumor morphology and clinical context. While sensitive, Pan-TRK IHC is not specific for NTRK gene fusions, as physiologic TRK expression may be seen in neural and smooth muscle tissues. Therefore, positive or equivocal results require confirmatory molecular testing, preferably with RNA-based next-generation sequencing for definitive detection of NTRK fusions. description: Serum IgG autoantibody profile for investigation of suspected paraneoplastic neurological syndromes (PNS), including paraneoplastic encephalitis. The panel detects six classical intracellular/onconeural antibodies: Amphiphysin, CV2.1/CRMP5, PNMA2 (Ma2/Ta), ANNA-1/Hu, ANNA-2/Ri and PCA-1/Yo. Paraneoplastic encephalitis is an immune-mediated neurological syndrome occurring in association with an underlying malignancy, in which the neurological presentation may precede detection of the cancer. It is typically associated with antibodies directed against intracellular neuronal antigens and is therefore diagnostically and biologically distinct from the more common neuronal surface/synaptic antibody-mediated autoimmune encephalitides. This panel should therefore not be used interchangeably with the Autoimmune Encephalitis Panel, which detects antibodies such as NMDA-R, AMPA-R, GABA-B-R, LGI1 and CASPR2. Those antibodies are directed predominantly against neuronal surface or synaptic targets and may occur with or without an associated malignancy. A positive result should be interpreted with the neurological phenotype and should prompt appropriate investigation for an underlying malignancy. A negative result does not exclude paraneoplastic encephalitis/PNS or antibodies not represented in this six-antigen panel. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Parathyroid Hormone Intact (PTH)
instructions: EDTA plasma sample is preferred as PTH is stable for >24 hours at room temperature in whole blood anticoagulated with EDTA. Serum collected using standard sampling tube (SST) should be centrifuged immediately because of instability of PTH in unseparated serum, and the sample should be kept at 2-8 degrees when transported to the lab within 2 days of collection.
description: ;; The Parathyroid Hormone Intact (PTH) test measures the level of parathyroid hormone in the blood to assess how well the parathyroid glands are functioning. PTH plays a key role in regulating calcium, phosphorus, and vitamin D levels in the body. This test is often ordered to help diagnose the cause of abnormal calcium levels. Low parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels typically suggest hypoparathyroidism, a condition where the parathyroid glands produce too little hormone. This can lead to low blood calcium levels, causing symptoms like muscle cramps, tingling, or even seizures. It may result from autoimmune disease, neck surgery, or certain genetic conditions. On the other hand, high PTH levels often indicate hyperparathyroidism, where one or more parathyroid glands produce too much hormone. This can lead to high calcium levels in the blood and symptoms such as bone pain, kidney stones, fatigue, and abdominal discomfort. Elevated PTH can also occur in response to low calcium or vitamin D levels, especially in chronic kidney disease. The test provides valuable information about bone metabolism and overall mineral balance. Quantitative determination of PTH in serum in the evaluation of Chronic Kidney disease- Mineral Bone disorder (CKD -MBD), Calcium and phosphate disorders and primary Parathyroid disease.

description: Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunohistochemistry test is used for identification of neoplasms expressing programmed cell death- ligand 1 (PD-L1). PD-L1 is an immune-related biomarker that can be expressed on the surface of many tissue types, including tumor cells. For certain types and stages of cancer, testing for PD-L1 expression may help to identify patients most likely to benefit from treatment with PD-1 inhibitors. Novel immunotherapies, known as immune checkpoint inhibitors, can interrupt signals generated by immune checkpoint proteins, such as PD-L1, and can enhance antitumor T-cell immunity. Several immune checkpoint inhibitors, including pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab, and others, have been approved for a number of clinical indications and are being evaluated in multiple malignancies. The FDA divides PD-L1 immunohistochemistry (IHC) tests into two groups: companion diagnostic tests, which provide information that is essential for the safe and effective use of a drug (test results are required for drug use), and complementary or codiagnostic tests, which may be used in treatment selection but are not considered essential for use of the corresponding therapy (test results are NOT required for drug use)
