instructions: General instructions Preferred start collection time is morning. Collect in detergent?free container. Acidify with hydrochloric acid after collection to a pH of less than 3 Empty the bladder first thing in the morning or at the start time and discard this urine. Note the time as this is the start time of the 24 hours. For example 6:00 am Collect every drop of urine voided over the next 24 hours (i.e. upto the next morning e.g. 6:am on a Tuesday to 6:00 am Wednesday). Should one need to defecate and urinate at the same time, this urine should also be collected. Try as much as possible not to contaminate the urine with faeces. Keep the urine cold either on ice or refigerated. Stop time should be within 20 minutes of the start time the day before. E.g. if start time was 6:00 am Tuesday, stop time is between 5:50 am and 6:10 am during which time any urine passed must be collected. FOR SUBMITTING LABORATORIES /HOSPITALS If submitting an aliquot of the 24 hour urine, note the volume of 24 hour urine submited. Mix the sample well to a homogenous mixture and aliquote into a clean container. Submit the aliquot with clear documentation of the duration of collection

description: Verdana; ;; "Phosphate testing helps diagnose and monitor phosphate imbalances such as hyperphosphatemia and hypophosphatemia in serum, plasma, or urine. About 85% of phosphate in the body is stored in the bones, while only a tiny amount is found in the blood. Phosphate levels are closely linked with calcium balance, and are regulated by the kidneys, intestines, and hormones like parathyroid hormone (PTH) and vitamin D. High phosphate levels (hyperphosphatemia) may result from kidney failure, hypoparathyroidism, or excess vitamin D. Low levels (hypophosphatemia) can be caused by poor intake, malabsorption, excessive urine loss, or conditions like rickets, hyperparathyroidism, or Fanconi syndrome. This test specifically measures inorganic phosphate, the active form in blood.."

description: This assay detects clinically significant mutations in the PIK3CA gene (Phosphatidylinositol-4,5-Bisphosphate 3-Kinase Catalytic Subunit Alpha) using targeted Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) technology on DNA extracted from tumour tissue or other validated specimen types. The test interrogates key hotspot regions and coding exons of the PIK3CA gene associated with oncogenic activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling pathway. Common actionable mutations include variants involving codons E542K, E545K, Q546K, H1047R, and H1047L, among others. PIK3CA mutations are encountered in multiple solid tumours including breast carcinoma, colorectal carcinoma, endometrial carcinoma, cervical carcinoma, ovarian carcinoma, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, and other malignancies. Detection of a PIK3CA mutation may provide diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive therapeutic information, including potential eligibility for targeted therapies such as PI3K inhibitors where clinically indicated. Results should be interpreted in conjunction with tumour histology, clinical findings, radiologic features, and other molecular or cytogenetic investigations. This assay is intended for clinical diagnostic use and does not exclude the presence of mutations outside the regions analysed. instructions: Submit representative tumour tissue (usually an FFPE block or approved alternative) with the histological diagnosis and estimated tumour content. description: POLD1 Gene Mutation Test; POLD1 NGS Analysis; DNA Polymerase Delta 1 Mutation Analysis; POLD1 Exonuclease Domain Mutation Analysis; POLD1 Single Gene NGS Assay LIS Test Description: POLD1 Mutation Analysis by Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) is a targeted solid tumour molecular assay designed to detect clinically significant pathogenic variants in the POLD1 (DNA polymerase delta 1 catalytic subunit) gene, particularly within the exonuclease proofreading domain. The assay is performed as a focused single-gene NGS test on DNA extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumour tissue or other validated solid tumour specimens. Pathogenic POLD1 mutations are associated with defective DNA proofreading and genomic hypermutation, contributing to tumourigenesis in selected solid tumours including colorectal, endometrial, and other malignancies. Alterations in POLD1 may be associated with elevated tumour mutational burden and may have potential prognostic and predictive significance, including possible relevance to immune checkpoint inhibitor responsiveness in selected clinical contexts. Germline POLD1 mutations are additionally associated with hereditary polymerase proofreading-associated cancer predisposition syndromes. Results should be interpreted in conjunction with histopathology, clinical findings, family history, MMR/MSI status, and other relevant molecular and genomic studies. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

instructions: Submit representative tumour tissue (usually an FFPE block or approved alternative) with the histological diagnosis and estimated tumour content. description: POLE Mutation Analysis by Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) is a molecular assay designed to detect clinically significant pathogenic variants in the POLE (DNA polymerase epsilon catalytic subunit) gene, particularly within the exonuclease proofreading domain. Mutations in POLE are associated with an ultramutated tumour phenotype characterized by exceptionally high tumour mutational burden and increased neoantigen formation. The test is primarily utilized in the molecular classification and prognostic stratification of endometrial carcinoma and may also have relevance in selected colorectal and other solid tumours. Identification of pathogenic POLE mutations is clinically important as POLE-mutated tumours often demonstrate favourable prognosis despite high-grade histologic features and may influence risk stratification, adjuvant treatment decisions, and eligibility for immunotherapy-based approaches in selected clinical contexts. Results should be interpreted together with histopathology, mismatch repair (MMR/MSI) status, p53 status, clinical findings, and other relevant molecular studies. description: Porphobilinogen (PBG) urine test measures the amount of PBG, a porphyrin precursor, in a urine sample to help diagnose or monitor conditions like acute porphyrias, particularly acute intermittent porphyria (AIP). PBG is a porphyrin precursor, a substance involved in the synthesis of heme, a component of hemoglobin in red blood cells. Porphyrins are normally found in small amounts in the body and are excreted through urine or stool. Elevated levels of PBG in urine can be a sign of a porphyria, a group of inherited or acquired disorders that affect the body's ability to produce heme. A positive qualitative test result should be confirmed by quantitative PBG test in 24-hour urine. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

instructions: Instructions for collection: Preferred start collection time is morning. Collect 24?hour urine without additives. Empty the bladder first thing in the morning or at the start time and discard this urine. Note the time as this is the start time of the 24 hours. For example 6:00 am Collect every drop of urine voided over the next 24 hours (i.e. upto the next morning e.g. 6:am on a Tuesday to 6:00 am Wednesday). Should one need to defecate and urinate at the same time, this urine should also be collected. Try as much as possible not to contaminate the urine with faeces. Keep the urine cold either on ice or refigerated. Stop time should be within 20 minutes of the start time the day before. E.g. if start time was 6:00 am Tuesday, stop time is between 5:50 am and 6:10 am Wednesday, during which time any urine passed must be collected. FOR SUBMITTING LABORATORIES /HOSPITALS If submitting an aliquot of the 24 hour urine, note the volume of 24 hour urine submited. Mix the sample well to a homogenous mixture and aliquote into a clean container. Submit the aliquot with clear documentation of the duration of collection and the volume of the 24 hour urine. description: Potassium is the primary intracellular cation essential for nerve and muscle function. description: This test provides definitive prenatal diagnosis of sickle cell disease through DNA-based analysis of the HBB (ß-globin) gene performed on amniotic fluid obtained at approximately 15-16 weeks gestation. Testing is performed using validated PCR-based methods and/or sequencing, with high analytical sensitivity and specificity (>99%). This test is diagnostic (not screening) and is primarily indicated in pregnancies where both parents are known carriers (HbAS) or where there is a family history of sickle cell disease. Results should be interpreted in conjunction with parental genotypes and clinical context. Testing is performed through an accredited partner reference laboratory, as this is a specialized assay not currently offered in-house. Clinically, this test is valuable in assessing ovulation, luteal phase adequacy, and progesterone-related disorders such as infertility or ectopic pregnancy. Elevated levels are expected in the luteal phase and throughout pregnancy, while low levels may suggest ovulatory dysfunction or luteal phase defects.

description: Red Blood Cell (RBC) Antibody Identification Panel or Monospecific DAT is a confirmatory immunohematology test used to identify and characterize unexpected red cell alloantibodies detected following a positive antibody screening test. Patient plasma or serum is tested against a panel of reagent red cells with known antigen profiles using the Indirect Antiglobulin Test (IAT) (gel card, column agglutination, or tube method). The reaction pattern allows identification of specific clinically significant antibodies such as Anti-D, Anti-C, Anti-E, Anti-c, Anti-K, Anti-Fya, or Anti-Jka, and detection of multiple antibodies where present. The test is essential for safe transfusion practice, antenatal care, and investigation of transfusion reactions. Identified clinically significant antibodies guide the selection of antigen-negative, crossmatch-compatible blood units and help prevent hemolytic transfusion reactions and hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN). Results are reported with antibody specificity, autocontrol status, and interpretive comments, and the antibody history should be permanently recorded in the patients transfusion record. description: Rhesus (Rh) antibody titre testing is performed to detect and quantify maternal alloantibodies, particularly anti-D antibodies, in Rh-negative pregnant women. This test helps assess the risk of hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN). A rising titre, especially above a critical threshold (commonly 1:16 or 1:32 depending on the laboratory), indicates increased risk of fetal hemolysis and necessitates closer monitoring, including ultrasound for signs of fetal anemia and possible referral for middle cerebral artery Doppler studies or intrauterine transfusion. Clinicians should order Rh antibody titres early in pregnancy for all Rh-negative women and repeat at intervals if antibodies are detected. It is essential to differentiate passive anti-D from prophylactic Rh immunoglobulin (RhIg) administration versus active immunization due to sensitization. Documentation of antibody specificity and monitoring of titre trends is vital for management decisions. name: Salivary Cortisol (Late Night Sample)
description: The salivary cortisol is measured using the Elecsys Cortisol II assay on the Roche cobas e801 platform, employing a competitive electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA). This method quantifies free (biologically active) cortisol in saliva, which correlates closely with the unbound serum fraction and is independent of cortisol-binding globulin. Salivary sampling is non-invasive and particularly suited for assessing circadian cortisol rhythm, with late-night salivary cortisol serving as a sensitive screening test for hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome). Interpretation is time-dependent and must consider collection timing and pre-analytical factors. Late-night values (23:00-24:00) are expected to be low (<6-7 nmol/L), while morning values (06:00-08:00) are highest (10 - 25 nmol/L) whereby abnormal elevation suggests loss of normal diurnal suppression. Results may be affected by blood contamination (e.g. gum bleeding), recent food intake, stress, or exogenous steroid exposure. Correlation with clinical findings and, where indicated, confirmatory testing (e.g. dexamethasone suppression test or 24-hour urinary free cortisol) is recommended.

instructions: Timing: Collect saliva at specific times depending on indication: late-night (23:00-24:00) for Cushing s screening, or morning/evening for diurnal rhythm assessment. Exact timing must be recorded on the sample. Preparation: Patients should avoid food, drinks (except water), smoking, chewing gum, or brushing teeth for at least 30 minutes before collection. Rinse mouth with water 10 minutes prior. Avoid gingival bleeding to prevent contamination. Collection: Use a salivette with a synthetic swab or direct drooling into the tube. For swabs, hold in the mouth for 1-2 minutes without chewing. Ensure a minimum of 0.5 mL saliva. Labelling and Storage: Label with patient ID, date, and collection time. Store samples at 2-8 \'b0C if delivered within 24 hours, otherwise freeze at -20 \'b0C. Repeated freeze-thaw cycles should be avoided. Transport: Send samples promptly to the lab, ideally within 24-48 hours, and keep cool during transport if delays occur.
description: Salivary cortisol provides a convenient, non-invasive measure of free cortisol, reflecting the biologically active fraction that diffuses into saliva independent of salivary flow rate. It is particularly useful for assessing diurnal rhythm and late-night cortisol levels in the evaluation of suspected Cushing syndrome, as well as for monitoring adrenal suppression or insufficiency. The Roche Elecsys assay employs an electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA) principle with high sensitivity and specificity for cortisol. It is validated for use on salivary samples, minimizing issues of cross-reactivity and interference seen in some earlier immunoassays. Pre-analytical handling remains critical-samples should be collected using synthetic swabs or direct expectoration, ideally at defined times (e.g., late-night 23:00-24:00 for Cushing s screening, or upon waking for diurnal rhythm studies), avoiding contamination from food, beverages, or dental products. Reference intervals are assay-specific and time-dependent. For late-night salivary cortisol, values below the assay cut-off reliably exclude hypercortisolism, whereas consistently elevated levels are highly suggestive and warrant confirmatory testing (e.g., dexamethasone suppression test, 24-hr urinary free cortisol). Interpretation should always be integrated with the clinical context, other biochemical investigations, and, if indicated, imaging findings.

name: SMAD4 Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
description: SMAD4 immunohistochemistry (IHC) is used to assess the integrity of the TGF-\'e2 signaling pathway by evaluating SMAD4 protein expression within tumor cells. In normal tissues, SMAD4 demonstrates diffuse nuclear and cytoplasmic staining, reflecting its role as a central mediator of intracellular signal transduction. In neoplastic contexts, retained (intact) SMAD4 expression is indicated by preserved nuclear staining in tumor cells, comparable to adjacent non-neoplastic elements, which serve as an internal positive control. Loss of SMAD4 expression -defined as complete absence of nuclear staining in tumor cells with retained staining in surrounding stromal, inflammatory, or epithelial cells-is indicative of SMAD4 inactivation, commonly due to gene mutation or deletion. This finding is clinically relevant in several malignancies, particularly pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and colorectal carcinoma, where SMAD4 loss may be associated with more aggressive tumor biology, poorer prognosis, and potential implications for disease progression and therapeutic stratification. Partial or heterogeneous staining patterns should be interpreted with caution and in correlation with morphology and other molecular findings.

Keep the urine cold either on ice or refigerated. Stop time should be within 20 minutes of the start time the day before. E.g. if start time was 6:00 am Tuesday, stop time is between 5:50 am and 6:10 am during which time any urine passed must be collected. FOR SUBMITTING LABORATORIES /HOSPITALS If submitting an aliquot of the 24 hour urine, note the volume of 24 hour urine submited. description: FISH for Y-chromosome sequences (SRY GENE BY FISH) is a molecular cytogenetic test that detects the presence of Y-chromosome DNA in cells using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). In this technique, fluorescently labeled DNA probes designed to bind to specific Y-chromosome regions-commonly including the SRY gene or Y-centromeric sequences-are applied to patient cells (such as peripheral blood, amniotic fluid, or tissue samples). If Y-chromosome material is present, the probes hybridize to the target DNA and produce visible fluorescent signals under a fluorescence microscope. Clinically, this test is used to determine whether Y-chromosome material is present or absent, particularly in the evaluation of disorders of sex development (DSD), suspected Y-chromosome mosaicism, Turner syndrome with possible hidden Y material, and prenatal sex determination. Detection of Y-chromosome sequences can have important diagnostic and management implications, for example identifying patients at risk of gonadoblastoma when Y-chromosome material is present in individuals with gonadal dysgenesis or Turner syndrome. description: This test performs automated identification (ID) and antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) of a previously isolated Streptococcus species using either the bioM\'e9rieux VITEK\'ae 2 or BD Phoenix\'99 automated microbiology system, depending on laboratory workflow and organism requirements. A standardized bacterial suspension prepared from a pure culture is inoculated into the appropriate identification and AST cards/panels. The system identifies the organism to the species level where possible, determines minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs), and categorizes antimicrobial susceptibility as Susceptible (S), Susceptible, Increased Exposure (I), or Resistant (R) according to current CLSI or EUCAST interpretive criteria, as configured by the laboratory. name: Strongyloides Agar Plate Culture Method (APC)
synonyms: Strongyloides culture (agar method);Larval culture on agar;Stool agar culture for Strongyloides
description: Strongyloides agar plate culture is a high-sensitivity stool-based method for the detection of Strongyloides stercoralis larvae. A fresh stool specimen is inoculated onto a nutrient agar plate and incubated, allowing motile larvae to migrate across the surface. As they move, they carry enteric bacteria that proliferate along their path, producing characteristic serpiginous tracks that signal larval presence. Recovered larvae can then be microscopically examined for morphological confirmation of species. This method is considered the most sensitive stool technique for Strongyloides detection and is particularly useful in low parasite burden or intermittent shedding, where routine stool microscopy may be negative. A positive result confirms active infection. However, the test requires fresh samples, controlled incubation conditions, and technical expertise, and may not be routinely available in all laboratories. In clinical practice, it is often used alongside routine microscopy on stool and blood serology testing to improve overall diagnostic yield.

description: Strongyloides serology detects IgG antibodies to Strongyloides stercoralis using ELISA and serves as the preferred initial screening test, particularly in patients with suspected chronic infection or low parasite burden where stool microscopy is frequently negative. It has high sensitivity (˜85?95%) and is especially valuable in pre-immunosuppression screening (e.g., prior to corticosteroids, chemotherapy, or transplantation), where missing infection carries a risk of life-threatening hyperinfection. A positive result supports exposure or infection and should be interpreted in clinical context, with consideration for confirmatory stool testing (agar plate culture or tissue) where feasible. However, serology cannot distinguish active from past infection and may show cross-reactivity with other helminths. A negative result does not fully exclude infection, particularly in immunocompromised patients, and further evaluation should be pursued if clinical suspicion remains high. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

description: Blood succinylacetone testing demonstrates elevated succinylacetone, which is diagnostic for hereditary tyrosinemia type I due to fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency. The presence of succinylacetone in blood is highly specific and can be detected even in the newborn period, making it a reliable screening and confirmatory marker. This finding indicates a block in tyrosine catabolism, leading to accumulation of toxic metabolites that cause progressive liver, renal, and systemic complications. In the clinical setting, this result necessitates urgent initiation of targeted therapy with nitisinone and dietary restriction of tyrosine and phenylalanine, as early treatment dramatically improves prognosis and reduces the risk of liver failure or hepatocellular carcinoma. Correlation with urine succinylacetone, plasma amino acids, liver and renal function, and confirmatory molecular genetic testing is advised. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

Detection of this metabolite confirms a defect in the tyrosine catabolic pathway and supports the diagnosis of hereditary tyrosinemia type I. In the appropriate clinical context (hepatomegaly, coagulopathy, renal tubular dysfunction, or failure to thrive in infancy/childhood), this result warrants prompt initiation of disease-specific therapy (e.g., nitisinone) along with dietary management. Early treatment is critical to prevent progression to acute liver failure, renal impairment, or hepatocellular carcinoma. Correlation with plasma amino acid profile, liver function tests, renal function, and genetic confirmation is recommended. Family counseling and genetic testing may also\\~be\\~indicated. instructions: Serum. Plasma: Li?heparin, K2?EDTA and K3?EDTA plasma.
description: The Total Testosterone test measures the overall level of testosterone in the blood, including both the hormone bound to proteins and the small amount that circulates freely. Testosterone is a key sex hormone involved in the development of male reproductive tissues, muscle mass, bone density, and body hair, though it is also present in females in smaller amounts. This test helps evaluate symptoms such as infertility, low sex drive, erectile dysfunction, irregular menstrual cycles, or signs of hormonal imbalance. It is commonly used to assess conditions like hypogonadism, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), and certain adrenal or pituitary disorders. Low total testosterone levels can be a sign of hypogonadism, where the body doesn t produce enough testosterone. In men, this may lead to symptoms like fatigue, reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, loss of muscle mass, and mood changes. It can result from aging, pituitary gland disorders, testicular injury, or chronic illnesses. In women, low testosterone is less common but may contribute to low libido and fatigue. Conversely, high testosterone levels in men may be due to testosterone supplementation, anabolic steroid use, or certain tumors. In women, high levels are often linked to conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), leading to symptoms such as excessive hair growth, acne, and irregular periods.

description: Thiopurine Methyltransferase (TPMT) is a key enzyme in the metabolism of thiopurine drugs such as azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, and thioguanine. Variability in TPMT activity, due to inherited genetic polymorphisms, directly influences drug tolerance and risk of toxicity. Patients with reduced or absent TPMT activity are unable to adequately inactivate thiopurines, predisposing them to severe, potentially life-threatening myelosuppression if treated with standard doses. Assessment of TPMT enzyme activity before initiating thiopurine therapy provides important guidance for individualized dosing. Patients with normal or high activity can usually receive standard dosing, while those with intermediate activity require reduced doses and close monitoring. Individuals with very low or absent activity should generally avoid thiopurine therapy, or only receive minimal doses under specialist supervision. Regardless of TPMT status, regular clinical and hematological monitoring remains essential, as other factors-including NUDT15 variants, concomitant medications, and underlying bone marrow function-also affect drug safety and efficacy. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

Confirm the referral laboratory's current specimen and transport requirements before collection.
description: Thiopurine Methyltransferase (TPMT) genotyping identifies common inherited variants in the TPMT gene that reduce or abolish enzyme activity. The presence of heterozygous or homozygous variants correlates with intermediate or deficient TPMT enzyme activity, respectively, and directly impacts the metabolism of thiopurine drugs such as azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, and thioguanine. Patients with low or absent enzyme function are at high risk of severe, dose-related myelosuppression when treated with standard thiopurine doses. Genotyping provides predictive information on thiopurine tolerance prior to therapy and helps guide dose adjustment or alternative treatment choices. Patients with no variants (wild-type) are usually suitable for standard dosing, while heterozygous carriers require reduced doses with close monitoring. Homozygous variant patients are generally contraindicated for standard thiopurine therapy and may only be considered for significantly reduced dosing under specialist care. Unlike enzyme activity assays, genotyping is not affected by recent transfusions, cytopenias, or intercurrent illness. However, it only detects known polymorphisms and does not capture all possible genetic or non-genetic factors influencing TPMT activity. For optimal patient safety, TPMT genotyping should be interpreted alongside clinical context, blood count monitoring, and, where relevant, consideration of additional pharmacogenetic variants such as NUDT15. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Thrombin Time (TT)
description: A coagulation assay performed using the transmission turbidity method to assess the final stage of the coagulation cascade. The sample is mixed with an appropriate amount of thrombin, which converts fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin. The resulting change in absorbance is measured, and the time taken for fibrin formation is reported as the Thrombin Time. The test is used to evaluate fibrinogen function and detect abnormalities such as hypofibrinogenemia, dysfibrinogenemia, increased fibrin degradation products, or the presence of thrombin inhibitors including heparin and direct thrombin inhibitors.

Results should be interpreted alongside TSH levels, treatment history and anti-thyroglobulin antibody status, as these antibodies may interfere with measurement. Serum Tg levels are primarily used to monitor for residual, recurrent, or metastatic disease following total thyroidectomy and radioiodine ablation. However, its interpretation must always consider the presence of anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (TgAb), which can interfere with Tg measurement and lead to inaccurate results. Tg may also be detectable in benign thyroid conditions, such as multinodular goiter or thyroiditis, and is not useful as a diagnostic test for thyroid cancer in patients with an intact thyroid gland.

description: The Toxocariasis serology test detects antibodies against Toxocara canis or T. cati, parasites responsible for toxocariasis in humans. It is primarily used to support the diagnosis of visceral or ocular larva migrans, especially in patients presenting with unexplained eosinophilia, hepatomegaly, pulmonary symptoms, neurological manifestations, or ocular involvement. A positive result suggests exposure or infection, but cannot differentiate between past and current infection, as antibodies may persist for years. Negative results usually exclude infection, although false negatives can occur in early disease or immunocompromised individuals This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Toxoplasma Antibody Igg Avidity
description: The Toxoplasma Antibody IgG Avidity test is used to help determine the timing of infection with Toxoplasma gondii, particularly in pregnant women. While standard IgG and IgM tests can indicate exposure, IgG avidity testing measures the strength of the IgG antibody binding to the antigen, which increases over time. A low avidity result suggests a recent infection (typically within the last 3-5 months), while high avidity indicates a past infection. This distinction is critical in assessing the risk of congenital toxoplasmosis and guiding further clinical management.

name: Toxoplasma IgG
instructions: Serum collected using standard sampling tubes or tubes containing separating gel. Li?heparin, K2?EDTA and K3?EDTA plasma.
description: "The Toxo IgG Antibody Test detects Immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies specific to Toxoplasma gondii, the parasite responsible for toxoplasmosis. This infection is typically acquired through consumption of undercooked meat containing tissue cysts or food and water contaminated with oocysts from infected cats. In most healthy individuals, infection is mild or asymptomatic and followed by a lifelong latent phase. The presence of Toxo IgG antibodies indicates previous exposure to T. gondii and suggests either a latent or past infection, or occasionally an ongoing one. While harmless in most people, toxoplasmosis poses significant risks to immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS, cancer, or organ transplants, in whom reactivation can cause severe complications, particularly brain lesions. The test is especially important in the context of pregnancy, as a newly acquired infection can cross the placenta and affect the fetus. While many congenitally infected infants show no symptoms at birth, serious complications including chorioretinitis, intellectual disability, psychomotor delay, and hearing or vision loss can appear later in life. The likelihood of transmission increases with gestational age, but earlier infections pose a higher risk of severe outcomes.Toxo IgG testing is commonly used to assess immune status before or during pregnancy, to guide management in immunosuppressed patients, and in combination with Toxo IgM testing to distinguish between acute, recent, and past infections. A diagnosis of acute toxoplasmosis is typically confirmed by seroconversion or a significant rise in IgG and/or IgM levels in paired samples over time."

name: Toxoplasma IgM
instructions: Serum collected using standard sampling tubes or tubes containing separating gel. Li?heparin, K2?EDTA and K3?EDTA plasma.
description: "The Toxo IgM Antibody Test detects Immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies specific to Toxoplasma gondii, the protozoan parasite responsible for toxoplasmosis. This infection is commonly acquired through ingestion of undercooked meat containing tissue cysts or food and water contaminated with oocysts shed by infected cats.In healthy individuals, toxoplasmosis is usually mild or asymptomatic and results in a lifelong latent infection. However, reactivation can occur in immunocompromised individuals-such as organ transplant recipients or people living with HIV/AIDS-and may lead to serious complications like meningoencephalitis. The Toxo IgM test is especially important in pregnancy, as T. gondii can cross the placenta and infect the fetus. While most congenitally infected newborns are asymptomatic at birth, they may develop serious long-term effects such as chorioretinitis, neurological impairment, or hearing loss. The risk of transmission increases with gestational age, but infections early in pregnancy are more likely to cause severe damage. The presence of Toxoplasma-specific IgM antibodies typically indicates a recent, acute, or possibly reactivated infection. However, IgM can persist for months, and therefore results should be interpreted alongside IgG testing and clinical history. A diagnosis of primary acute infection during pregnancy is confirmed by seroconversion or a significant rise in both IgG and/or IgM titers in serial samples. Early detection and treatment during pregnancy are essential to reduce the risk or severity of congenital toxoplasmosis"

synonyms: Anti TSH Receptor Antibody; Thyrotropin receptor antibody (TRAb); Anti-TSHR;TRAb
instructions: Serum collected using standard sampling tubes or tubes containing separating gel. Li?heparin, K2?EDTA and K3?EDTA plasma.
description: Anti - TSHR / TRAb antibody testing is carried out in the investigation suspected auto-immune thyroid diseases. e.g. hyperthyroidism (Grave's disease) The TSH Receptor Antibody (TRAb) test is a specialized blood test used to detect the presence of autoantibodies that target the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptor. These antibodies are most commonly associated with Graves disease, an autoimmune condition that causes the thyroid gland to become overactive, resulting in hyperthyroidism. In this condition, the antibodies mimic the action of TSH, overstimulating the thyroid and leading to excessive production of thyroid hormones. The TRAb test is an important tool for confirming a diagnosis of Graves disease, especially in cases where clinical symptoms or imaging results are unclear. It is also used to monitor treatment response, assess the likelihood of disease relapse after therapy, and evaluate the risk of neonatal thyrotoxicosis in pregnant women with current or past Graves disease, as the antibodies can cross the placenta. While the test is highly specific for Graves disease, some patients may not have detectable antibody levels, particularly at early or late stages of the condition. Additionally, results may be influenced by recent treatments such as radioiodine therapy or by interfering substances in the blood. Overall, the TSH Receptor Antibody test provides valuable information in the diagnosis and management of autoimmune thyroid disorders and is most effective when interpreted alongside clinical findings and thyroid function tests.

It is a useful test when first-line thyroid antibodies tests in hyperthyroidism fail to confirm autoimmune etiology as it is more specific than TPOAb or TgAb. Patients who are candidates for anti-thyroid drug therapy may not respond to this treatment when TSI levels are markedly elevated. The determination of TSI can also assist in predicting hyperthyroidism in neonates due to placental transmission of the immunoglobulins from mothers with hyperthyroidism. description: This test detects both IgG and IgM antibodies to Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV) in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) to aid in the diagnosis of central nervous system (CNS) infections caused by VZV, such as encephalitis, meningitis, myelitis, or vasculopathy. Presence of IgM suggests a recent or active infection, while IgG, especially when found in higher levels than in serum or with evidence of intrathecal synthesis, supports ongoing or past infection with possible CNS involvement. description: The IDS VZV IgG test quantitatively detect IgG antibodies against Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) in serum or plasma, aiding in assessing immunity or past infection. VZV, also known as Human Herpes Virus-3 (HHV-3), is the cause of varicella (chickenpox) and can remain latent, later reactivating as herpes zoster (shingles), especially in the elderly or immunocompromised individuals. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets or direct skin contact, with symptoms including fever, malaise, and characteristic vesicular rashes. Complications can include bacterial infections, pneumonia, and CNS issues. IgG antibodies appear within days of symptom onset, persist for years, and rise sharply during reactivation, making this test useful for evaluating immunity, guiding vaccination decisions, and confirming infections when combined with IgM results. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

Detection of VZV IgG in CSF may indicate intrathecal antibody production, which supports the diagnosis of central nervous system (CNS) involvement, such as VZV encephalitis, meningitis, or vasculopathy. When interpreted alongside serum IgG levels and IgM findings, this test helps evaluate recent or past exposure and possible viral reactivation affecting the CNS.

description: The VZV IgM quantitatively detect IgM antibodies against Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) in serum or plasma, aiding in the diagnosis of recent or active infection. Transmission occurs mainly through respiratory droplets or direct contact, with symptoms such as fever, malaise, headache, abdominal pain, and a characteristic vesicular rash. name: Vet Blood Culture – Aerobic & Anaerobic
description: This test involves the aseptic collection of blood into a specialized aerobic culture bottle designed to support the growth of aerobic and facultative anaerobic microorganisms. The specimen is incubated in a continuous-monitoring automated blood culture system, such as the BACTEC blood culture system or BacT/ALERT system, which detects microbial growth based on metabolic activity. When growth is detected, a Gram stain is performed promptly, followed by organism identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) as clinically indicated. The standard incubation period is 5 days (120 hours), which is sufficient to detect the vast majority of clinically significant bloodstream pathogens, most of which flag positive within the first 24 72 hours. Positive results are reported immediately upon detection of growth to facilitate timely targeted therapy. If no growth is detected, the culture is finalized and reported as No growth after 5 days of incubation. Extended incubation (up to 7 14 days) may be undertaken in specific clinical scenarios such as suspected infections with fastidious organisms (e.g., HACEK group, Brucella) or certain fungal pathogens based on clinician request or laboratory protocol.

name: Voltage Gated Potassium Channel (VGKC) Antibodies - LGI1 and CASPR2
synonyms: LGI1 (leucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1) Antibodies CASPR2 (contactin-associated protein-like 2) Antibodies
instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Voltage Gated Potassium Channel (VGKC) Antibodies - LGI1 and CASPR2 and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: This assay, historically reported as the voltage-gated potassium channel (VGKC) antibodies test, primarily detects antibodies directed against proteins associated with the VGKC complex rather than the potassium channel itself, specifically LGI1 (leucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1) and CASPR2 (contactin-associated protein-like 2). These are now recognised as the true, clinically relevant antigens. Only the presence of LGI1 or CASPR2 antibodies is considered pathogenic and diagnostically meaningful; isolated, non-specific VGKC positivity in the absence of these antibodies is generally of limited clinical significance and must be interpreted in the context of the patients clinical phenotype. LGI1 antibodies are strongly associated with autoimmune limbic encephalitis, typically presenting with subacute memory impairment, confusion and seizuresparticularly faciobrachial dystonic seizuresand frequently accompanied by hyponatraemia, with characteristic medial temporal lobe changes on MRI. CASPR2 antibodies are linked to a broader clinical spectrum, including peripheral nerve hyperexcitability, Morvan syndrome, dysautonomia, neuropathic pain and, less commonly, limbic encephalitis, with a stronger association with thymoma and other malignancies. Both conditions are usually highly responsive to early immunotherapy, and detection should prompt neurological evaluation, targeted neuroimaging, CSF/EEG studies, appropriate malignancy screening (particularly in CASPR2-positive cases), and timely initiation of treatment. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.

name: Von Willebrand Factor Activity

instructions: Collect blood into a correctly filled light blue top tube maintaining the 9:1 blood-to-anticoagulant ratio. Mix gently by inversion and centrifuge promptly to obtain platelet-poor plasma. Avoid hemolyzed, clotted, or underfilled specimens. Transport refrigerated at 2-8?C; if testing is delayed beyond 4 hours, separate plasma and freeze at -20?C or lower.
description: This assay measures the functional activity of von Willebrand factor and evaluates its ability to mediate platelet adhesion through interaction with platelet glycoprotein Ib. It is a key investigation in patients with mucocutaneous bleeding, easy bruising, menorrhagia, epistaxis, or a suspected inherited or acquired von Willebrand disorder. Results should be interpreted together with the von Willebrand factor antigen level and, where indicated, ristocetin cofactor activity and factor VIII levels. name: Von Willebrand Factor Antigen
instructions: • Collect the sample when the patient is not acutely ill or post-surgery, as inflammation or stress may affect levels. · Use a light blue-top tube containing 3.2% sodium citrate (Na citrate) as anticoagulant. · Ensure the tube is filled to the correct volume (9 parts blood to 1 part anticoagulant). · Avoid prolonged tourniquet application (not more than 1 minute) or traumatic draws(do not probe or use small needles) to prevent falsely elevated levels. · Immediately and gently invert the tube 4-6 times to mix blood with anticoagulant.Do not shake vigorously. · Transport to the laboratory within 4 hours of collection.Keep sample at room temperature (18-24?C). description: This assay quantitatively measures circulating von Willebrand factor antigen and is used to assess the amount of VWF present in plasma. name: Water Microbiological Analysis (Total Coliforms/Total Viable Count)
instructions: To test water for Total Coliforms and Total Viable Count (TVC), collect the sample in a sterile, sealable bottle-preferably one containing sodium thiosulfate if the water is chlorinated. name: Y-Chromosome STR (Yfiler™ Plus) Paternal Lineage Analysis x1 Individual
synonyms: Yfiler™ Plus Y-STR Analysis; Y-STR Kinship Test; Paternal Lineage DNA Test; Male Lineage DNA Analysis; Male Kinship DNA Test.
instructions: DNA Paternity Testing Specimen - Buccal Swab (Cotton Swab) or dried blood spot on treated or untreated paper. Buccal Swab Specimen Collection Instructions 1. Prepare the Collection Kit: Ensure the kit contains sterile buccal swabs (minimum 2 per individual), labeled collection envelopes or tubes, gloves, and a consent form. 2. Label each envelope or tube clearly with the individual's full name, date of birth, and collection date. 3. Ensure Proper Identification: Verify and record the identity of each donor using a valid form of identification. 4. Complete the chain-of-custody form if required. 5. Pre-Collection Instructions: Do not eat, drink, smoke, chew gum, or brush teeth for at least 30 minutes prior to sample collection. Rinse the mouth with clean water and wait 10 minutes before swabbing. 6. Swab Collection Procedure: Wear gloves throughout the procedure. Using one sterile swab, firmly rub the inside of the cheek in a back-and-forth motion for 30-60 seconds to collect epithelial cells. Repeat with a second swab on the opposite cheek. Allow swabs to air dry for at least 15-20 minutes. Do not blow on or touch the swab head. 7. Packaging the Samples: Place the dried swabs into the labeled paper envelope or specimen tube (do not use plastic bags or airtight containers). 8. Ensure each sample is properly sealed and labeled. 9. Documentation: Complete and sign all required documentation, including consent and identification forms. Ensure accurate linkage of sample ID to the donor's identity. 10. Transport to Laboratory: Place all labeled envelopes, consent forms, and chain-of-custody documents in the collection kit or transport bag. Deliver to the laboratory under standard room temperature conditions. Avoid exposure to moisture or heat.
description: Y-Chromosome Short Tandem Repeat (Y-STR) analysis is a molecular genetic test used to evaluate biological relationships through the paternal lineage by analysing polymorphic short tandem repeat (STR) markers located on the male-specific Y chromosome. Using the Thermo Fisher Scientific Yfiler\'99 Plus PCR Amplification Kit, the assay amplifies 27 Y-STR loci following DNA extraction, with subsequent capillary electrophoresis, allele calling, Y-haplotype generation and statistical kinship analysis. Buccal (oral) swabs are the preferred specimen, although EDTA whole blood is also suitable. The expected turnaround time is *3 working days* from receipt of an adequate specimen. The test is primarily indicated for paternal lineage verification, including father-son, paternal grandfather-grandson, brother-to-brother and paternal uncle-nephew relationship testing, as well as forensic human identification, missing persons investigations, disaster victim identification and complex kinship cases where the alleged father is unavailable or deceased. Matching Y-STR haplotypes are consistent with a shared paternal lineage but do not independently establish a specific biological relationship, since males from the same paternal family generally share identical or highly similar Y-chromosome profiles. Conversely, non-matching haplotypes effectively exclude a shared recent paternal lineage, except in the rare event of a Y-STR mutation. As this assay evaluates only the paternal lineage, it cannot distinguish between closely related males within the same paternal family or assess maternal relationships. It should not replace autosomal STR analysis for routine paternity testing when the alleged father is available. Reports include specimen details, the Y-STR haplotype, comparison of tested individuals, an interpretation of whether the findings are consistent with or exclude a shared paternal lineage, and an interpretive comment outlining the limitations of Y-STR analysis together with recommendations for complementary autosomal STR testing where appropriate.

description: Yellow Fever Serology detects antibodies (IgG) against the Yellow fever virus in serum, using ELISA immunoassay method. The presence of IgG antibodies reflect past exposure or immunity due to prior infection or vaccination. Interpretation should consider potential cross-reactivity with other flaviviruses such as dengue. Clinically, this test helps assess immunity status against Yellow Fever virus and supports the diagnosis of past infection in appropriate epidemiological and clinical contexts. Results should be correlated with vaccination history, travel exposure, and clinical presentation. For diagnosis of active infection, confirmatory testing with PCR should be considered where necessary. instructions: Collect the laboratory-approved specimen for Zinc Transporter 8 Antibodies (ZNT8) and label it with patient identity and collection time. Send any relevant clinical information needed to interpret this test. Confirm the current referral-laboratory requirement if this test is sent out.
description: The Zinc Transporter 8 (ZNT8) antibody test is used to support the diagnosis of autoimmune Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM). ZNT8 is a \'df-cell-specific protein, and the presence of autoantibodies against it indicates immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic \'df-cells. The test is especially useful in distinguishing T1DM from Type 2 or monogenic diabetes in cases with atypical features or adult-onset diabetes. It is typically used in conjunction with other autoimmune markers such as GAD65, IA-2, and insulin autoantibodies to increase diagnostic sensitivity. A positive ZNT8 result supports a diagnosis of autoimmune T1DM and may also help assess the risk of disease development in first-degree relatives of T1DM patients. However, a negative result does not exclude the diagnosis, especially in long-standing cases where antibody levels may have declined. The test is performed on serum samples, and results should always be interpreted in the clinical context. This test is referred to a partner reference laboratory when it is not available in-house at DKL.
